# Research report — NCD IPOs open in India on 8 December 2025
Executive summary
- This report analyzes the Non‑Convertible Debenture (NCD) public offers that evidence shows were open for subscription on 8 December 2025: Edelweiss Financial Services Ltd., Muthoot Mercantile Ltd., and KLM Axiva Finvest Ltd. Each issuer/issue is profiled against the research brief items where evidence is available. Major evidence gaps (notably issuer audited financial statements and many balance‑sheet and cash‑flow line items required for leverage/solvency metrics) are identified and listed; results and recommendations are provided with explicit caveats where those gaps limit any credit or allocation decision. Evidence sources are listed at the end; all factual statements are cited to those sources.

Methodology and assumptions
- Scope: Only facts and figures contained in the supplied research findings were used. No external facts, rates or issuer financials were added. Where the brief requested calculations that require missing inputs (for example debt/equity), the report states the gap rather than guessing.
- Tax assumptions (as requested in the brief): Post‑tax yield calculations below use the representative marginal tax rates specified in the brief: 30%, 20% and 10% for a "generic investor." For the "senior‑citizen" scenario, a provisional marginal tax rate of 20% is used for the comparative table below (the brief invited confirmation; this provisional assumption is used so the report can present direct generic vs senior comparisons — the senior‑citizen marginal rate can be changed on request and results recomputed). Where post‑tax arithmetic is performed it is: post‑tax yield = gross yield × (1 − marginal tax rate). All such computations are shown exactly and cite the gross (pre‑tax) yield source.
- Automatic leverage flag rule: per brief, a default flag is triggered if total debt / total equity > 2.0 (or >50% above industry median). Application of the flag requires issuer total debt and total equity; when those items are not present in the evidence the flag cannot be computed and is reported as Not Available (see Evidence gaps).

Issues open on 8 December 2025 — short overview
- Edelweiss Financial Services Ltd. — NCD public offer open 5–11 December 2025 (there is a conflicting close date in other sources; see conflicts below). Coupon range 8.85%–10.10% p.a.; effective yield 10.10% reported; tenors 24, 36, 60 and 120 months; face value ₹1,000; minimum lot 10 NCDs (₹10,000); base issue ₹125 crore, green‑shoe up to ₹125 crore (total up to ₹250 crore). Listed/available on BSE (and some series shown on NSE approvals). Rated A+ (Stable) by CRISIL in multiple sources; one corporate filing in the evidence indicates a CRISIL AA+ (Stable) reference — see conflict note. [1], [2], [3], [11], [16]
- Muthoot Mercantile Ltd. — NCD public offer open 4–17 December 2025. Secured, redeemable NCDs; coupon examples up to 10.75% p.a., effective yields reported 9.71%–11.73% depending on series; tenors include 400 days, 24, 36, 60 and 75 months; face value ₹1,000; base issue size ₹75 crore (green‑shoe up to ₹75 crore). Minimum lot 10 NCDs (₹10,000). Rated BBB (Stable) by India Ratings (IND BBB Stable / IND BBB). [8], [9], [10], [13]
- KLM Axiva Finvest Ltd. — NCD public offer open 1–12 December 2025 (active on 8 December). Base issue ₹50 crore (total up to ₹100 crore). Coupon rates range ~9.50%–11.10% per series; effective yields per series in the 9.92%–11.30% range depending on series; face value ₹1,000; minimum lot 5 NCDs (₹5,000). Rated BBB (Stable) by Acuité. [5], [6], [7]

Detailed issuer-by-issuer analysis

1) Edelweiss Financial Services Ltd. (issue open 5–11 Dec 2025)
1.1 Issuer & offer identifiers and prospectus/offer terms (evidence)
- Offer opened 5 December 2025 (subscription data point shows open on 8 Dec), listed on BSE; base issue size ₹125 crore with green‑shoe up to ₹125 crore (total up to ₹250 crore); face value ₹1,000; tenors 24, 36, 60 and 120 months; coupons 8.85%–10.10% p.a.; effective yield reported 10.10%; minimum lot 10 NCDs (₹10,000). [1], [2], [3], [11]

1.2 Current credit rating(s) and links to rating rationale
- CRISIL A+ (Stable) is reported for the issue in several public listings and investor pages. [1], [2], [3]
- Conflicting evidence: a separate filing referencing NSE listing/approvals notes CRISIL AA+ (Stable) reaffirmed on 17 November 2025 for a specified Edelweiss NCD series; this conflicts with other sources that report A+ Stable for the December 2025 retail NCD offer. The evidence does not resolve whether the AA+ reference relates to a different series/issue or is an alternative rating for a different instrument. [4] — conflict noted; see Evidence‑gaps and conflicts section.

1.3 Coupon, YTM and post‑tax yields (exact figures and worked calculations)
- Gross (reported effective) yield used for calculations: 10.10% p.a. (effective yield reported). [3]
- Post‑tax yields computed as gross × (1 − tax rate). Using generic investor marginal rates 30%, 20%, 10% and senior provisional rate 20%:

  - Gross yield = 10.10% (0.1010)
  - Post‑tax @ 30% = 0.1010 × (1 − 0.30) = 0.07070 = 7.07% p.a. [3]
  - Post‑tax @ 20% = 0.1010 × (1 − 0.20) = 0.08080 = 8.08% p.a. [3]
  - Post‑tax @ 10% = 0.1010 × (1 − 0.10) = 0.09090 = 9.09% p.a. [3]
  - Senior‑citizen (provisional) @ 20% = 8.08% p.a. (same arithmetic as 20% marginal). [3]

Notes: coupon schedule (periodic vs cumulative) varies by series but the evidence provides the reported effective yield above; YTM calculations at investor‑level would require series‑specific cashflow timing and price (issue price is ₹1,000 face), which the evidence provides partly (face value), but market price and exact payment schedule per series are not fully recorded in the evidence for a full YTM curve by series. The effective yield figure cited is used as the representative gross yield. [1], [3]

1.4 Issuer financials & specific metrics (evidence and calculations)
- Evidence includes high‑level corporate facts (founded Nov 1995, 27 subsidiaries as of 30 June 2025; 254 domestic offices and 3 international offices) but does not supply audited balance‑sheet line items required by the brief (total debt, total equity, EBITDA, interest expense, operating cash flow, free cash flow, current ratio, maturity profile, liquidity headroom). Therefore none of the precise financial ratios requested (debt/equity, debt/EBITDA, interest coverage, etc.) can be computed from the evidence. [1]

1.5 Automatic leverage/solvency flag
- Cannot be computed: total debt and total equity are not present in the evidence. Therefore automatic flag (debt/equity > 2.0) is Not Available (data gap). [Evidence gaps]

1.6 Relative value & competitive positioning (vs peer NCDs, corporate bonds, bank FDs)
- Relative position among contemporaneous retail NCD offers: Edelweiss carries a higher reported rating (A+ Stable in several sources) than the BBB‑rated NBFC offers below while offering an effective yield of ~10.10% — i.e., a comparatively higher rating for roughly the same yield bucket offered by lower‑rated NBFCs in the same primary window. This makes the Edelweiss offer comparatively attractive on a rating‑for‑yield basis within the documented sample. [1], [3], [6], [8]
- Specific spread vs bank FDs, corporate bond curves, or swaps is not computable from the evidence because benchmark FD rates, swap curves or contemporaneous corporate bond yields are not included in the supplied material. (See Evidence gaps.) [Evidence gaps]

1.7 Historical precedents / pattern recognition
- Subscription data shows strong retail demand for the Edelweiss offer (subscribed 3.30x at closure in one report). Retail appetite was higher than institutional uptake in this offer. This pattern aligns with the contemporaneous window where retail appetite picked higher yield NCDs; see Comparative Subscription section. [11]

1.8 Risk assessment (scenarios & tail risks)
- Principal risk indicators available in the evidence: credit rating A+ (Stable) reported — positive indicator versus BBB peers. The evidence contains no issuer solvency metrics (debt maturity profile, interest coverage, liquidity headroom) that would allow quantification of runway under stress, downgrade/default probability, or vulnerability to an interest‑rate shock. Therefore scenario quantification is Not Available. Qualitative risk points supported by the evidence:
  - Rating sensitivity: A downgrade from A+ to lower categories (not quantified in the evidence) would increase required yields for new issuance and secondary trading spreads; absence of leverage metrics prevents estimating magnitude. [1]
  - Retail concentration: retail heavy subscription suggests retail investor reliance; retail‑dominated demand may affect future primary pricing if retail appetite shifts. [11]
- Conclusion: Cannot quantify tail‑risk numerically due to missing issuer balance sheet and cash‑flow data. [Evidence gaps]

1.9 Regulatory & policy implications
- No SEBI/RBI circulars or specific regulatory actions linked to the Edelweiss issue are present in the provided evidence. [Evidence gaps]

1.10 Forward indicators (yield curve / primary pipeline / flows)
- No swap curve, government‑yield curve, bank FD rates nor foreign flow data in the evidence; cannot compute forward credit spread directionality or primary subscription risk beyond contemporaneous subscription rate (3.30x at close). [Evidence gaps], [11]

1.11 Investment thesis & recommendation (evidence‑backed)
- Evidence points: higher reported rating among the Dec 2025 retail NCD sample and a representative effective yield ~10.10% with strong retail subscription. However, audited issuer balance‑sheet metrics required for full credit diligence are missing.
- Recommendation (evidence‑backed, with caveats): Conditional Hold / Buy for investors who accept retail‑market liquidity and rely on external ratings — the A+ rating plus 10.10% effective yield makes it comparatively attractive versus BBB‑rated peers in this sample. Institutions or investors needing full balance‑sheet diligence should require audited financials (missing in the evidence) before a buy decision. Confidence level: Moderate (limited by evidence gaps). [1], [3], [11]

------------------------------------------------------------

2) Muthoot Mercantile Ltd. (issue open 4–17 Dec 2025)
2.1 Issuer & offer identifiers and prospectus/offer terms (evidence)
- NCDs are secured, redeemable and listed on BSE; base issue size ₹75 crore (green‑shoe up to ₹75 crore); face value ₹1,000; tenors include 400 days, 24, 36, 60 and 75 months; coupon examples up to 10.75% p.a.; effective yields reported in range 9.71%–11.73% depending on series; minimum investment 10 NCDs (₹10,000). Issue subscribed 2.35x at closure in one report. [8], [9], [10], [13]

2.2 Current credit ratings and links
- Rated BBB (Stable) by India Ratings & Research (IND BBB Stable). The evidence does not show CRISIL or ICRA treatment for this specific December 2025 issue. [8], [9], [10]

2.3 Coupon, YTM and post‑tax yields (exact figures and worked calculations)
- Use the highest reported effective yield for downside comparison: 11.73% p.a. (reported maximum effective yield). [9]
- Post‑tax calculations:

  - Gross yield = 11.73% (0.1173)
  - Post‑tax @ 30% = 0.1173 × (1 − 0.30) = 0.08211 = 8.21% p.a.
  - Post‑tax @ 20% = 0.1173 × (1 − 0.20) = 0.09384 = 9.38% p.a.
  - Post‑tax @ 10% = 0.1173 × (1 − 0.10) = 0.10557 = 10.56% p.a.
  - Senior‑citizen (provisional) @ 20% = 9.38% p.a. [9]

Notes: The evidence lists series‑level coupons (e.g., coupon 10.75% p.a. for a particular series) and effective yields. Use effective yields where available as representative gross yields. [8], [9]

2.4 Issuer financials & specific metrics
- Evidence includes the scale of the gold‑loan portfolio as of 30 Sep 2025: principal amount Rs 1,064.36 crore (this represents the gold‑loan portfolio principal; the evidence does not provide full balance sheet line items such as total debt, total equity, EBITDA, interest expense, current ratio, operating cash flow, free cash flow, or overall maturity profile). Therefore requested ratios (debt/equity, debt/EBITDA, interest coverage, liquidity headroom) cannot be computed from the evidence. [13]

2.5 Automatic leverage/solvency flag
- Not computable: total debt and total equity are not provided; therefore automatic leverage flag cannot be evaluated. [Evidence gaps]

2.6 Relative value & competitive positioning
- Muthoot Mercantile offers yields in the ~9.71%–11.73% band for secured NCDs while carrying a BBB (Stable) rating — higher yields than the A+‑rated Edelweiss issue but lower credit rating. The Muthoot issue appears to be competing on yield to attract retail investors (subscription 2.35x), which is consistent with retail demand for higher coupon NBFC NCDs in the period. [8], [9], [11], [13]

2.7 Historical precedents / pattern recognition
- The December 2025 NCD was Muthoot Mercantile’s 7th debt offering since Dec 2020 (evidence supports repeated debt issuance by the issuer), which provides precedent for repeated access to debt markets, but the evidence does not include performance (defaults, downgrades) of those prior issues. High retail subscription in this tranche (2.35x) indicates consistent retail investor interest. [13]

2.8 Risk assessment (scenarios & tail risks)
- Evidence constraints prevent quantified stress testing. Qualitative points from evidence:
  - The issue is secured — a mitigating factor vs unsecured paper (evidence: “secured, redeemable NCDs” noted). [8], [9]
  - The issuer’s predominant business appears to be gold‑loans (portfolio reported), which implies business concentration; evidence of portfolio size is provided but not portfolio performance metrics (NPLs, yields, provisioning). This concentration is a single‑business risk not quantifiable from current evidence. [13]
- Quantification of downgrade/default scenarios, interest coverage, or runway under liquidity shock is Not Available due to missing financials. [Evidence gaps]

2.9 Regulatory & policy implications
- No SEBI/RBI circulars or specific regulatory actions relating to Muthoot Mercantile’s NCDs are present in the provided evidence. [Evidence gaps]

2.10 Forward indicators
- Subscription was 2.35x at close — indicates retail demand. No swap/sovereign curve or FD rate data is available for calculating spread movement. [13], [11]

2.11 Investment thesis & recommendation
- Evidence summary: secured structure and a track record of multiple debt raises are positive; BBB (Stable) rating and higher yields (up to 11.73% effective) compensate for lower credit rating relative to A+ peers. Missing financials prevent rigorous solvency assessment.
- Recommendation (evidence‑backed): Conditional Hold / Selective Buy for yield‑seeking investors who accept BBB‑rated NBFC credit risk and who value secured status; retirement investors seeking capital preservation should treat this as higher credit risk than A+ paper and limit allocation accordingly (see Monitoring Triggers). Confidence level: Low‑to‑Moderate (due to missing balance‑sheet and cash‑flow metrics). [8], [9], [13]

------------------------------------------------------------

3) KLM Axiva Finvest Ltd. (issue open 1–12 Dec 2025)
3.1 Issuer & offer identifiers and prospectus/offer terms (evidence)
- Offer opened 1 December 2025 and closed 12 December 2025 (thus open on 8 Dec). Base issue ₹50 crore, total up to ₹100 crore; coupons across series range ~9.50%–11.10% p.a.; effective yields reported per series 9.92%–11.30%; face value ₹1,000; minimum lot 5 NCDs (₹5,000). Rated BBB (Stable) by Acuité. [5], [6], [7]

3.2 Current credit ratings and link
- Rated BBB (Stable) by Acuité Ratings & Research for the December 2025 NCD issue. (No CRISIL or ICRA rating for this specific December 2025 offer is present in the evidence.) [5], [6], [7]

3.3 Coupon, YTM and post‑tax yields (exact figures and worked calculations)
- Representative gross yield (use highest reported effective yield series for conservative comparison): 11.30% p.a. (Series 8 effective yield, reported). [6]
- Post‑tax calculations:

  - Gross yield = 11.30% (0.1130)
  - Post‑tax @ 30% = 0.1130 × (1 − 0.30) = 0.07910 = 7.91% p.a.
  - Post‑tax @ 20% = 0.1130 × (1 − 0.20) = 0.09040 = 9.04% p.a.
  - Post‑tax @ 10% = 0.1130 × (1 − 0.10) = 0.10170 = 10.17% p.a.
  - Senior‑citizen (provisional) @ 20% = 9.04% p.a. [6]

3.4 Issuer financials & specific metrics
- The supplied evidence for KLM Axiva Finvest does not include audited financial statements or balance‑sheet line items required to compute total debt, total equity, debt/equity, debt/EBITDA, interest coverage, current ratio, operating cash flow, free cash flow, maturity profile, or liquidity headroom. [Evidence gaps]

3.5 Automatic leverage/solvency flag
- Not computable: missing total debt and total equity data. [Evidence gaps]

3.6 Relative value & competitive positioning
- KLM yields (up to 11.30% effective) place the issuer at the higher end of the yield band among the Dec 2025 NCD offers; rating BBB (Stable) is lower than Edelweiss’s reported A+ and similar to Muthoot’s BBB, implying higher yield for lower rating. Minimum lot size (5 NCDs / ₹5,000) and subscription multiples (3.15x total subscription reported) indicate retail accessibility and demand in primary. These facts position KLM as a higher‑yield, lower‑rated, retail‑friendly NBFC paper in this window. [5], [6], [7], [11]

3.7 Historical precedents / pattern recognition
- The subscription multiple reported for KLM (3.15x total; retail 3.24x etc.) indicates strong retail demand for this type of NBFC paper in the period. The evidence does not provide prior default history or track record beyond this subscription performance. [6], [11]

3.8 Risk assessment (scenarios & tail risks)
- Missing issuer financials preclude quantified stress scenarios. Qualitative risks drawn from the evidence:
  - BBB (Stable) rating implies non‑investment‑grade/standalone credit sensitivity relative to higher‑rated peers; yields compensate for this. [5], [6]
  - The NCD structure (security status not clearly specified in the evidence for all series) must be confirmed before relying on recovery assumptions. [5], [6]
- No quantitative runway under stress can be calculated from the provided facts. [Evidence gaps]

3.9 Regulatory & policy implications
- No regulatory circulars or sector‑specific policy actions in the provided evidence for KLM Axiva Finvest. [Evidence gaps]

3.10 Forward indicators
- Subscription 3.15x at close signals retail demand. No yield‑curve, swap or FD rate data to compute spread movement. [6], [11]

3.11 Investment thesis & recommendation
- Evidence summary: KLM provides higher yields (up to 11.30% effective) than the A+‑rated Edelweiss offering but carries a BBB (Stable) rating. Retail demand strong. Missing financials prevent a full credit assessment.
- Recommendation (evidence‑backed): Selective Buy for investors targeting higher income who accept BBB‑rated NBFC credit risk and short/mid tenor exposure; retirees seeking capital preservation should treat this as higher credit risk than A+ paper. Require audited financials and security/covenant details before increasing position size. Confidence level: Low‑to‑Moderate (limited by evidence gaps). [5], [6], [11]

------------------------------------------------------------
Cross‑issue synthesis, comparative observations and portfolio implications

A. Comparative yield vs reported rating (synthesis)
- Among the Dec 2025 retail NCD sample open on 8 Dec:
  - Edelweiss: reported effective yield ~10.10% with reported CRISIL A+ (Stable) in several sources (conflict noted elsewhere). [1], [3]
  - Muthoot Mercantile: effective yields up to 11.73% with India Ratings BBB (Stable). [8], [9]
  - KLM Axiva: effective yields up to 11.30% with Acuité BBB (Stable). [5], [6]
- Synthesis: lower‑rated NBFCs (BBB) offered higher effective yields (~11–11.7%) than the higher‑rated Edelweiss offer (~10.10%) — consistent with conventional credit‑spread compensation for lower rating, as visible in the primary window evidence. [1], [3], [5], [6], [8], [9]

B. Subscription / demand patterns
- All three issues documented strong retail subscription: Edelweiss reported 3.30x (at closure), KLM reported 3.15x total, Muthoot 2.35x. Retail appetite was a material driver of primary demand in this issuance window. [11], [6], [13]

C. Security / covenant differences (high‑level)

- Edelweiss: sources describe secured, subordinated Tier II style instruments for certain series in exchange filings (but also A+ rating references) — the instrument/subordination/SEC specifics vary by series and some files note Tier II classification; precise covenant language for the retail offer is not fully present in the evidence. [1], [4]
- KLM: security status is not explicitly detailed in the available evidence for each series. [5], [6]

- Evidence shows repeated issuance by some issuers (Muthoot Mercantile’s multiple debt offerings since Dec 2020) and frequent strong retail subscription across offerings — a pattern of retail appetite for higher coupon NBFC NCDs in this period. # New Zealand structural steel fabrication market: 2018–2024
Executive summary  
The New Zealand structural-steel fabrication sector is a small, capacity-constrained subsector within fabricated metal product manufacturing. Industry-sourced trade association reports (Steel Construction New Zealand, SCNZ) show recent annual structural-steel fabrication output of roughly 100,000 tonnes and industry capacity estimates that rose from ~120,000 tpa (Dec 2021 / Mar 2023) to 150,000 tpa (Sep 2023) with spare capacity reported at 31% (Dec 2021) and 41% (Sep 2023) — these statements are internally inconsistent and attributed to different SCNZ publications (see Section 1) [1][11]. Official national statistics are reported at broader ANZSIC levels (fabricated metal products C222/C2221) and provide employment counts that differ substantially depending on whether the broader structural-metal grouping (C222) or the narrow structural-steel fabricating class (C2221) is used; the broader class shows ~15,100–15,500 employees in 2023–2024 while class‑level estimates for structural‑steel fabricating show ~4,524 (2018) and an industry association figure of ~5,000 employees (Dec 2021) [1][13]. Tariff policy is mixed: the New Zealand tariff framework uses the Harmonised System and some steel goods attract 5–10% duties, but the specific tariff rates by HS subheading (7207–7216) are not provided in the available evidence [23][11]. Project demand evidence is strongest for the City Rail Link (CRL), for which ~25,000 tonnes of locally produced reinforcing steel have been identified; comparable published tonne estimates are not available in the evidence for other large NZ infrastructure projects cited in the brief [13][11].

Recommended immediate data‑collection priorities (one page): see final section.

------------------------------------------------------------
## 1. Market size and growth (2018–2024): revenue, employment, tonnage
Summary statement (data coverage and method): Primary official sources at the detailed class level (ANZSIC C2221 Structural Steel Fabricating) are not provided in the evidence for an annual 2018–2024 time series of revenue, FTE employment and tonnage. The available evidence combines (a) industry association supply‑side measures for structural steel tonnage/capacity/output (SCNZ), (b) a secondary market-size estimate for the wider fabricated metal product manufacturing market (IBISWorld), and (c) employment counts reported for both the broad structural-metal product group (ANZSIC C222) and narrower structural-steel fabricating (C2221) from studies/reports. The table below consolidates what is directly reported, and then (separately) presents a secondary-data based estimated revenue series for the broader fabricated metal product manufacturing market where IBISWorld figures exist (labelled clearly as secondary-source estimates and not structural-steel‑only).

Table A — Directly reported primary/industry datapoints (only facts stated in the evidence)
- Table columns limited to 5 as required.

| Year | Total industry revenue (NZD) — structural steel (reported) | Total employment — structural steel (reported) | Total tonnage fabricated — structural steel (reported) | Source (publication date) |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| 2018 | Not reported for structural‑steel revenue in evidence | Structural steel fabricating employed 4,524 (2018) | Not reported | Sustainablesteel report (21 Dec 2021) [12] |
| 2021 | Not reported | Industry association estimated structural steel industry employs ~5,000 | Annual output of structural steel in past 12 months ≈ 100,000 t | SCNZ Infrastructure Update Dec 2021 (Dec 2021) [1] |
| 2023 | Not reported | Not reported at class‑level in SCNZ Mar 2023 (but SCNZ reports 153 companies) | Annual output of structural steel in past 12 months ≈ 100,000 t; capacity estimated 120,000 tpa (Mar 2023) | SCNZ Mar 2023 (Mar 2023) [1] |
| Sep 2023 | Not reported | Not reported | Annual output ≈ 100,000 t; current annual capacity estimated 150,000 tpa; spare capacity 41% | SCNZ Sep 2023 (Sep 2023) [1] |
| 2024 | Not reported | Structural metal product manufacturing (ANZSIC C222) employed 15,100 (2024) — broader industry, not C2221 | Not reported | Figure.nz / Business Demography dataset (dataset meta, release noted) [13] |

Notes and source mapping:
- Structural-steel specific tonnage and capacity figures are from Steel Construction New Zealand (SCNZ) industry updates: Dec 2021, Mar 2023 and Sep 2023 — the reports state output ≈100,000 t and give two different capacity estimates (120,000 tpa and 150,000 tpa) [1].
- Employment figures for the narrowly defined structural‑steel fabricating class (ANZSIC C2221) are available in a 2018 sector study (4,524 employees) and an SCNZ association statement (~5,000 employees, Dec 2021) [12][1].
- The broader structural metal product manufacturing grouping (ANZSIC C222) shows larger employment counts (15,100 in 2024; 15,500 in 2023) as reported in the Business Demography dataset compiled by figure.nz (dataset meta in findings) — this is a broader industry classification that includes more activities than structural-steel fabricating [13].

Table B — Secondary-source estimated revenue series for the broader Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing (ANZSIC C222) (IBISWorld-based; labelled secondary)
Method and assumptions: IBISWorld reported a market size of NZ$1.5 billion in 2024 for fabricated metal product manufacturing and stated the sector declined at a -7.4% CAGR between 2019 and 2024. The series below applies that CAGR backward from the 2024 value to produce an illustrative 2019–2024 revenue series for the broader ANZSIC C222 market; this is a secondary-source estimate and is not a structural‑steel‑only figure. (2018 is outside IBISWorld CAGR span and thus not estimated here without additional evidence.)

| Year | Estimated revenue (NZD, ANZSIC C222) — secondary (IBISWorld) |
|---:|---:|
| 2019 (estimated) | NZ$2,203,000,000 [derived from IBISWorld 2024 value and CAGR] [23] |
| 2020 (estimated) | NZ$2,039,000,000 [23] |
| 2021 (estimated) | NZ$1,888,000,000 [23] |
| 2022 (estimated) | NZ$1,748,000,000 [23] |
| 2023 (estimated) | NZ$1,618,000,000 [23] |
| 2024 (IBISWorld reported) | NZ$1,500,000,000 [23] |

Uncertainty and caveats:
- The IBISWorld figures are for the broader fabricated metal product manufacturing market (ANZSIC C222), not structural steel only. Using these figures to represent structural steel revenue would overstate the narrow structural‑steel fabricating segment unless a validated allocation factor is available; no such allocation factor is present in the supplied evidence.
- SCNZ tonnage figures provide the best direct measure of structural-steel output (≈100,000 t in recent 12‑month windows), but no year‑by‑year public official statistics for 2018–2024 structural-steel tonnage are presented in the available evidence.
- The SCNZ capacity estimates conflict between reports (120,000 tpa vs 150,000 tpa); both figures are reported in evidence and must be presented as conflicting primary industry statements [1].

Primary-source vs secondary-source labelling:
- Primary / industry sources: SCNZ reports (Dec 2021, Mar 2023, Sep 2023) — structural steel tonnage/capacity/employment statements [1]. Sustainablesteel sector study (Dec 2021) — 2018 employment for C2221 [12].
- Secondary: IBISWorld market-size and CAGR for fabricated metal product manufacturing (used for revenue series estimates) [23]. figure.nz compilation of business demography (ANZSIC C222 employment numbers) is treated as secondary evidence in the findings [13].

Evidence gaps (short):
- No authoritative year-by-year (2018–2024) structural‑steel‑fabrication revenue series from Stats NZ or MBIE in the provided evidence.
- No official annual tonnage series for 2018–2024; only point estimates (~100,000 t) were available in industry reports for recent 12‑month periods.
- No complete FTE series for C2221 2018–2024 in the evidence; only 2018 and association snapshots exist.

------------------------------------------------------------
## 2. Top‑5 structural-steel fabricators (2023 ranking) — data, ownership, and source notes
Evidence availability and approach: The provided evidence does not include a comprehensive, audited ranked list of NZ structural-steel fabricators by 2023 revenue or 2023 tonnage capacity. The dataset contains company-level financials for selected firms that participate in steel manufacture/distribution or have disclosed structural‑steel activities. The table below compiles the five firms for which the evidence includes revenue/tonnage or output-relevant disclosures; ranking is by reported 2023 revenue when available, otherwise by available tonnage/volume or other disclosed metric. Each datum cites the original evidence. Where values are not specified in the evidence the cell states "not reported" and the data gap is described.

Table C — Top‑5 (evidence‑based, ranked by 2023 revenue where available)

| Rank | Company (structural scope) | Ultimate ownership / status | 2023 revenue or tonnage (reported) | Headcount (if available) | Sources (report & pub date) |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | Steel & Tube Holdings Ltd (steel distribution & downstream fabrication activities) | Listed company (NZX) — public | FY2023 revenue NZ$589.1 million | Not reported in evidence (company-level headcount not given) | Steel & Tube FY2023 results release (year ended 30 Jun 2023) — published FY2023 results page (date in filing) [23] |
| 2 | Fletcher Building (produces structural steel for projects; includes downstream fabrication for some scopes) | Listed company (Fletcher Building) | Group FY2023 revenue NZ$8,469 million (group; not structural-steel-only) — note: 4,000 tonnes of structural steel produced for Winstone Wallboards in FY2023 | Fletcher Building employed >14,970 people (30 Jun 2023) — group level | Fletcher Building FY2023 Annual Report (FY2023) [23] |
| 3 | New Zealand Steel / BlueScope New Zealand (steel producer supplying reinforcing and other products) | Owned by BlueScope / New Zealand Steel Limited (BlueScope group) | New Zealand Steel estimated revenue (secondary source) NZ$209.9 million (growjo estimate) — FY not specified in evidence; production ~650,000 tpa (steelmaking) | New Zealand Steel employs ~523 (growjo estimate) — secondary | BlueScope FY2023 investor materials and New Zealand Steel news (BlueScope FY presentation, investor report; NZ Steel news on CRL) — BlueScope FY2023 investor presentation & FY report (2023); NZ Steel news (date in posting) [13][11] |
| 4 | Pacific Steel (local manufacturer of reinforcing bar, wire rod and coil; supplied CRL rebar) | Private NZ manufacturer (founded 1963) | Reported/quoted annual revenue NZ$62.5 million (secondary estimate) | Employs between 101–200 people (secondary estimate in evidence) | Prospeo company profile / Pacific Steel news: Pacific Steel CRL rebar announcement (NZ Steel / Pacific Steel news) [23][11] |
| 5 | Culham Engineering Company Limited (regional fabricator) | Private; Culham Holdings (Whangarei) Limited holds 100% of shares | Revenue/tonnage not reported in evidence | Not reported (directors listed) | Company registration data (companyhub.nz/companyDetails) — company registration info (registered 18 May 1962) [13] |

Notes on ranking and data gaps:
- Steel & Tube has the only directly reported FY2023 revenue in the evidence for a downstream steel business that spans distribution and fabrication (NZ$589.1m) [23]. Fletcher Building’s group revenue is large but is a conglomerate and only a small portion relates to structural steel activities; evidence reports a disclosed production quantity (4,000 t) for one internal client in FY2023 but not company-level structural-steel revenue [23].
- New Zealand Steel is the only domestic integrated steelmaker and produces ~650,000 tpa steel (BlueScope reporting); it is the key domestic upstream mill supplying local fabricators, but New Zealand Steel itself is a producer rather than primarily a structural-steel fabricator [13].
- For Pacific Steel, the evidence shows it manufactured reinforcing bar used on the City Rail Link and a secondary revenue/headcount profile is present in the findings; company filings or audited annual reports were not included in the supplied evidence for Pacific Steel [23][11].
- Culham Engineering appears in the evidence only as a registered company (ownership structure is in the company registration record); no 2023 revenue/tonnage disclosed [13].
- The available evidence does not provide audited 2023 revenue figures for many NZ structural fabricators. Several fabricators are active but not named in the provided evidence; therefore the table above is necessarily partial and uses the best‑available datapoints present in the evidence.

Data gaps and how missing values would be estimated (if additional data collection allowed):
- Missing company revenues/tonnages could be estimated by collecting Companies Office annual financial statements, audited annual reports, or SFC (Steel Fabrication Certification) participant disclosures; these authoritative filings are not included in the evidence set.
- Ownership shareholder registers and NZ Companies Office filings would be used to determine ultimate owners and major shareholders where missing.

------------------------------------------------------------
## 3. New Zealand import tariff environment for raw/semi‑finished steel (HS 7207–7216) and tariff impact methodology
Evidence summary on tariffs and HS framework:
- New Zealand uses the Harmonised System nomenclature; the Working Tariff Document (Part I Standard Tariff; Part II Preferential Tariff) is maintained by NZ Customs and sets tariff rates; MBIE states most goods have no import tariffs but some steel and steel‑related products have tariffs of 5% or 10% — the evidence does not list NZ tariff rates by HS subheading for 7207–7216 [23][11].

What the evidence provides:
- High-level policy: "Most goods imported into New Zealand have no import tariffs" and "Tariffs of 5 or 10 per cent apply to some imported goods including ... steel" [23].
- Customs documentation structure: the Working Tariff Document is published in two parts; Harmonised System is used for tariff classification [23][23].
- HS headings definitions for flat‑rolled steel (example HS7212) are present in the evidence (third‑party HS explanatory pages) but the evidence does not contain a New Zealand Customs Tariff schedule extraction showing the NZ tariff rate for each HS 7207–7216 subheading [23].

Conclusion on tariff schedule data availability in the evidence:
- The required specific NZ tariff rates per HS 7207–7216 subheading (New Zealand Customs Tariff schedule entries and exact percentage rates) are not present in the supplied evidence. Therefore, exact NZ Customs tariff rates per subheading cannot be reported from the available material.

Tariff impact on a representative local fabricator — what can be shown given evidence constraints:
- Evidence items that would be inputs to a worked tariff impact calculation are missing: the evidence contains no per‑tonne landed‑cost data (FOB, freight, insurance) or firm-level margin benchmarks for typical NZ structural fabricators. The only directly usable margin-like metric in the evidence is Steel & Tube’s FY2023 EBITDA (NZ$51.9m) and FY2023 revenue (NZ$589.1m), implying an FY2023 EBITDA margin around 8.8% for that business (EBITDA / revenue) — this single company-level margin can be used as an illustrative benchmark only for Steel & Tube’s corporate performance and not as a universal fabricator margin [23].
- MBIE indicates tariffs of 5–10% may apply to some steel goods, which would, ceteris paribus, raise landed input costs on those imports by the tariff percentage plus any additional handling/clearance costs [23].

Worked‑calculation approach (methodology to be applied once required input data are obtained):
1. Define import mix by HS code (% by tonne): e.g., hollow sections (HS 7306/7308), hot‑rolled beam sections (HS 7308), flat hot‑rolled plate (HS 7208/7210/7211), cold‑rolled/coated sections (HS 7210/7212), reinforcing bar (HS 7213/7214). (The evidence does not contain an NZ import‑mix breakdown for structural fabrication inputs; this must be collected from NZ Customs trade data.)
2. For each HS line, obtain NZ tariff rate from the Working Tariff Document (NZ Customs), and apply duty to FOB + freight + insurance to compute duty-per-tonne. (NZ tariff rates by subheading are not in the evidence; source: NZ Customs Working Tariff Document is the required primary source.) [23]
3. Apply duty-per-tonne to the fabricator’s input tonnage mix to compute additional landed cost per tonne attributable to tariffs. Compare incremental landed-cost per-tonne to the fabricator’s gross margin per tonne (or company EBITDA margin as a top-line proxy) to derive percentage-of-margin impact. (Gross margin / cost-per-tonne data are not present in the evidence; Steel & Tube EBITDA margin ~8.8% may serve as a high-level reference for one company only.) [23]

Evidence gaps (critical for calculation):
- NZ Customs tariff rates by HS subheading (7207–7216) for New Zealand (specific % per subheading) are not present in the provided evidence; the Working Tariff Document must be consulted to get exact rates [23].
- Import mix by HS code for typical structural fabricators (percentages of beams, hollow sections, plate, reinforcing, etc.) is not provided.
- Landed cost inputs (FOB prices, freight, insurance) and fabricator gross‑margin per tonne are not provided. Without these, numerical per‑tonne or percentage‑of‑margin tariff impact estimates cannot be calculated from the supplied evidence.

## 4. Major infrastructure project demand (three projects; one must be City Rail Link)
The evidence strongly supports one project (City Rail Link) with a published steel tonnage; for other projects the evidence identifies programmatic demand drivers or project business‑case documents but does not publish structural‑steel tonne requirements. The three items below summarise evidence, available tonnage statements, and estimation notes.

Project A — City Rail Link (CRL)
- Project description/owner: City Rail Link — New Zealand’s first underground railway (3.45 km twin‑tunnel), project news and supply announcements in evidence [11].
- Structural steel demand (reported): Approximately 25,000 tonnes of locally produced reinforcing steel will be used over a three‑to‑four‑year period for the City Rail Link — reported by New Zealand Steel / Pacific Steel in a public news item on local steel for CRL [13].
- Completion timeline and certainty: The CRL project was reported as due for completion in 2024 in the NZ Steel news item (project timeline in evidence) — a public project with awarded contracts and visible procurement; the reported reinforcing-tonnage is a supplier announcement and considered a high‑certainty figure within the evidence [13].
- Source: NZ Steel news and Pacific Steel supply announcement (publication date in the linked news item) [13].

Project B — Northern Busway Enhancements (Auckland Transport)
- Project description/owner: Northern Busway Enhancements — Auckland Transport (AT) business case document in evidence [13].
- Structural steel demand (reported): Not specified in the provided evidence.
- Method / how to estimate (evidence‑based approach): The AT business‑case document identifies Northern Busway as a high‑priority rapid-transit corridor requiring enhancements to infrastructure; based on that role the project would likely require structural elements (platforms, canopies, structural retaining works). However, the evidence does not include a Bill of Materials (BOM), contractor tender, or published steel‑tonnage. Therefore no tonnes can be reported from the evidence. Certainty: project is described in a business case (planning stage) in evidence [13].
- Source: AT Northern Busway Enhancements Detailed Business Case (publication date in doc) [13].

Project C — Cyclone Gabrielle residential recovery (programme-level demand driver)
- Description/owner: MBIE building/construction sector reporting identifies substantial residential recovery work resulting from Cyclone Gabrielle and models workforce requirements; this recovery work is a material driver of construction demand over multiple years [11].

- Method / how to estimate (evidence‑based approach): The evidence provides workforce and program length estimates but no construction‑material quantities; therefore no tonnes can be reported from the evidence. Certainty: MBIE modelling suggests a significant and ongoing program of works (moderate certainty as a public-sector forecast) [11].

Notes on estimation and sensitivity:
- Except for CRL (25,000 t of reinforcing steel reported), the evidence does not include published BOMs, tender BOQs, contractor ECI documents, or engineering procurement announcements that disclose project-level structural-steel tonnes for major projects. Any tonne estimates for Northern Busway or Cyclone Gabrielle recovery would therefore be speculative without additional primary procurement or tender documentation (an evidence gap).

Evidence gaps (project demand):

## 5. Strategic analysis — top 3 risks and top 3 opportunities for NZ structural fabricators
All items below cite evidence supporting each claim (primary or secondary).

Top 3 strategic risks

1) Tariff exposure and policy ambiguity (evidence: MBIE tariff summary)
- Explanation: MBIE states that while most imports are tariff‑free, "Tariffs of 5 or 10 per cent apply to some imported goods including ... steel" and New Zealand maintains a Working Tariff Document; this creates potential cost volatility for fabricators importing raw/semi‑finished steel if tariffs apply to critical input lines or if preferential rates change [23].
- Evidence: MBIE tariffs explanation and NZ Customs working tariff document structure (no NZ subheading rates provided in supplied evidence) [23].

2) Supply-chain concentration / upstream mill dependence (evidence: BlueScope / New Zealand Steel)
- Explanation: New Zealand Steel (BlueScope) is the only domestic integrated steel producer in New Zealand and produces ~650,000 tpa; fabricators depend on this single domestic mill plus imported materials. Upstream concentration means domestic mill outages or strategic decisions (e.g., production focus, capacity allocation) could materially affect downstream fabricators' input availability and prices [13].
- Evidence: BlueScope reporting that New Zealand Steel produces around 650,000 tonnes of steel per year and is the only steel producer in NZ [13].

3) Project‑pipeline and labour volatility (evidence: MBIE building sector and Stats NZ employment indicators; SCNZ spare capacity figures)
- Explanation: Construction sector employment and project workloads are volatile: Stats NZ employment indicators show construction filled jobs fell 5.8% in Nov 2024 vs Nov 2023, MBIE reports difficulty recruiting tradespeople, and SCNZ reports spare capacity (31–41% depending on report) meaning demand swings can create revenue/ utilisation volatility and labour shortages/skill gaps for fabricators [11][1][13].
- Evidence: MBIE building and construction sector trends (difficulty recruiting tradespeople); Stats NZ employment indicators (construction jobs down Nov 2024); SCNZ spare capacity reporting (Dec 2021 and Sep 2023) [11][13][1].

Top 3 strategic opportunities

1) Local‑content wins on major projects (evidence: NZ Steel / Pacific Steel CRL announcement)
- Explanation: The CRL used ~25,000 tonnes of locally produced reinforcing steel (Pacific Steel / NZ Steel announcement). Demonstrated project-scale local sourcing suggests fabricators who can align to local procurement and quality assurance schemes (e.g., SFC participation referenced by SCNZ) can capture substantial project volumes and reduce import dependency [13][1].
- Evidence: NZ Steel / Pacific Steel announcement on CRL rebar supply (~25,000 t) and SCNZ note that 90% of sector output is delivered by SFC‑qualified fabricators (Mar 2023 report) [13][1].

2) Decarbonisation / local low‑carbon steel transition (evidence: BlueScope EAF project)
- Explanation: BlueScope announced an accelerated feasibility study to build an electric arc furnace at New Zealand Steel, targeted operational by 2026 and co‑funded by the NZ Government; a local shift to lower‑carbon domestically produced steel creates differentiation opportunities for fabricators willing to market and certify low‑carbon structural steel supply chains to project owners seeking embodied‑carbon reductions [13].
- Evidence: BlueScope FY2023 investor materials describing EAF project targeting operation by 2026, NZ$300m project with government co‑funding and emission reductions ~45% [13].

3) Spare capacity and capability to deliver (evidence: SCNZ capacity/capability statements)
- Explanation: SCNZ reports that the NZ structural steel industry has proven capability and spare capacity (31% in Dec 2021; 41% in Sep 2023) and that fabrication generally shortens programmes vs alternatives; fabricators can capitalise on this by pursuing larger project contracts or quicker delivery windows and by marketing domestic availability to reduce offshore procurement for timelines-sensitive projects [1].
- Evidence: SCNZ reports of spare capacity and claimed delivery performance (Dec 2021, Mar 2023, Sep 2023) [1].

## Evidence gaps and data‑collection recommendations (one page)
Priority data collection steps to close major gaps (short list, actionable and linked to sources to consult):

1) Obtain NZ Customs Working Tariff Document extract for HS 7207–7216 (Part I Standard Tariff) and record tariff rates by NZ Customs subheading. # Recent evolution of deepfake detection (since 2022): video, audio, multimodal methods, evaluation, risks, and policy evidence gaps

## Executive summary
Since 2022 the research literature shows continued progress on deepfake detection across video and audio modalities, with three simultaneous trends: (1) specialized signal‑analysis approaches (frequency / spectral, temporal consistency, physiological cues) that maintain competitive benchmark performance; (2) widespread adoption of transformer‑style and hybrid CNN/transformer architectures (including parameter‑efficient adaptation of large pretrained encoders); and (3) increasing emphasis on multimodal fusion and on measuring cross‑dataset and in‑the‑wild generalization, which reveals large performance gaps relative to controlled benchmarks. Reported top results on canonical benchmarks (FF++, DFDC, ASVspoof 2019) are very strong for in‑domain tests (AUCs or low EERs often in the high‑90s % AUC or sub‑1% EER), but multiple recent evaluations and new “in‑the‑wild” benchmarks show dramatic drops (examples include ~50% AUC drops on one open benchmark and EERs rising from sub‑1% to >10–20% on cross‑domain audio tests). Evidence about regulatory responses (laws, proposals) is not present in the provided research findings; that gap is noted below. [1], [2], [15]

## 1. Scope and timeframe
- The review period is “since 2022” through the present; the body of work summarized here includes papers, benchmark reports, dataset papers, and preprints released in 2022–2026 that were provided in the evidence set. A consolidated discussion of datasets, metrics, and benchmarking practices across multiple datasets was published as part of a NeurIPS datasets/benchmarks survey that documents the proliferation of deepfake datasets and benchmark fragmentation leading to inconsistent evaluations across methods [1]. New dataset efforts and explainability/benchmarking work continued into 2024–2026 (examples: explainable video dataset ExDDV and multilingual audio‑video benchmarks mentioned in a WACV 2026 dataset paper) [2].

## 2. Technical methods (organized by modality, then joint methods and privacy/foundation‑model integration)

### 2.1 Video‑only detection — representative classes and recent advances
- Spatial / frequency analysis. Several recent works exploit frequency‑domain inputs or combined RGB+frequency representations to reveal generation artifacts. A Frequency Domain Filtered Residual Network reported 98.85% AUC on FaceForensics++ (C0) using combined RGB+frequency inputs, while also noting failure modes where tampering is highly localized (e.g., Face2Face mouth‑only edits) that confuse frequency classifiers [4]. Frequency‑blending defenses (FreqBlender) reported strong DFDC performance (94.59% AUC) and claimed robustness to common perturbations [5]. More recent triple‑branch, frequency‑aware networks extend this direction by explicitly modeling multiscale frequency cues [29]. [4], [5], [29]
- Temporal inconsistency and motion cues. Work extending spatial frequency approaches to explicitly include temporal/frequency components (pixel‑wise temporal frequency analysis) finds that temporal frequency features expose dynamic inconsistencies not captured by spatial methods alone [3]. Thumbnail/temporal layout methods that add temporal modeling to transformer backbones (TALL added temporal modeling to Swin and reported substantial AUC improvements on Celeb‑DF and DFDC when trained on FF++ (HQ)) demonstrate the value of temporal aggregation for video models [6]. [3], [6]
- Physiological / biometric signals (rPPG/heartbeat). Approaches using remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) or visual heartbeat rhythms detect physiological anomalies introduced or removed by generation pipelines; a review and experimental papers report high AUCs in some datasets (examples: rPPG approaches reporting 91.2% and 99.7% AUC on two datasets; DeepRhythm used attentional visual heartbeat rhythms) but these methods may be sensitive to video quality and editing that preserves or synthetically injects physiological signals [11], [12].
- Multi‑scale CNNs and hybrids. Multi‑scale convolutional modules (dilated, depthwise‑separable) combined with Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones have been shown to improve detection across both high‑ and low‑quality deepfakes [14].
- Transformer‑based and hybrid architectures. Hybrid CNN+ViT and pure ViT models have been widely explored. Reported behavior is sensitive to architecture and training: one hybrid ViT reported very high numbers on FF++ (a hybrid ViT: 99.28% AUC, 98.92% F1, 99.28% accuracy on FF++; a standalone ViT performed much worse on the same data), showing that ViT architecture choice and fusion with convolutional/local features matter [7]. Parameter‑efficient tuning techniques (adapters, LoRA, Mixture‑of‑Experts) have been applied to adapt large pretrained vision encoders efficiently for detection tasks [8]. CLIP/OpenCLIP adaptation (SigLIP‑2 / OpenCLIP and LNCLIP‑DF approaches) shows a line of work that reuses large contrastively pretrained encoders and either fine‑tunes small parameter subsets (e.g., LNCLIP‑DF fine‑tunes only LayerNorm parameters) or adds lightweight temporal decoders for video forgery detection, and these approaches claim state‑of‑the‑art results across multiple datasets [10], [11]. [7], [8], [10], [11]
- Observed tradeoffs and failure modes. Frequency methods can be misled by highly localized manipulations, and pure ViT models can underperform unless combined with inductive bias (locality) or hybrid convolutional modules; this motivates hybrid CNN/transformer backbones and temporal decoders for video detection [4], [7], [6], [3].

### 2.2 Audio‑only detection — architectures, features, and SSL integration
- Spectral vs raw‑waveform approaches and classical front ends. Traditional handcrafted spectral front ends (LFCC, MFCC, CQCC, mel‑spectrograms) continue to be strong baselines for audio anti‑spoofing tasks; studies summarize the use of LFCC/CQCC and mel features in earlier detection work and show that LFCC can preserve high‑frequency artifacts helpful for unseen attacks [20].
- CNN / ResNet / end‑to‑end raw waveform systems. CNN families (ResNet, ResNeXt, LCNN) and end‑to‑end raw‑waveform systems (RawNet variants) are widely used; repositories and community codebases (e.g., media‑sec‑lab) catalog many competitive systems and their reported t‑DCF/EER numbers on ASVspoof splits [23].
- Audio transformers & spectrogram transformers. The Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) (12 transformer blocks, 8‑head MHSA) reported strong performance on ASVspoof 2019 (EER 4.06%, AUC 99.9%) and matched or outperformed raw‑waveform systems in several open‑set evaluations [17].
- Self‑supervised pretrained audio encoders. SSL models (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, WavLM, XLS‑R) are frequently used as feature extractors or frozen encoders; wav2vec 2.0 gave 0.82% EER (ASVspoof 2019 LA) in one evaluation and combined variants (wav2vec+VIB, XLS‑R + SLS) have produced sub‑0.2% EERs on ASVspoof 2019 LA in strong reported setups, demonstrating the power of large SSL models for in‑domain detection [18], [19], [29].
- Lightweight and efficient detectors. Architectures like SpecRNet (LFCC + CNN‑GRU) and other CPU/GPU‑friendly models reported very low in‑domain EERs on benchmarks such as WaveFake (SpecRNet EER 0.15%), illustrating practical tradeoffs between speed and accuracy [20]. [17], [18], [20], [23]
- Privacy‑preserving audio detectors. SafeEar (a content privacy‑preserving audio deepfake detector) uses acoustic tokens only and reported EER 2.02% with a very high word error rate (WER > 93.9%), illustrating a deliberate privacy/performance tradeoff where content is not reconstructible but detection remains effective [22].
- Observed tradeoffs and failure modes. As with video, very low in‑domain EERs do not imply robust real‑world performance: strong ASVspoof results (sub‑1% EER) often degrade sharply on unseen generation methods or in‑the‑wild corpora (see Section 4) [18], [19], [31].

### 2.3 Multimodal (audio‑visual) detection and fusion strategies
- Fusion strategies. Multimodal detectors use early fusion (joint spectro‑visual inputs), late fusion (separate modality classifiers combined), and cross‑attention or co‑attention mechanisms; contrastive and retrieval‑augmented approaches have also been proposed for embedding‑level interaction. Large benchmarking efforts integrate multiple state‑of‑the‑art multimodal methods to compare fusion strategies [13], [14].
- Representative results. DeepfakeBench‑MM (a multimodal extension of DeepfakeBench) reports high AUCs for top multimodal entries (example numbers: MRDF AUC 0.970, FRADE AUC 0.994) and attributes high performance to audio‑visual interaction modeling and adapting pretrained ViT architectures to multimodal inputs [14]. The AST (audio) model was also reported to outperform prior methods on FakeAVCeleb in open‑set evaluation contexts in one benchmark [17]. [13], [14], [17]
- Benchmarks and multilingual datasets. New multimodal benchmarks (e.g., multilingual audio‑video open‑set MAVOS‑DD mentioned in dataset work) and curated multimodal suites enable systematic comparison across audio, visual, and joint methods [2].

### 2.4 Cross‑dataset generalization techniques
- Observed degradation and mitigation directions. Multiple recent studies quantify large cross‑dataset drops and investigate mitigation: the Deepfake‑Eval‑2024 benchmark reports that open‑source SOTA video models can suffer ~50% absolute AUC drop when evaluated on that benchmark, highlighting severe generalization limitations for models tuned to legacy datasets [15]. In audio, CD‑ADD (a 300‑hour dataset of zero‑shot TTS outputs with simulated noise) demonstrates that models trained only on ASVspoof datasets show large performance drops on CD‑ADD; some fine‑tuning on specific TTS outputs improves generalization to other TTS systems but not uniformly (performance varied widely across generator types) [25], [26].
- Effective strategies. Reported mitigation approaches include (a) large SSL pretraining (wav2vec / XLS‑R / WavLM) used as robust feature extractors; (b) fine‑tuning on in‑the‑wild data which reduces EER substantially in some cases (examples: fine‑tuning on ItW reduced many models’ audio EERs into the 23–39% range from much worse baselines in one evaluation, and fine‑tuning RawNet3 improved EER from 63.7% to 26.7% and AUC from 31.79% to 79.95%); (c) augmentation and augmented training sets to stabilize performance across communication conditions; and (d) retrieval‑augmented detection or embedding retrieval approaches that report low EERs on certain datasets [31], [16], [27], [24]. [31], [16], [27], [24]
- Domain adaptation & test‑time adaptation. Parameter‑efficient tuning of pretrained encoders (adapters, LoRA) and lightweight temporal decoders (for frozen CLIP encoders) have been proposed to adapt vision encoders with small data budgets and can help handle dataset shifts [8], [10].

### 2.5 Foundation model integration (vision/audio/language)
- Reusing large pretrained encoders. Several works adapt CLIP/OpenCLIP or other large pretrained vision encoders for forgery detection; LNCLIP‑DF reported fine‑tuning only LayerNorm parameters (0.03% of total parameters) of a CLIP vision encoder and claimed state‑of‑the‑art performance across many video datasets [10]. Other works freeze CLIP image encoders and add spatial/temporal decoders to enable temporal reasoning for video‑forgery detection [11].
- Audio foundation models. Large SSL speech encoders (wav2vec 2.0, WavLM, XLS‑R) are used as frozen or fine‑tuned backbones and achieve state‑of‑the‑art in‑domain results when combined with anti‑spoofing backends; XLS‑R with sensitive‑layer selection (SLS) and other careful selection methods were reported to reach sub‑2% EER on ASVspoof 2021 DF in one SUPERB‑style evaluation [29], [19].
- Early multimodal language integration. Proposals include using text modalities (e.g., CLIP text tokens) to guide visual feature extraction for forgery detection; such CLIP‑based multi‑frame architectures and text‑guided encoders have been proposed as research directions in recent preprints [11].

### 2.6 Privacy‑preserving techniques
- Techniques and tradeoffs. Approaches include federated learning, differential privacy, synthetic‑data training, and specialized model designs that avoid reconstructable content. High‑level descriptions emphasize federated learning for local training, differential privacy for mathematical privacy guarantees, and synthetic data to reduce exposure of real sensitive data; these are discussed in non‑peer publications and project pages as viable techniques but without uniform, peer‑reviewed quantification of detection/privacy tradeoffs in the provided evidence set [28].
- Concrete example (audio). SafeEar is a privacy‑preserving detector that uses non‑reconstructible acoustic tokens; it reported EER 2.02% but a very high WER (>93.9%), demonstrating an explicit utility/privacy tradeoff where content cannot be recovered while detection remains available [22]. [28], [22]

## 3. Evaluation: metrics, benchmarks, and reported performance

### 3.1 Key public benchmarks and datasets highlighted in the evidence
- Video/image benchmarks commonly reported: FaceForensics++ (FF++), DFDC (Facebook Deepfake Detection Challenge), Celeb‑DF, DeeperForensics, ForgeryNet and consolidated benchmark suites; dataset and benchmark fragmentation is documented in the NeurIPS datasets/benchmarks survey [1]. Newer dataset and benchmark releases include ExDDV (explainable deepfake video dataset) and multilingual audio‑video benchmarks (MAVOS‑DD) [2], and larger “gen‑video” scale evaluation preprints appear in the recent dataset literature. [1], [2]
- Audio benchmarks: ASVspoof (2019, 2021) remains a canonical anti‑spoofing benchmark; ADD (Audio Deepfake Detection) challenge and ADD datasets (2022/2023) provide additional evaluation tracks; WaveFake, FakeAVCeleb and in‑the‑wild corpora and new multilingual in‑the‑wild (ML‑ITW) benchmarks appear in recent evidence [32], [17], [25], [27]. [32], [17], [25], [27]

### 3.2 Representative published performance numbers (selected examples)
- Video detection:
  - Frequency Domain Filtered Residual Network: 98.85% AUC on FF++ (C0) (reported in the method’s paper) [4].
  - GenConViT (hybrid ViT): reported 98.5% accuracy on DFDC, 97% on FF++, and 90.94% on Celeb‑DF for their configurations; a hybrid ViT variant reported 99.28% AUC / 98.92% F1 / 99.28% ACC on FF++ whereas a standalone ViT in the same work performed much worse (77.10% AUC) — illustrating sensitivity to architecture and training [7].
  - TALL (temporal modeling added to Swin): reported CDF AUC improvement of 7.6% and DFDC AUC improvement of 3.6% over Swin alone when trained on FF++ (HQ) and claimed state‑of‑the‑art on Celeb‑DF, DFDC, and Deeper‑Forensics in reported experiments [6].
  - FreqBlender: reported 94.59% AUC on DFDC and improved robustness to common perturbations [5].
- Multimodal video+audio:
  - DeepfakeBench‑MM entries: MRDF achieved AUC 0.970 and FRADE AUC 0.994 (multimodal entries using audio‑visual interactions and adapted ViT architectures) [14].
- Audio detection:
  - Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST): EER 4.06% on ASVspoof 2019, AUC 99.9% on ASVspoof 2019 reported in that study; AST claimed strong open‑set performance on FakeAVCeleb and in‑the‑wild datasets in one evaluation [17].
  - Self‑supervised encoders: wav2vec 2.0 reported EER 0.82% and min t‑DCF 0.109 on ASVspoof 2019 LA in one evaluation (no anti‑spoofing backend), and variants (wav2vec+VIB, XLS‑R, RawNet2) have been reported to reach EER 0.12% and min t‑DCF 0.0032 in specific experimental setups [18], [19].
  - Lightweight and efficient models: SpecRNet (LFCC + CNN‑GRU) reported EER 0.15% on WaveFake while being CPU/GPU friendly in one compilation of results [20].
  - Privacy‑preserving detector SafeEar: EER 2.02%, WER >93.9% (illustrates privacy/utility tradeoff) [22].

(Each of the above figures is quoted from the cited source; differences in reported metric definitions and evaluation protocols are reported in the cited studies.) [4], [5], [7], [6], [14], [17], [18], [19], [20], [22]

### 3.3 Benchmarks versus realistic/in‑the‑wild performance (quantified gaps)
- Large and reproducible decreases are documented when models are evaluated outside the test distribution used for training:
  - Deepfake‑Eval‑2024 reported that open‑source SOTA video models’ AUCs dropped by roughly 50% when tested on its curated evaluation benchmark versus their reported in‑domain values [15].
  - In audio, CD‑ADD and VoiceWukong style evaluations show dramatic degradations: models that perform well on ASVspoof or similar benchmarks can see EERs increase from sub‑1% to double‑digit percentages on zero‑shot TTS outputs or in‑the‑wild data; e.g., VoiceWukong analyses reported many detectors with EER >20% on English and Chinese evaluations, with only a few models achieving AUC >0.9 and EERs ~13.5% in cross‑language tests [24], [25].
  - Fine‑tuning on in‑the‑wild data does help: one WACV 2026 evaluation (audio detectors vs real fraud) reported that fine‑tuning on ItW reduced EERs of most models into the 23–39% range and that RawNet3 improved EER from 63.70% to 26.70% and AUC from 31.79% to 79.95% after ItW fine‑tuning — still considerably worse than in‑domain numbers but markedly improved compared with unadapted baselines [31], [15], [24].
- Synthesis: top reported in‑domain benchmark results can be excellent, but multiple independent benchmark efforts and in‑the‑wild evaluations reveal large, sometimes order‑of‑magnitude, degradations on realistic data or unseen generation methods. These quantified discrepancies are central evidence that benchmark‑reported state‑of‑the‑art does not imply robust real‑world detection out of the box. [15], [24], [31]

## 4. Robustness and generalization evidence (cross‑dataset experiments and adversarial effects)
- Cross‑dataset evaluations demonstrate substantial drops. Deepfake‑Eval‑2024 documented ~50% AUC drops for video when SOTA models were tested on that benchmark; CD‑ADD shows that ASVspoof‑trained audio systems do not generalize uniformly to zero‑shot and noisy TTS outputs; VoiceWukong reported high EERs across languages on real‑world audio testbeds [15], [25], [24].
- Mitigation effectiveness (quantified examples). Fine‑tuning on in‑the‑wild data reduced EERs and raised AUC substantially in specific audio evaluations (RawNet3 EER from 63.7% to 26.7% and AUC from 31.8% to 79.95% after ItW fine‑tuning) [31]. Pretraining with large SSL audio encoders and selecting sensitive layers (XLS‑R + SLS) yielded sub‑2% EER on ASVspoof 2021 DF in a SUPERB‑style evaluation, indicating that SSL pretraining plus targeted adaptation strongly improves in‑domain robustness (but in‑the‑wild generalization remains a separate issue) [29].
- Adversarial / perturbation robustness. Some video frequency‑blending methods report robustness to common perturbations (FreqBlender). Pixel‑wise temporal frequency methods highlight that temporal perturbations and motion magnification can expose forgeries beyond spatial frequency methods, suggesting that combining spatial and temporal frequency analyses increases robustness [5], [3]. Frequency methods also have documented failure cases where localized edits (mouth‑only manipulations) reduce classifier effectiveness [4].
- Evidence gaps. There is limited evidence in the supplied materials quantifying robustness to targeted adversarial attacks (adaptive forgery methods deliberately optimized to evade detectors), codec‑level attacks, or systematic adversarial perturbations across large cross‑dataset suites with standardized adaptive threat models; this is an evidence gap in the provided findings.

## 5. Ethical, social, and technical risks identified in the literature
- Commonly emphasized harms. The provided research findings and method papers highlight risks including misinformation via manipulated audio/video, non‑consensual explicit content generation, identity and privacy harms, surveillance/misattribution concerns, bias and unequal detection performance across demographic groups, and dual‑use concerns for research and tooling (detection methods can inform better generators and vice versa). The evidence set also includes work focused explicitly on fairness—e.g., a fairness‑aware detection framework using temporal feature learning reported improved fairness metrics (Spearman correlation >0.84 on evaluated datasets) alongside detection performance, indicating the field is measuring demographic and fairness concerns in some research threads [30].
- Empirical bias measurements. Recent fairness‑aware method work reports large improvements on four datasets with Xception backbones and quantifies statistical correlations relevant to fairness (Spearman >0.84, p<10⁻¹¹), providing direct empirical study of bias mitigation in detection models [30].
- Privacy tradeoffs. Privacy‑preserving detectors (e.g., SafeEar) explicitly trade content recoverability for detection capability and quantify that tradeoff (EER 2.02% with WER >93.9%) [22].
- Evidence gaps. The supplied evidence set contains limited direct large‑scale social science studies measuring real‑world harms (e.g., quantifying misinformation spread, psychological harms, or legal outcomes resulting from deepfakes). The literature in the evidence set is primarily technical and benchmark‑oriented; additional empirical social‑impact studies are not present in the provided materials.

Note: this prioritized list selects representative, high‑impact items that appear in the provided evidence (peer‑reviewed conference/journal items prioritized; when peer‑reviewed versions were not available the entry is labeled as preprint).

- Video‑only / spatial & frequency:
  1. Frequency Domain Filtered Residual Network — FF++ 98.85% AUC (method paper) [4].
  2. FreqBlender — frequency‑blending method with 94.59% AUC on DFDC (NeurIPS 2024) [5].
  3. Pixel‑wise temporal frequency (ICCV 2025) — temporal frequency analysis beyond spatial methods [3].

  1. TALL (Thumbnail Layout + Swin) — ICCV 2023; temporal modeling for Swin with reported AUC gains on Celeb‑DF/DFDC [6].

## 8. Evidence gaps and explicit limitations of this report
- Regulatory/policy texts: no official or authoritative EU, US, or international laws, bills, platform policy texts, or government analyses were included in the provided evidence; the report therefore cannot summarize enacted or proposed regulation and must treat that topic as an evidence gap. (User provision of policy sources would enable that section.) [— no citation available —]
- Large‑scale social‑impact empirical studies: the provided findings do not include systematic empirical social science studies quantifying misinformation spread or other social harms tied to detected deepfakes at scale; this is an evidence gap for claims about real‑world social effects.
- Systematic adversarial robustness: the supplied materials include some robustness claims and perturbation tests but do not provide a uniform, standardized evaluation of adversarially adaptive forgery attacks across the major model classes; this remains an area where the supplied evidence is incomplete.

## 9. Practical conclusions for researchers and practitioners
- For controlled benchmarks, modern methods (hybrid CNN/ViT, frequency‑aware networks, SSL audio encoders) can achieve excellent in‑domain numbers; however, these numbers often collapse under dataset shift, unseen generators, or in‑the‑wild noise. Reported specific examples show in‑domain AUCs/EERs in the very strong regime but cross‑dataset evaluation can reduce AUC by tens of points or increase EER from <1% to >10–20% in audio/video cases [4], [5], [7], [15], [24], [31].
- Robust deployment requires: (a) careful cross‑domain validation (including zero‑shot generators and in‑the‑wild corpora), (b) planned adaptation pipelines (SSL pretraining, parameter‑efficient tuning, targeted fine‑tuning on realistic samples), (c) multimodal fusion where available, and (d) transparent reporting of expected error rates and demographic fairness metrics; some methods and benchmarks explicitly demonstrate these needs and partial mitigation strategies [8], [10], [14], [29], [31], [30].
- Privacy‑preserving detection is feasible with quantifiable tradeoffs; practitioners must decide acceptable utility/privacy balances (SafeEar is one concrete instantiation) [22], [28].
