# Fortive: Post‑Precision Technologies separation — segment economics, momentum, and portfolio prioritization

Executive summary
- Q2 2025 segment operating margins (GAAP, as reported): Intelligent Operating Solutions (IOS) 24.7%, Precision Technologies 17.8%, Advanced Healthcare Solutions (AHS) 12.2% — computed from Fortive’s Q2 2025 segment revenue and operating income [1].  
- Using Fortive’s 2024 segment figures disclosed in the company’s FY‑2024 results release, the comparable 2024 margins are IOS 28.1%, Precision 20.0%, AHS 13.7% (see discussion of a material data ambiguity below); Q2 2025 vs 2024 shows margin contractions of ~3.4 ppt (IOS), ~2.2 ppt (Precision), and ~1.5 ppt (AHS) [2].  
- Material one‑time items and reporting comparability issues (notably separation‑related costs in 2025 and an inconsistency between available 2023 and 2024 segment totals in the provided evidence) limit clean year‑over‑year segment margin comparisons; adjusted/normalized comparisons cannot be completed at the segment level with the available evidence because separation costs are not allocated to segments in public disclosures [1], [6], [8].  
- Company‑level operating margin fell Q1 2025 vs Q1 2024 (operating income ÷ revenue): Q1 2025 = 302.2 / 3,049.0 = 9.9%; Q1 2024 = 164.1 / 1,525.0 = 10.8% — a decline of ~0.9 ppt; management cited near‑term margin pressure in certain businesses and one‑time separation items across the period covered by the spin process [9], [13], [11].  
- Strategic assessment: IOS shows the strongest unit economics (highest absolute margins and adjusted EBITDA disclosure), but momentum is mixed (management reports flat revenue in Q2 2025). Evidence that the Precision spin strengthened the remaining businesses is limited to clearer portfolio focus and shareholder capital allocation (large buybacks) rather than documented increases in reinvestment or segment reinvigoration; more granular evidence (post‑spin segment capex/R&D, segment‑level guidance, or reallocated M&A authority) is not present in the supplied findings and is listed below as an evidence gap [4], [5], [11].

Methodology and primary evidence used
- Operating margin formula: operating margin = (segment operating income ÷ segment revenue). GAAP segment operating income and revenue from Fortive’s Q2 2025 filing were used to calculate Q2 2025 margins [1]. 2024 segment revenue and operating income were taken from Fortive’s FY‑2024 results release in the supplied findings [2]; the report flags and documents a material ambiguity between the available 2023 and 2024 segment totals that affects year‑over‑year growth calculations (see “Comparability and evidence gaps” below) [8].  
- All numeric calculations show the formula used and are rounded to one decimal place in tables. Sources for each factual block are cited at the end of the paragraph (single citation per paragraph where possible) to avoid repeated citations of the same source.

Key Q2 2025 and 2024 segment results (calculations and comparability note)
Note on source ambiguity (critical): the supplied evidence includes (A) Q2 2025 GAAP segment revenue and operating income from Fortive’s Q2 filing and (B) a Fortive press release that labels certain segment values “for fiscal year 2024.” However, the magnitudes of the 2024 segment figures in that press release are inconsistent with earlier 2023 segment totals included in the supplied evidence (the 2023 segment totals are much larger), creating a conflict about whether the cited 2024 numbers are full‑year figures or quarterly/fourth‑quarter figures. This report uses the Fortive FY‑2024 figures as reported in the provided FY‑2024 press release for the requested 2024 comparisons but documents the conflict and the resulting limitations below [2], [8].

Per‑segment calculations (Q2 2025 figures from Fortive’s Q2 filing; 2024 figures from Fortive FY‑2024 release) [1], [2]:

Intelligent Operating Solutions (IOS)
- Q2 2025 revenue = $675.7 million; Q2 2025 operating income = $166.7 million. Operating margin (Q2 2025) = 166.7 ÷ 675.7 = 24.7% [1].  
- 2024 (company‑reported in FY‑2024 release): revenue = $710.8 million; operating income = $199.6 million. Operating margin (2024) = 199.6 ÷ 710.8 = 28.1% [2].  
- Margin change = 24.7% − 28.1% = −3.4 ppt (relative change = −3.4 ÷ 28.1 = −12.2%). (Formula shown: margin change (ppt) = Q2‑2025 margin − 2024 margin) [1], [2].

Precision Technologies
- Q2 2025 revenue = $523.6 million; Q2 2025 operating income = $93.2 million. Operating margin (Q2 2025) = 93.2 ÷ 523.6 = 17.8% [1].  
- 2024 (company‑reported in FY‑2024 release): revenue = $567.7 million; operating income = $113.6 million. Operating margin (2024) = 113.6 ÷ 567.7 = 20.0% [2].  
- Margin change = 17.8% − 20.0% = −2.2 ppt (relative change = −2.2 ÷ 20.0 = −11.0%) [1], [2].

Advanced Healthcare Solutions (AHS)
- Q2 2025 revenue = $319.5 million; Q2 2025 operating income = $39.1 million. Operating margin (Q2 2025) = 39.1 ÷ 319.5 = 12.2% [1].  
- 2024 (company‑reported in FY‑2024 release): revenue = $341.8 million; operating income = $46.9 million. Operating margin (2024) = 46.9 ÷ 341.8 = 13.7% [2].  
- Margin change = 12.2% − 13.7% = −1.5 ppt (relative change = −1.5 ÷ 13.7 = −10.8%) [1], [2].

Concise per‑segment tables (broken into two small tables per segment to respect the five‑column table limit)

Table A — Q2 2025 and 2024 headline amounts (per segment)
- Intelligent Operating Solutions: Q2‑2025 revenue $675.7M; Q2‑2025 operating income $166.7M; 2024 revenue $710.8M; 2024 operating income $199.6M. [1], [2]  
- Precision Technologies: Q2‑2025 revenue $523.6M; Q2‑2025 operating income $93.2M; 2024 revenue $567.7M; 2024 operating income $113.6M. [1], [2]  
- Advanced Healthcare Solutions: Q2‑2025 revenue $319.5M; Q2‑2025 operating income $39.1M; 2024 revenue $341.8M; 2024 operating income $46.9M. [1], [2]

Table B — Derived margins and deltas (per segment)
- Intelligent Operating Solutions: Q2‑2025 margin 24.7%; 2024 margin 28.1%; change −3.4 ppt (−12.2%). [1], [2]  
- Precision Technologies: Q2‑2025 margin 17.8%; 2024 margin 20.0%; change −2.2 ppt (−11.0%). [1], [2]  
- Advanced Healthcare Solutions: Q2‑2025 margin 12.2%; 2024 margin 13.7%; change −1.5 ppt (−10.8%). [1], [2]

Notes on one‑time items, restructuring/separation costs, and comparability adjustments
- Fortive reported $41 million of separation‑related costs in Q2 2025 (three months ended June 27, 2025) and $64 million for the six months ended June 27, 2025; the Q2 filing treats Precision as a continuing operation for Q2 but notes that beginning in Q3 2025 Precision will be classified as discontinued [1], [5]. These separation costs are recorded at the consolidated level in the Q2 filing; the supplied evidence does not allocate those costs to segments, so segment‑level adjusted margins excluding separation costs cannot be reliably calculated from the supplied evidence alone [1].  
- Fortive reported discrete restructuring charges of $4.9 million in Q2 2025 in its Q2 earnings presentation; Q1 2025 also carried discrete restructuring items reported in the supplied evidence [6], [10]. Q1 2025 included a $63.1 million gain on sale of property in the Precision segment (a one‑time gain) reported in the Q1 2025 filing; that one‑time item materially affects 2025 year‑to‑date comparatives and any attempt to annualize or compare to 2024 without restatement [9].  
- Because separation costs and certain Q1 one‑offs are reported at consolidated or non‑segment levels in the supplied evidence, any “adjusted” segment margin that excludes separation or restructuring amounts would require management’s allocation methodology; that allocation is not present in the supplied facts and therefore was not applied here [1], [6], [9].

Segment revenue momentum: 2023→2024 growth (evidence limits)
- The supplied evidence contains FY‑2023 segment totals (Intelligent Operating Solutions $2,612.2M; Precision $2,132.8M; AHS $1,320.3M) in an SEC exhibit and also contains a Fortive FY‑2024 press release with much smaller segment amounts (710.8M / 567.7M / 341.8M) labeled “for fiscal year 2024.” These two sets of figures are inconsistent in magnitude; therefore the supplied evidence does not permit a reliable 2023→2024 percentage growth calculation at the segment level without external clarification or the company’s formal restated comparatives [8], [2].  
- The 2023 totals in the SEC exhibit and the 2024 press‑release numbers cannot be reconciled from the supplied facts, so 2023→2024 growth rates are not computed here to avoid producing misleading results. This is a material evidence gap for the requested year‑over‑year momentum analysis (see Evidence Gaps below) [8], [2].

Company‑level operating margin trend: Q1 2025 vs Q1 2024
- Q1 2025 company operating income = $302.2 million; Q1 2025 revenue = $3,049.0 million → operating margin = 302.2 ÷ 3,049.0 = 9.9% [9].  
- Q1 2024 company operating income = $164.1 million; Q1 2024 revenue = $1,525.0 million → operating margin = 164.1 ÷ 1,525.0 = 10.8% [13].  
- Change = −0.9 ppt (relative −8.3%). Management commentary and the Q2 call highlight margin pressure in some businesses, adjusted gross‑margin declines in IOS versus the prior year, and near‑term impacts from separation costs and restructuring actions; management also reported robust adjusted free cash flow and significant share repurchases during the spin process [11], [9].  
- Reconciliation to segment trends: Q2 segment margins are down versus 2024 across all three segments (see Table B), consistent with management’s reporting of margin headwinds at the segment level; however Q1 vs Q2 intra‑year variability (e.g., a Q1 gain in Precision) and unallocated corporate/separation costs complicate a simple reconciliation of quarter‑to‑quarter movements. The supplied evidence shows Q2 consolidated operating income can be reconstructed from segment operating profits less unallocated corporate loss (segment profits sum to $299.0M; unallocated corporate loss $76.8M → consolidated operating income $222.2M for Q2 2025) and that Fortive reported additional separation costs in Q2 2025 ($41M) [1]. This reconstruction shows Q2 company margin is sensitive to non‑segment items and one‑offs and therefore segment‑driven margin comparisons must be interpreted cautiously [1].

Strategic assessment and portfolio prioritization (qualitative synthesis)
- Which segment shows the strongest unit economics and trajectory?  
  - Based on Q2 2025 GAAP operating margins and available adjusted metrics disclosed in the Q2 earnings call materials, IOS demonstrates the strongest unit economics: highest GAAP operating margin in Q2 2025 (24.7%) and management‑reported adjusted EBITDA/adjusted gross margins highlighting IOS profitability (adjusted EBITDA margin ~33.8% and adjusted gross margin ~66.1% as called out in the earnings call transcript) [1], [11]. However, IOS revenue growth in Q2 2025 was reported as flat by management, which tempers the trajectory argument despite stronger unit economics [11].  
- Did the Precision separation strengthen the remaining businesses? Evidence available in the supplied findings supports several limited, observable changes but does not demonstrate clear operational strengthening at the segment level:  
  - Portfolio focus and governance: Fortive completed the spin‑off of Precision (Ralliant) on June 28, 2025 and will classify Precision as a discontinued operation beginning Q3 2025, sharpening the remaining company around IOS and AHS and simplifying the corporate portfolio framework; Fortive also appointed a new CEO effective June 28, 2025 (organizational focus signal) [4], [5].  
  - Capital allocation shift toward shareholders during the spin: from the spin announcement through completion Fortive allocated over 75% of consolidated free cash flow to share repurchases and repurchased about $140M in Q2 2025 — a demonstrable prioritization of shareholder returns during the separation process rather than redeploying cash into rapid, visible reinvestment in remaining segments [11].  
  - One‑time costs and near‑term margin impacts: separation‑related costs ($41M in Q2 2025; $64M year‑to‑date) and restructuring charges were incurred in 2025, creating near‑term margin headwinds for the continuing company and obscuring a clean read on underlying operational improvement attributable to the spin [1], [6].  
  - No supplied evidence of material reallocation of capex, R&D budgets, or a marked increase in M&A appetite directed to the remaining segments post‑spin; such metrics and management guidance are not present in the supplied findings and therefore cannot be used to conclude that the spin materially strengthened competitive positioning via reinvestment or accelerated go‑to‑market changes. This lack of evidence is noted as a gap below.  
- Contextual competitiveness: the supplied findings include no peer benchmark data for segment margins and revenue growth; therefore comparative assessment to industry peers cannot be completed from the provided evidence and is noted as an evidence gap.

Investment / portfolio‑prioritization implications (3–5 bullets)
- IOS appears the highest‑quality, higher‑margin business within the continuing Fortive (best unit economics); however, Q2 2025 shows margin compression and flat revenue momentum, implying emphasis should be on restoring margin drivers (cost/mix/pricing) even as cash is temporarily prioritized to shareholder returns [1], [11].  
- The Precision spin has delivered clarity (corporate simplification and governance change) and enabled substantial cash returns (share repurchases) but the supplied evidence does not show re‑investment of proceeds into material growth programs for the remaining segments; investors should therefore treat the separation as portfolio re‑shaping plus shareholder returns rather than a clear operational re‑acceleration of IOS/AHS [4], [11].  
- AHS shows mixed signals: modestly lower absolute margins and slightly negative revenue momentum as provided, but management reports improved adjusted gross margin in AHS; this suggests selective operational improvement potential but not yet a consistent growth/margin breakout relative to IOS [1], [11].  
- Near‑term margin comparisons are clouded by separation‑related and restructuring items; conservative analysis should use adjusted metrics only if management’s allocation of separation costs to segments is disclosed (not present in the supplied evidence) or wait for Q3 2025 onward when Precision is reported as discontinued and comparatives are restated [1], [5].

Short judgement (evidence‑supported)
- The Precision separation created a simpler portfolio (two continuing segments) and enabled a pronounced shareholder‑return policy during the spin, but the supplied evidence does not demonstrate clear, immediate operational strengthening (higher segment reinvestment, reallocated capex/R&D, or materially improved segment margins) of the remaining businesses. IOS retains the strongest unit economics, but its revenue momentum in Q2 2025 was flat and margins declined versus 2024 in the supplied figures; thus the separation’s primary observable effects were governance/capital‑allocation shifts rather than documented near‑term performance acceleration of the remaining units [1], [2], [4], [11].

Evidence gaps and limitations (required by brief)
- No definitive full‑year 2024 segment revenue and operating income figures that reconcile with FY‑2023 segment totals in the supplied evidence: the FY‑2024 segment numbers present in the supplied FY‑2024 press release are inconsistent in magnitude with the FY‑2023 segment totals included elsewhere in the supplied findings, creating an inability to compute reliable 2023→2024 growth rates from the supplied evidence alone [2], [8].  
- No allocation of separation‑related costs to segments in the supplied facts (only consolidated separation costs are reported), preventing segment‑level adjusted margins that exclude separation costs [1], [6].  
- Missing post‑spin (Q3 2025 onward) segment‑level capex, R&D, and M&A guidance or actuals in the supplied evidence — these are needed to evaluate whether capital is being redeployed to strengthen the remaining segments.  
- No peer or industry benchmark margin and growth data in the supplied findings to contextualize Fortive’s segment economics versus competitors.  
- Proposed remedies / best alternative data sources (recommended): obtain Fortive’s 2024 Form 10‑K and the company’s Q4 2024 and FY‑2024 full segment note disclosures on SEC EDGAR (these will provide definitive FY‑2024 segment totals and any management restatements), Fortive’s Q3 2025 10‑Q and investor presentation (for post‑spin comparatives and discontinued‑operation restatements), and sell‑side / industry reports for peer benchmarking.

Appendix — calculation formulas and a quick consolidated Q2 2025 company reconstruction
- Operating margin (segment) = segment operating income ÷ segment revenue. (Used for each segment above.)  
- Q2 2025 company‑level reconstruction from supplied facts: Sum(segment operating income) = 166.7 + 93.2 + 39.1 = $299.0M; unallocated corporate costs (operating loss) = $76.8M → consolidated operating income (Q2 2025) = 299.0 − 76.8 = $222.2M. Q2 2025 consolidated revenue = $1,518.8M → consolidated operating margin (Q2 2025) = 222.2 ÷ 1,518.8 = 14.6% [1]. Note this consolidated calculation is sensitive to how separation costs and other corporate items are presented and is shown to illustrate the impact of unallocated corporate costs in the supplied facts [1].

# vTv Therapeutics Inc. — Equity‑Financing and Dilution Profile (evidence‑based)

## Executive summary
- The legal entity is vTv Therapeutics Inc., ticker VTVT, listed on NASDAQ. [1]  
- Reported GAAP total share‑based compensation rose from $2,757,000 in fiscal 2024 to $3,775,000 in fiscal 2025 — an absolute increase of $1,018,000 (≈36.9%). This is the available audited year‑to‑year comparison in the filings; a 2023 figure is not present in the available evidence so the requested 2023→2024 comparison cannot be computed from the provided sources. [2], [3]  
- Quarterly breakdowns (stock‑based compensation split to Research & Development and General & Administrative for Q3 2024 and Q3 2025) are not reported in the provided disclosures; the Q3 2025 Form 10‑Q supplies other quarter metrics and the outstanding share count but does not disclose the per‑quarter R&D/G&A stock‑based compensation line items needed for the requested Q3→Q3 calculation. Consequently the Q3‑to‑Q3 summed comparison cannot be completed from the available evidence. [5]  
- Disclosed option grants during the period include: a June 10, 2025 grant of an option to purchase 4,000 shares (vesting on the one‑year anniversary or the next AGM, whichever is sooner) and a Board amendment providing each non‑employee director an option to purchase 8,000 shares (or equivalent in RSUs/cash), vesting monthly over three years. Summary compensation tables show very large option award values to executives (PEO option awards reported as $5,601,712 in 2025 versus $2,949,001 in 2024), suggesting materially larger equity grants to management in 2025. Exercise prices, per‑grant share counts beyond those noted, expirations, and comprehensive outstanding warrant details are not disclosed in the provided findings. [4]  
- The only fully confirmed basic share count from the filings is 3,938,018 Class A shares outstanding as of September 30, 2025. Known, discrete option grants (4,000 shares) would cause immaterial dilution by themselves (~0.10% incremental shares). However, the disclosure of a large $80 million financing involving Class A shares and pre‑funded warrants in 2025 (reported in a recent 8‑K summary) indicates potential for materially larger dilution that cannot be quantified from the available summaries because counts, strike prices and terms are not provided. [5], [6]

The sections below present the numerical calculations that are possible from the evidence, an analysis of option grant terms that are disclosed, a constrained dilution model using only documented instruments, a sensitivity sketch (for documented items only), and an explicit list of evidence gaps that prevent a full, definitive dilution calculation.

## Legal entity and ticker
vTv Therapeutics Inc. is the legal entity; the company’s NASDAQ ticker is VTVT. [1]

## Full‑year share‑based compensation (audited GAAP figures)

Year comparison requested by brief: 2023 → 2024
- Evidence gap: no FY2023 total share‑based compensation figure is present in the provided findings, so the requested 2023→2024 computation cannot be completed from the available sources. [2]

Available audited comparison (2024 → 2025)
- Fiscal 2024 total share‑based compensation (GAAP, audited) = $2,757,000.  
- Fiscal 2025 total share‑based compensation (GAAP, audited) = $3,775,000.  
- Absolute increase = $3,775,000 − $2,757,000 = $1,018,000.  
- Percentage increase = $1,018,000 / $2,757,000 = 36.9% (approx).

Table 1 — Full‑year share‑based compensation (audited; available data)
| Fiscal year | Total share‑based compensation (GAAP) | Absolute change vs prior year | % change vs prior year |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2024 | $2,757,000 | — | — |
| 2025 | $3,775,000 | $1,018,000 | +36.9% |

Sources for table: FY totals and the FY change note. [2], [3]

## Q3‑to‑Q3 stock‑based compensation (R&D + G&A)
The brief requested a Q3 (earlier year) → Q3 (later year) comparison by summing Research & Development and General & Administrative stock‑based compensation for each quarter.

- Evidence gap: The filings available in the evidence set (including the September 30, 2025 Form 10‑Q) do not supply line‑item quarterly breakdowns of stock‑based compensation split between R&D and G&A for Q3 2024 or Q3 2025 in the facts provided. Therefore the requested Q3‑to‑Q3 summed numeric comparison cannot be computed from the provided findings. The Q3 2025 10‑Q does provide other quarterly metrics (operating expenses, net loss, and basic shares outstanding) but not the R&D/G&A stock‑based compensation split needed. [5]

Source: absence of per‑quarter R&D/G&A stock‑based compensation figures in the provided Form 10‑Q extract. [5]

## Disclosed option grants and compensation award details (what is available)
- June 10, 2025: option to purchase 4,000 shares granted; vesting on the one‑year anniversary of the grant date or the annual meeting of stockholders following the grant date, whichever is sooner. [4]  
- 2025 Board amendment (non‑employee director compensation): each non‑employee director receives an option to purchase 8,000 shares (or equivalent in restricted stock, RSUs, or cash), vesting monthly over a three‑year period. The number of non‑employee directors and therefore aggregate potential shares from this program are not stated in the provided facts. [4]  
- Summary compensation disclosures show substantially larger option award values to executives in 2025 than 2024 (PEO option awards reported as $5,601,712 in 2025 vs $2,949,001 in 2024; CFO option awards reported $928,619 in 2024). These dollar values are presented in the summary compensation table (likely representing grant‐date fair value of option awards disclosed for executives). [4]

What the disclosed grant details imply (qualified by available evidence)
- Timing and size (dollar value) of executive option awards materially increased in 2025 versus 2024, as reflected in the summary compensation table; this is consistent with a shift toward larger equity awards to executives in 2025. [4]  
- Director awards (8,000 options each, vesting monthly over three years) signal continued use of equity instruments as part of non‑employee director compensation and a multi‑year retention schedule. [4]  
- The single small employee grant that is numerically specified (4,000 shares) has a relatively short‑form retention condition (one‑year or next AGM vesting), indicating a short‑term retention/incentive structure for that grant. [4]  
- Absent exercise prices, expiration dates, and per‑grant share counts for the large executive option awards, the inferences about moneyness (grants at/above/below market at grant) and the degree to which option awards substitute for cash compensation cannot be definitively established from the provided evidence. The substantial increase in option award dollar value to the CEO between 2024 and 2025 suggests heavier reliance on equity as incentive/retention compensation for management in 2025. [4]

## Outstanding dilutive instruments — documented pieces and limits of the record
Documented, verifiable items from the findings:
- Class A common shares outstanding: 3,938,018 as of September 30, 2025 (basic share count). [5]  
- Documented option grants: the 4,000‑share grant (June 10, 2025) and Board‑level change setting 8,000 options per non‑employee director (vesting monthly over 3 years). [4]  
- Corporate financing event reported in recent 8‑K(s) describing an approximately $80 million private placement of Class A common shares and pre‑funded warrants (summary reported); the filings referenced in the tracking summary indicate such a financing existed but the provided facts do not include the number of shares or warrants issued, exercise prices, expiration dates, or the exact dilutive impact. [6]

Not disclosed / evidence gaps (critical for a complete dilutive instruments schedule)
- Comprehensive list of outstanding options (total number outstanding), exercise prices, grant dates, grant date fair values by grant, expiration dates, vesting schedules (beyond the two items above), and grantee classes.  
- Number, strike/exercise price, expiration and other terms of any outstanding warrants (including pre‑funded warrants) and their moneyness.  
- Any outstanding convertible securities (notes, preferred stock) and their conversion terms.  
Because of these gaps, a full accounting of outstanding dilutive instruments (as requested by the brief) cannot be produced from the available evidence. [4], [5], [6]

## Dilution modeling (restricted to documented instruments)
Given the incomplete instrument schedule, the dilution model below is conservative and uses only verified counts.

Base (documented) shares outstanding (basic): 3,938,018 (Class A, as of 9/30/25). [5]

Documented incremental instruments (counts confirmed in filings):
- June 10, 2025 option grant: 4,000 shares (vesting condition noted). [4]  
- Director program: 8,000 options per non‑employee director (number of directors not provided — excluded from numeric model). [4]

Scenario A — Exercise of documented 4,000 option grant (the only discrete option count provided)
- Pro‑forma shares = 3,938,018 + 4,000 = 3,942,018.  
- Incremental shares = 4,000.  
- Percentage dilution to existing holders = 4,000 / 3,938,018 ≈ 0.1016% (≈0.10% dilution).  
- Cash proceeds to company if exercised: cannot be computed — exercise price for the 4,000‑share option is not provided in the available evidence. [4]

Scenario B — Exercise of all documented options where counts are unknown (not computable)
- Evidence gap: aggregate outstanding option count, warrants and their exercise prices are not provided; therefore a full “all in‑the‑money” or “all outstanding” exercise model cannot be computed from the provided facts. [4], [6]

Sensitivity for the single documented option grant (4,000 shares)
- 25% exercise (1,000 shares): incremental dilution ≈ 0.025% of outstanding shares.  
- 50% exercise (2,000 shares): incremental dilution ≈ 0.051%.  
- 75% exercise (3,000 shares): incremental dilution ≈ 0.076%.  
- 100% exercise (4,000 shares): incremental dilution ≈ 0.102%.  
Cash proceeds and net dilution per dollar raised: cannot be computed for any of these partial exercise scenarios because exercise prices are not disclosed. [4]

Qualitative observation on the larger, undisclosed financing and warrant overhang
- The summary reporting of an $80 million financing involving Class A shares and pre‑funded warrants signals a potentially material future dilution source if shares/warrants are exercised or if warrants convert — but the required instrument counts and terms to quantify that dilution are not in the provided evidence, so the magnitude, timing and cash proceeds from that event cannot be modeled here. [6]

## Effects on shareholder dilution risk, EPS and market signaling (synthesis)
- Near‑term dilution magnitude (documented portion): trivially small based on the documented, specific option counts (4,000 shares), producing ≈0.10% incremental dilution if exercised; director plan changes and the small employee grant disclosed do not materially move the share base by themselves. [4], [5]  
- Longer‑term dilution risk: materially dependent on undisclosed items. The increase in total share‑based compensation (≈36.9% year‑over‑year, 2024→2025) and the larger option award values to executives suggest an uptick in equity use for compensation; coupled with the reported $80 million financing with pre‑funded warrants, there is a credible pathway to meaningful dilution, but quantification is not possible from the available facts. [2], [3], [4], [6]  
- Earnings per share (EPS) impact: with a small documented incremental share count, the near‑term EPS effect from the disclosed 4,000 options is negligible. However, if the financing and pre‑funded‑warrant instruments noted in the financing summaries convert/exercise into shares, the EPS dilution could become material; the filings provided do not include the number of shares/warrants and exercise terms, so a back‑of‑envelope EPS calculation cannot be performed with certainty. [2], [5], [6]  
- Market signaling and governance risks: larger executive option award values in 2025 relative to 2024 indicate management is receiving more compensation in equity form; combined with director grant program changes this signals reliance on equity for retention and governance alignment. The presence of a large financing with pre‑funded warrants can create an “overhang” that markets perceive as potential future supply, risking dilution fatigue among investors if and when the company must replenish equity plans or if warrants convert. Absent specific plan replenishment disclosures, the degree of governance risk (e.g., shareholder approval needs, equity plan limits) cannot be fully evaluated from the evidence. [4], [6]  
- Reliance on equity vs other financing: evidence shows both increased equity‑based compensation and a sizable private placement that included pre‑funded warrants — together, these items point to meaningful use of equity instruments both for compensation and for financing in 2025. Whether that pattern continues is not determinable from the provided findings, but the 2024→2025 trends documented indicate materially greater reliance on equity in 2025 than in 2024. [2], [3], [4], [6]

## Evidence gaps (material items missing from the available findings)
The following items are necessary to fully satisfy the research brief but are not present in the provided evidence:
- Fiscal 2023 total share‑based compensation (audited GAAP) — prevents 2023→2024 full‑year comparison. [2]  
- Quarterly line‑item stock‑based compensation amounts split between Research & Development and General & Administrative for Q3 2024 and Q3 2025 — prevents Q3→Q3 summed comparison. [5]  
- Comprehensive schedule of all outstanding dilutive instruments: total outstanding stock options (by grant and exercise price), RSUs/restricted stock, warrants (including pre‑funded warrants) with counts, exercise/pre‑funding prices, expiration dates, vesting/convertibility conditions and typical per‑grant grant‑date fair values. [4], [6]  
- Exercise prices and expected proceeds for exercise of documented instruments (including the 4,000 option grant and any warrants or pre‑funded warrants). [4], [6]  
- Number of non‑employee directors to compute aggregate potential shares from the 8,000‑option per‑director program. [4]  
- Detailed 8‑K/Exhibit text for the reported $80M financing (to extract number of shares/warrants issued, strike prices, expiry, and any anti‑dilution or registration arrangements). [6]

Because those items are missing, several deliverables requested in the brief (complete dilutive instrument schedule; full pro forma fully diluted share count under “all outstanding exercised” scenarios; cash proceeds from full exercise; net dilution per dollar raised) cannot be computed from the evidence provided.

## Conclusion — strategic and shareholder‑impact implications (concise)
- vTv is using equity more intensively in 2025 than it did in 2024: total GAAP share‑based compensation grew ~36.9% from $2.757M to $3.775M (2024→2025), and executive option award values shown in the summary compensation table rose materially in 2025, indicating elevated equity grants to management as a retention/incentive tool. [2], [4]  
- The discrete documented option grants (4,000 shares; 8,000 options per director plan) imply modest direct dilution from those line items alone (the 4,000 grant is ~0.10% of shares outstanding), but the company also engaged in a large financing reported as ~$80M with pre‑funded warrants — an instrument class that can produce material dilution depending on counts and exercise terms. The available evidence does not provide those counts or strike prices, so material dilution from the financing cannot be quantified here. [4], [5], [6]  
- For existing shareholders, the likely implication is increased dilution risk relative to 2024 driven by (a) higher aggregate equity compensation, and (b) recent financing activity that introduced pre‑funded‑warrant overhang. The near‑term EPS/dilution effect from the specifically documented option grants is negligible, but the broader financing and elevated executive option award values create an overhang risk that could be meaningful if and when those instruments convert or further equity issuances occur. [2], [4], [6]  
- Final assessment: vTv’s observable strategy in 2025 strongly favors using equity both for compensation (to retain and incentivize executives and directors) and as a financing tool. That approach conserves cash but transfers dilution risk to shareholders; the magnitude and timing of that risk hinge on instrument counts and exercise terms that are not disclosed in the provided findings. Absent disclosure of the full instrument schedule and terms, shareholders face uncertainty about potential future dilution and its effect on per‑share metrics.

# Cold‑weather fleet selection for Mongolia: Caterpillar, Komatsu, Volvo CE and Russian alternatives (focus: sustained −40 °C open‑pit mining)

Executive summary
- For sustained operation near −40 °C, Volvo CE and Russian heavy‑duty mining designs (BelAZ ultra‑class examples, and factory pre‑heated systems on some Russian trucks) document components and kits explicitly rated at or below −40 °C; Caterpillar and Komatsu provide winterization packages and dealer support in Mongolia but many OEM standard cold packages documented in evidence are rated to between about −32 °C and −35 °C and therefore require confirmed arctic kit options or aftermarket heaters for reliable continuous operation at −40 °C. [21], [1], [5], [24], [27]  
- Local support in Mongolia is already established for Caterpillar (Barloworld Mongolia) and Komatsu (Transwest Mongolia), including component rebuild centres, parts warehouses, field service teams and dealer training; Volvo CE offers arctic kits and training globally but evidence of a dedicated Volvo dealer network capacity in Ulaanbaatar is not documented in the findings. [6], [7], [14], [15], [16], [17], [47]  
- Russian/CIS alternatives (BelAZ, KAMAZ and other Russian producers) have documented cold‑start and heater technologies and a visible presence in Mongolia (many BelAZ trucks in use and a local distributor), but regional trade, sanctions and logistics complexities introduce measurable procurement and operational risks that must be weighed against lower list prices and cold‑rating claims. [27], [29], [30], [36], [39], [44]

See "Evidence gaps" at the end for the specific contact requests required to close these gaps.

Structure of this report
- Manufacturer summaries (Caterpillar, Komatsu, Volvo CE) with representative model shortlists and documented cold‑weather features.  
- Russian/CIS alternatives (BelAZ, KAMAZ) and regional trade considerations.  
- Cross‑topic synthesis: cold‑start and hydraulic behavior, batteries and heaters, local service & training, parts and repair turnaround, fuel behaviour at −40 °C, and practical recommendations.  
- Evidence gaps and suggested local contacts.

## 1. Manufacturer summaries and representative models

### 1.1 Caterpillar — documented cold features, models and Mongolia presence
- Representative mining classes and model examples found in the evidence: mid‑class excavator — Cat 320D / 320D L (excavator class commonly used in construction/mining), large hydraulic shovel — Cat 6060 (next‑generation hydraulic mining shovel delivered to a Mongolian mine), large haul truck class evidence: Cat 777 dump truck and Cat 793F mining truck referenced in deliveries and spec material. [1], [6], [5]  
- Cold‑weather documentation and factory/optional features in evidence: the 320D/320D L is offered with a cold‑weather package rated to −32 °C and includes air starting plus two additional maintenance‑free batteries; other Cat models (793F) show antifreeze/coolant protection to −35 °C and engine coolant/oil heaters for cold starts. Caterpillar winter guidance recommends use of #1 diesel or winter‑blended fuel, approved fuel additives to prevent gelling, daily tank‑fill practice to avoid condensation and use of approved battery, coolant and oil heaters. Cat also publishes operator and service training programmes and Customer Value Agreements (CVAs) for mining that keep parts on hand and provide planned maintenance. [1], [5], [2], [9], [8]  
- Mongolia dealer/service capability evidence: Barloworld Mongolia is the official Cat dealer in Mongolia; it operates a Component Rebuild Centre (CRC) in Ulaanbaatar and multiple regional branches and has delivered large Cat mining equipment to Mongolian mines. Barloworld offers CVAs for mining fleets including parts inventory, planned maintenance kits and on‑site dealer services. [7], [6], [47]  

(Reference used: Cat 320D/320D L cold package and related Cat winter/delivery / dealer evidence) [1], [2], [6], [5], [7], [9], [8], [47]

- Representative examples: Komatsu HM400‑5 articulated dump truck (44.1 t payload, SAA6D140E‑7 engine with ~473 hp gross) and Komatsu HB365LC‑3 hybrid hydraulic excavator (271 hp gross Tier 4 Final engine) are representative Komatsu mining/off‑highway products present in the documentation. (Reference used: Komatsu HM400/HB365 brochures and Transwest/KOMCAT dealer evidence) [11], [12], [14], [15], [16], [17], [19], [18], [20]

### 1.3 Volvo Construction Equipment — cold‑rating, arctic kits and testing
- Volvo CE documents arctic‑grade options that are directly relevant to −40 °C operation: Volvo offers engine block heaters, diesel‑powered coolant heaters, water‑separator heaters and hoses rated to −40 °C; Volvo recommends synthetic/multi‑grade hydraulic and engine oils for sub‑zero operation, dedicated winter/arctic diesel and filling tanks to >70% to reduce condensation; and Volvo documents increasing coolant concentration to 50% for protection down to −50 °C in guidance. ## 2. Cold‑weather operational reliability and readiness (−40 °C focus)

Synthesis of documented OEM capabilities and observed field testing
- OEM documented cold packages cover a range: Volvo documents arctic‑rated hoses and full immersion heater kits rated to −40 °C and presents testing well below −30 °C; BelAZ documents full system protection to −50 °C for at least one ultra‑class model; Caterpillar’s documented model cold packages cited are typically rated to about −32 °C (320D cold package) and Cat mining truck base cold protection to about −35 °C on some models, though Caterpillar winter guidance recommends additional heaters and practices to extend low‑temperature operability; Komatsu brochures include cooling and fan features that improve efficiency in cool climates but explicit −40 °C rating statements in the provided Komatsu materials are not shown. This means that for continuous operation at sustained −40 °C, Volvo arctic kits and BelAZ designs have explicit documented low‑temperature ratings in the evidence, while Cat and Komatsu require confirmation of available arctic‑rated options beyond the standard documented cold packages. [21], [27], [1], [5], [12]  
- Documented cold‑start systems and pre‑heaters: Caterpillar recommends block heaters (1,250–1,500 W ranges referenced by Cat‑dealer guidance) and the use of approved battery, coolant and oil heaters; Volvo lists engine block heaters and diesel‑powered coolant heaters; KAMAZ and some Russian truck designs document fuel‑heating/pre‑heater systems able to heat fuel to 60–80 °C before injection to enable reliable cold starts. These are the primary mechanical mitigations cited in the evidence for sub‑zero starting. [3], [21], [32]  
- Batteries and cranking: a general industry reference in the findings reports that battery available starting power drops sharply as temperature falls (a fully charged battery at −1.4 °F ≈ −18 °C has roughly 40% of normal starting power, and at −20.2 °F ≈ −29 °C only about 18% remaining), highlighting the need for additional batteries, battery heaters, air or electric starts and/or auxiliary starting systems for −40 °C conditions. Caterpillar documents use of two additional maintenance‑free batteries in a cold package on the 320D and the inclusion of glow plugs on some models. [49], [1], [4]  
- Hydraulic behavior and oils: Volvo recommends synthetic or multi‑grade hydraulic and engine oils for sub‑zero operation and arctic hoses rated to −40 °C; Cat guidance recommends warming fluids before heavy work and using extended‑life coolant and heaters. Viscous fan clutches or other temperature‑responsive cooling components (documented on Komatsu HB365LC‑3) help manage engine temperatures and oil thermal state in cold ambient conditions. Evidence of specific viscosity grades, pump priming behaviour at −40 °C or quantified hydraulic response times at −40 °C is not provided. [21], [3], [12], [2]  

Known failure modes and operational limitations in evidence
- Diesel gelling and filter plugging: Cenex guidance in the evidence indicates No.2 diesel cloud points and CFPP characteristics that make No.2 diesel vulnerable well above −40 °C, and recommends straight No.1 diesel when temperatures fall below ~−30 °F (~−34 °C) to avoid gelling. Caterpillar’s winter checklist likewise recommends #1 diesel or winter‑blended fuel and approved additives; Volvo recommends dedicated winter/arctic diesel. Failure modes include fuel gelling, water in fuel filters/plugging and DEF freezing for SCR systems (DEF freezes at ~12 °F / −11 °C), which is relevant for Tier 4 machines that use DEF unless machine systems provide heaters/evacuation procedures. Evidence documents machine heater strategies and daily draining of fuel water separators as mitigations. [50], [2], [21]  
- DEF (diesel exhaust fluid) freeze risk is noted generally in the evidence (DEF freeze point ~12 °F) and construction equipment guidance notes that machines with internal tank heaters evacuate DEF before shutdown. Specific OEM procedures at −40 °C for DEF systems in the cited materials are not detailed. [49], [2]  

Implication for −40 °C continuous operation
- To operate continuously at or near −40 °C, OEM documented base cold packages rated to −32 to −35 °C (Cat 320D, Cat 793F) are insufficient per the evidence without additional arctic kits, immersion heaters and dedicated fuel systems; Volvo’s documented arctic kits (rated to −40 °C or designed to protect to −50 °C coolant concentrations) and BelAZ’s documented −50 °C protection are the only items in the evidence that directly claim protective coverage at or below −40 °C. Komatsu material in the evidence demonstrates design features favorable to cool‑temperature efficiency but does not document a factory arctic kit rating to −40 °C in the provided documents. [1], [5], [21], [24], [27], [12]

- Caterpillar / Barloworld Mongolia: Barloworld Mongolia is the official Caterpillar dealer in Mongolia, operates a Component Rebuild Centre (CRC) in Ulaanbaatar that performs critical component repairs and rebuilds, maintains branches in multiple mining provinces and has delivered major Cat mining equipment to Mongolian mines (including Cat 6060 shovels and Cat 777 trucks). Cat CVAs for mining are documented and provide parts-on‑hand, planned maintenance kits and dealer labour options. The evidence supports strong on‑island rebuild capability and organized warranty/service programs but does not specify typical response times to remote breakdowns or the number of mobile service teams available. [7], [6], [47], [8]  
- Komatsu / Transwest Mongolia and KOMCAT: Transwest Mongolia is an authorized Komatsu dealer with a Ulaanbaatar parts warehouse (stocks undercarriage parts), field service teams and rebuild shops able to repair diesel engines, transmissions, hydraulic cylinders and electrical components; Transwest documents over 60 factory‑trained tradespeople supporting field service and has run Komatsu Academy technical instructor training locally. KOMCAT provides fleet‑management and overhaul workshops including extensive hydraulic and engine overhaul capability. The evidence supports a robust Komatsu repair and parts presence in Ulaanbaatar with in‑country remanufacturing capacity, but specific guaranteed response times to remote sites are not documented in the evidence. [14], [15], [16], [17], [19], [18]  
- Volvo CE in Mongolia: Volvo CE publishes arctic kits and operator training but the evidence does not show a documented Volvo dealer network presence in Ulaanbaatar or on‑site rebuild capability comparable to the detail documented for Cat and Komatsu in the provided materials. [21], [26], [25]  
- Russian/CIS dealers & aftermarket in Mongolia: BelAZ has an established dealer/distributor presence (United BelAZ Machinery) and historical shipments of BelAZ trucks into Mongolian operations are recorded; aftermarket parts suppliers and specialist BelAZ parts providers (and case studies of local part-supplier partnerships) are documented. The evidence does not quantify the number of mobile service teams for these Russian brands. [27], [29], [30], [28], [38]  

Summary: Caterpillar (Barloworld) and Komatsu (Transwest/KOMCAT) have the most documented in‑country capability in Ulaanbaatar (component rebuild centre, parts warehouses and field teams). Volvo’s documented arctic technical capability is strong but the evidence does not document a similarly detailed Volvo dealer footprint in Ulaanbaatar. BelAZ has an active distributor and installed base in Mongolia. Specific response‑time guarantees and counts of mobile teams are absent from the evidence and listed as an evidence gap below. [7], [14], [15], [16], [27], [21]

Transwest documents an on‑site parts warehouse stocking OEM undercarriage parts for Komatsu and the ability to perform pin & bushing turns and other repair actions in country. A Mongolian spare‑parts supplier (Spareparts.mn) offers OEM and aftermarket parts and lists experience in sourcing engine, hydraulic and electrical parts. These items indicate options for consignment/spare pools and in‑country reman/rebuild capability. [47], [7], [17], [16], [38]  
- Documented limitations and missing specifics: the evidence does not provide precise inventory counts, SKU‑level on‑hand spare lists for Ulaanbaatar, or lead‑time tables for non‑stocked parts. Specifics on estimated turnaround times for major repairs (engine, hydraulic pump, final drives) are not provided. Evidence shows that component rebuilds can be materially cheaper than buying new (Barloworld claims up to 30% cheaper in one presentation), but does not quantify repair turnaround days for each class of repair. [47], [16]  

Implication
- Dealers in Ulaanbaatar can provide undercarriage items, common hydraulic and engine components, and component rebuild services that materially reduce downtime risk compared with purely import‑dependent strategies; however, for continuous −40 °C operation, explicit spare pools for arctic‑rated heaters, immersion heater elements, battery heater kits and winter fuel equipment must be verified with dealers because documentation of those parts’ local stocking and lead times is not present in the evidence. [17], [7], [38]

## 5. Fuel efficiency and diesel engine performance in extreme cold

Documented fuel‑related risks and mitigations
- Diesel gelling: Cenex evidence explains No.2 diesel cloud point and CFPP characteristics and recommends straight No.1 diesel when ambient temperatures go below about −30 °F (~−34 °C); cold‑flow improvers have effectiveness limits above that temperature. Caterpillar’s winter checklist similarly recommends #1 diesel or winter‑blended fuel plus approved additives, daily tank fills to reduce condensation and draining of fuel water separators at the end of each day. Volvo recommends using a dedicated winter or arctic diesel and maintaining fuel tanks above ~70% to limit condensation risk. KAMAZ documentation demonstrates fuel pre‑heating systems that heat fuel to 60–80 °C prior to injection as a cold‑start solution. These measures are the principal documented mitigations for gelling and cold‑start risks in the evidence. [50], [2], [21], [32]  
- Fuel‑consumption impacts: the evidence includes a high‑level vehicle example (BelAZ 75710 consumption estimate) and statements about fuel‑efficiency improvements for specific new Cat shovels, but it does not provide quantified, model‑specific percentage penalties in fuel consumption at −40 °C for the mainstream excavator and haul‑truck models in scope. The Cat 6060 shovel is documented to achieve 10–15% better fuel efficiency than its predecessor (but this is not a cold‑temperature penalty measurement). No measured, model‑specific fuel consumption penalties at −40 °C are present in the evidence. [27], [6]  
- DEF and aftertreatment: DEF freeze behaviour (freeze point ~12 °F / −11 °C) is noted generally in industry guidance; the evidence does not present OEM‑specific procedures for Tier‑4 machines at −40 °C beyond advising use of heated/evacuated DEF tanks where machines provide internal heaters. [49], [2]  

Operational best practices supported by the evidence
- Use No.1 diesel or appropriately winter‑blended fuels and approved cold‑flow additives when ambient temperatures approach or fall below the CFPP/cloud point ranges for local fuels; operate fuel‑heating/pre‑heating systems where available; keep tanks topped daily to avoid condensation and drain water separators after each day’s use; and equip machines with battery and coolant/oil heaters and insulated covers as specified by OEM arctic kits. These recommendations are supported by Caterpillar, Volvo and independent diesel‑fuel guidance in the evidence. [2], [21], [50], [32]  

Evidence gap: direct measured fuel‑efficiency penalties (percent change in L/h or t/km) for the specific excavator/hauler models at −40 °C are not present in the provided evidence.

What is documented
- Caterpillar: Cat offers operator, service‑technician and safety training programs, including customizable operator training, instructor‑led on‑site training and simulator training; Cat says operator courses can train 3–6 employees per session. Cat training is an available dealer/OEM option to upskill local staff. [9], [10]  
- Komatsu / Transwest: Transwest completed Komatsu Academy Asia Technical Instructor Qualification Course (TIQC) and has gold‑level instructor certification among staff, indicating availability of Komatsu‑standard instructor training in Mongolia and train‑the‑trainer capability. Transwest also runs in‑country remanufacture and technical training as part of its service offering. [19], [15], [16]  
- Volvo: Volvo operator training combines classroom instruction with field practice to improve safety and uptime; Volvo’s published training emphasis includes minimizing wear and operating machines to reduce costs. [26]  
- Local training capacity: Transwest and Barloworld both document in‑country technical capability (workshops, remanufacturing and component rebuild centres) that supports hands‑on technician training on large mining equipment; a dealer partnership for mine‑site support (MacLean & ULE) exemplifies specialist partnerships for site‑specific training/support arrangements. Specifics about training delivered in Mongolian or Russian languages, class durations, costs or throughput (number of technicians/operators trained per year) are not provided in the evidence. [16], [7], [48]  

Evidence gap: explicit statements that training is delivered in Mongolian or Russian (or both), precise course costs, timeframes, class sizes beyond the Cat statement and annual training capacity numbers for local dealers are not present in the given materials.

## 7. Commercial, supply‑chain and regional trade considerations for Russian alternatives

Key points supported by evidence
- Mongolia trade routes and customs: Mongolia’s land links run through Russia and China; rail routing is dominated by the Russian 1520 mm gauge (gauge change implications for some routes) and major road and rail links to China are frequently used for imports. Mongolia applies MFN customs duty (commonly ~5–10%), but a seasonal additional duty (15%) may apply between August 1 and April 1 according to one source; import documentation and tariff practices are variable and may allow exemptions for priority foreign‑invested projects. Evidence also documents existing dependence on Russian petroleum imports. These facts affect logistics, fuel sourcing and spare‑parts routing for any fleet. [44], [40], [41], [42], [43], [46]  
- Sanctions and political risk: independent analysis in the evidence notes that Western sanctions on Russia and Belarus target extractive industries and restrict certain equipment, finance and re‑export provisions. Evidence specifically points to increased costs and delays related to sanctions and that Western exporters may require “no re‑export to Russia” clauses, complicating transits that involve Russian territory or suppliers. OFAC listings (example in evidence: a Mongolia‑based company on an SDN list) and export restrictions were documented in the material, highlighting a non‑zero risk that political measures can disrupt parts or service flows tied to Russian suppliers. Evidence also records temporary Russian export restrictions in 2023‑2024 having caused immediate shortage anxiety in Mongolia’s mining sector in a historical context. [39], [37], [44]  
- Russia/CIS supplier presence vs risk tradeoff: BelAZ and other Russian/CIS vendors have strong installed bases and local dealer networks for some product lines in Mongolia (BelAZ number of vehicles in country documented), offering spare‑parts pipelines and local representation; however, evidence also notes logistics challenges (rail routing, seasonal duties, shifting tariff rates) and sanction‑related exposure that can increase lead times, costs and long‑term reliability of supply chains. For example, BelAZ shipments and local dealer operations are documented, but broader sanctions and logistics constraints are separately documented and raise procurement risk. [27], [29], [30], [39], [44]  

Supply‑chain routing and lead‑time implications
- The evidence supports that most imports transit either Chinese or Russian routes (with gauge and transhipment constraints noted) and that rail transit times to Mongolia commonly are 15–20 days in standard cases; however, seasonally higher customs duties and ad‑hoc export restrictions can materially change total lead time and landed cost estimates. The evidence does not provide SKU‑level lead‑time estimates for specific parts lines. [44], [43], [42]  

Implication
- Procuring Russian/CIS machines or parts can provide clear cold‑rating advantages documented for some models (BelAZ −50 °C rating) and local dealer presence, but buyers must weigh the documented political/logistics risks (sanctions, variable duties, railway routing constraints) that can add TCO volatility and spare‑parts availability risk over the equipment life. Detailed contractual protections and alternative sourcing plans (local aftermarket, consignment stock, rebuild programmes) are therefore strongly indicated. [27], [29], [39], [44], [47]

## 8. Practical recommendations (synthesis for fleet manager in Mongolia)

1. Prioritize machines that have documented arctic kits rated to or below −40 °C or confirm OEM‑approved retrofit arctic kits:
   - Volvo A45G with Siberian/arctic kit and Volvo guidance documents protection to −40/−50 °C are explicit in the evidence and therefore present a lower‑uncertainty option for −40 °C operation if the kit is procured and installed. [24], [21]  
   - BelAZ ultra‑class trucks document −50 °C protection for at least one model; where haul capacity and local distributor support match task requirements, BelAZ is documented as a candidate for extreme cold. [27], [29], [30]  
   - Caterpillar and Komatsu machines documented in the evidence have documented cold packages to around −32 to −35 °C; to use them at −40 °C, require documented OEM arctic kit options or add robust aftermarket heater packages (engine/coolant/oil heaters, battery heaters, fuel heaters and insulated hoses) and confirm dealer stocking of these items. [1], [5], [21], [12]

2. Use dealer CVAs and local component rebuild capability to reduce downtime risk:
   - Structure procurement with Cat CVAs or Komatsu service agreements that include on‑site PM kits, parts consignment and rebuild commitments where possible; validate local CRC and Transwest rebuild throughput and ask for guaranteed on‑site spares lists for arctic heaters, battery kits and fuel heating components. Evidence shows both Barloworld and Transwest provide rebuild and inventory services. [47], [16], [7], [14], [15]

3. Fuel strategy and cold‑flow mitigation:
   - For routine operation at −40 °C, plan on using No.1 diesel or dedicated arctic diesel blends and approved cold‑flow additives, implement fuel‑heating systems or pre‑heaters, keep tanks >70% to reduce condensation and implement a strict daily fuel‑water separator draining routine; these are explicit mitigations in Caterpillar, Volvo and diesel‑fuel guidance. Also verify DEF system heaters or shutdown/evacuation procedures for Tier‑4 machines since DEF freezes at much higher temperatures. [50], [2], [21]

4. Local spares & training investments:
   - Require suppliers to commit to local consignment spare pools for critical arctic items (immersion heater elements, battery heater kits, fuel heaters, fuel‑line insulation, arctic hoses) and to provide train‑the‑trainer courses locally. Evidence shows Cat, Komatsu and local dealers run training programs and have instructors/curricula that can be used; Transwest and Barloworld have in‑country rebuild and training capability. Negotiate explicit stocking and response‑time commitments in contracts. [9], [10], [19], [16], [7]

5. Contractual protections for Russian/CIS procurement:
   - If acquiring BelAZ or KAMAZ equipment, require contractual remedies and alternative parts‑supply clauses to mitigate sanctions/logistics risk (e.g., local parts consignment, allowed third‑party rebuilds, multi‑year parts commitments). Evidence documents both the operational cold‑rating advantages of some Russian models and the documented regional sanctions/logistics complications that elevate procurement risk. [27], [29], [39], [44]

- For continuous year‑round operation at sustained −40 °C, the evidence supports prioritizing machines with documented arctic ratings at or below −40 °C (Volvo arctic kits and BelAZ −50 °C documented protection) or requiring verified, OEM‑approved retrofit arctic kits and local dealer commitments for Cat and Komatsu machines whose documented base cold packages are rated in the −32 to −35 °C range.
