# Evolution of vertical‑integration strategies (2018–2024): Barry Callebaut, Cargill, Olam — upstream investments, sustainability certification, EUDR readiness, and premium‑supply positioning

Executive summary  
This report synthesizes verified, source‑level evidence (company reports, sector case studies, donor/project pages and reputable trade press) to compare how Barry Callebaut, Cargill and Olam evolved their vertical‑integration strategies from 2018–2024, with emphasis on upstream investments in West African cocoa cooperatives, participation in sustainability/certification programmes, capital investments in origin‑country processing (Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana), documented farmer income outcomes, EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) responses (traceability and mapping), and implications for premium chocolate supply. Key takeaways:
- All three traders/processors increased upstream vertical integration and digital/first‑mile traceability between 2018–2024, but differ in scale, reporting detail and claims on direct sourcing versus broker purchases. Evidence quality varies: company self‑reports predominate; where independent studies exist they are cited explicitly.
- Cargill and Olam show explicit, reported capital projects with project-level financing figures for West Africa; Barry documents capacity expansions but provides fewer public project‑level capex figures in the evidence set.
- Measured farmer income outcomes are reported by all three, but sources mix company monitoring, programme reports and limited independent studies; sample sizes and methodologies are variably disclosed and so affect confidence in attribution.
- Each company has deployed digital first‑mile traceability and mapping to meet EUDR requirements, with Olam and Barry making stronger public claims of near‑complete farm‑level traceability for direct supply; Cargill reports first‑purchase‑point traceability and ongoing scaling efforts.
- Evidence of premium‑supply commercial positioning is clearest for Barry (renewed long‑term customer agreements); direct evidence linking Cargill/Olam to preferred‑supplier status with Lindt, Ferrero, Mondelēz is not present in the reviewed findings.

The body of the report below presents company‑level syntheses (evidence and data quality notes), a cross‑company comparison, explicit evidence gaps, and a short methodology/data‑quality section.

## 1. Barry Callebaut (summary of evolution 2018–2024)

- Strategic evolution and upstream investments: Barry expanded upstream integration via its Forever Chocolate programme, steadily enlarging farmer coverage, agroforestry and mapping activities between 2018 and 2024; its reports show additions of farmers, hectares and agroforestry plots and continuing investments in premiums and farmer services. Barry reports adding almost 120,000 new cocoa farmers to sustainability programmes (a 35% increase) and mapping hundreds of thousands of farm plots over 2022–24, while reporting large numbers of farmers lifted above poverty‑line thresholds under its monitoring approach. [1], [2], [3]

- Direct‑sourced versus broker‑purchased cocoa (reported definitions and volumes): An IDH traceability case study (December 2020) reports that 40% of Barry Callebaut’s cocoa was sourced through its “direct supply chain” (i.e., directly procured by Barry rather than purchased via intermediaries/brokers); the report also documents SAP‑based Katchilè as the company’s batch/farmer data application. Barry’s own reporting shows a mix of sustainability‑verified volumes and broad product metrics (e.g., >50% of products sold containing 100% sustainable/verified cocoa in the 2023/24 reporting year), but the firm does not provide a single consolidated metric in the supplied evidence that converts its total cocoa‑tonnage purchases into a contemporaneous metric‑tonnes split (direct vs broker) for 2018–2024. This creates a reporting gap between the 40% direct‑supply figure (IDH, 2020) and later sustainability coverage claims. Data sources: IDH case study (40% direct supply) and Barry sustainability/Forever Chocolate reports (sustainable product percentages; mapping and traceability counts). [4], [1], [3]

- Origin‑country processing capex (Côte d’Ivoire & Ghana): Barry’s 2018/19 annual report documents opening a cocoa‑processing unit in Abidjan in March 2019 that raised local capacity materially (report states capacity increased by >40% by 2022), but the available evidence does not disclose a project‑level capital expenditure amount for that Abidjan unit in the supplied documents. Barry’s other 2022–24 reports describe broadened on‑the‑ground investments (agroforestry hectares, premium payments and mapping) but do not present a project‑level capex figure for a new Ghana/CI processing plant in the evidence set. [5], [1]

- Farmer income outcomes and evaluation detail: Barry reports progress against poverty thresholds: for example, an annual figure that 269,762 farmers in its supply chain are no longer in poverty (USD 2.15/day line) and later reporting (2024/25) that 557,739 farmers were above the poverty line; Forever Chocolate reports CHF 43.5 million in premiums paid for Cocoa Horizons products in 2023/24 and mapping claims of 669,174 farm plots in 2023/24. However, the supplied evidence contains limited information on independent baseline vs endline methodologies, counterfactuals or systematic independent impact evaluations tied to representative samples (Barry’s Agrilogic white paper documents a farmer survey of 561 Ivorian farmers but is limited in scope). Therefore attribution confidence is moderate for company‑reported outcomes but lower for independent causal attribution. [1], [3], [23], [24]

- EUDR / traceability responses (technology and mapping): Barry reports that traceability to farm level for cocoa volumes in its direct supply chain reached ~83% in 2023/24 and that mapping initiatives expanded to cover hundreds of thousands of cocoa farm plots (e.g., 669,174 plots reported for 2023/24), with the company using its Katchilè (SAP‑based) application for batch traceability and farmer data collection per the IDH traceability case study. Barry also reported in 2024/25 that it had achieved the traceability level required by the EU Deforestation Regulation for mapped volumes and that for volumes supplied to facilities in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire it achieved 100% deforestation‑free sourcing in 2024/25; CDP reporting shows a small share of reported volume certified as deforestation‑free and a portion from unknown origins (see Data quality and gaps). [3], [4], [1], [8]

- Commercial/premium customer positioning: Barry publicly renewed long‑term strategic supply agreements with large customers (e.g., Mars Wrigley LAN renewed 9 October 2023, and Unilever extended a long‑term global agreement in June 2023) demonstrating continued market leadership in supplying large confectionery and industrial customers and implying access to scale demand for sustainably‑sourced cocoa; the company’s reporting highlights premium receipts from Cocoa Horizons and digital premium payments. Direct evidence of preferred‑supplier status with Lindt, Ferrero or Mondelēz was not present in the supplied evidence. [6], [7], [3]

Data‑quality notes (Barry): most figures are company‑reported via annual/sustainability progress reports; the IDH case study provides an external traceability snapshot (2020). Where available, sample sizes are limited (e.g., Agrilogic farmer survey: 561 farmers). Several Barry metrics (e.g., number of farmers above poverty) are internally computed and reported without detailed independent baseline/endline study documentation in the supplied evidence.

## 2. Cargill (summary of evolution 2018–2024)

- Strategic evolution and upstream investments: Cargill continued to scale first‑mile services, farmer coaching and digital traceability (Promise platform and CocoaWise™ 360), linking farmers to financial services and expanding mapping and deforestation‑risk assessments in its direct supply chain while committing to EUDR readiness roadmaps. Cargill reports active farmer programmes across Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana with hundreds of thousands of farmers engaged in its Cocoa Promise network over the decade. [9], [14]

- Direct‑sourced versus broker‑purchased cocoa (definitions and reported volumes): An IDH case study (Cargill) reported an approximate 60% share of Cargill’s cocoa supply chain as “directly sourced” versus ~40% indirectly sourced (bought via intermediaries) in the period covered by that case study. Cargill’s own 2023/24 reporting provides crop‑year sourcing numbers by country (e.g., 98,619 metric tonnes from Côte d’Ivoire and 6,079 metric tonnes from Ghana in 2023/24) and reports 25,376 metric tonnes of cocoa directly sourced and traceable from farm to first purchase point in the 2023/24 crop year (Cargill’s definitions place “first point of purchase” as the first buying location where traceability records are attached). The IDH 60/40 snapshot and Cargill’s crop‑year tonne figures are both company‑linked reports but use differing units and scopes; they cannot be algebraically reconciled into a single, authoritative % direct vs broker number for every year 2018–2024 using only the supplied evidence. [13], [9]

- Origin‑country processing capex (Côte d’Ivoire & Ghana): Cargill publicly announced and executed multi‑year investments in West African processing: in 2019 an investment package of US$113 million was announced (US$100 million for a 50% capacity increase at Yopougon, Côte d’Ivoire; US$13 million for a 20% capacity increase at Tema, Ghana), and Cargill reported completing a US$100 million expansion of its Yopougon cocoa‑processing facility in November 2021 (with the Tema expansion commissioning also reported in November 2021). Cargill’s reporting associated part of these investments with announced linked investments in farmer coaching and traceability (e.g., a ~$13 million additional allocation including farmer coaching and traceability projects). The 2019/2021 project‑level amounts and commissioning dates are explicitly documented in Cargill’s disclosures. [11], [12]

- Farmer income outcomes and evaluation detail: Cargill’s published programme documents and impact reports (e.g., “A Decade of Impact” and other Cocoa Promise materials) report yield and income improvements for participating farmers: examples include programme‑reported increases such as a 25% yield increase in some projects and a 29% rise in average farmer income where reported (PROCOCO, Ghana: average farmer income reported to have risen from US$72 to US$239 for the programme participants), and programme ROI statements (net income increase US$194 per farmer in one report). Some project documents provide participant counts (e.g., PROCOCO trained 9,625 farmers; broader Cocoa Promise farmer counts are reported in the hundreds of thousands), but many Cargill income claims are programme monitoring outputs rather than independent, peer‑reviewed impact evaluations; sample sizes and methodologies are variably disclosed across documents. [14], [9], [13]

- EUDR / traceability responses (technology, mapping and supply‑map completion): Cargill reports that 100% of cocoa in its direct supply chain is traceable to the first point of purchase and documents active mapping (reporting 28,000 farms mapped total active in direct supply chain and crop‑year mapping), with platforms such as CocoaWise™ 360 and digital first‑mile traceability used to capture bag‑level and farmer‑ID data; Cargill reported that 76.6% of farmers delivered cocoa through its digital First Mile Traceability within the Promise supply chain in 2024 and that it had begun phased EUDR compliance work in early 2023 with further implementation through 2025. Cargill’s reporting includes deforestation‑risk assessment hectare counts and mapping totals; however, the supplied evidence does not include a public company disclosure of volumes (metric tonnes or %) formally excluded as non‑compliant under EUDR screening. [9], [10], [15]

- Commercial/premium customer positioning: Cargill’s investments in local grinding capacity (Yopougon, Tema) and digital traceability position it to serve processing‑and‑manufacturing customers that require traceable supply, but the supplied evidence does not include direct, public documentation of preferred‑supplier agreements or explicit supply contracts with Lindt, Ferrero or Mondelēz in the period 2018–2024. [12], [9]

Data‑quality notes (Cargill): reporting includes program monitoring reports and company progress reports; some figures (mapping counts, farm numbers, tonnes from specific countries, % sustainable volumes) are specific and auditable in principle but are company disclosures that lack (in the supplied evidence) consistent independent verification statements or standardized third‑party audit reporting for every metric. IDH and other sector case studies provide external snapshots (e.g., the 60/40 direct/indirect split).

## 3. Olam / ofi (summary of evolution 2018–2024)

- Strategic evolution and upstream investments: Olam (including ofi/Olam Food Ingredients) continued to integrate upstream by scaling farmer programmes (living‑income targets, Farm Development Plans), acquiring ADM’s cocoa business in 2015 (establishing a larger global cocoa platform) and investing in processing capacity and traceability tools; it emphasises AtSource/AtSource+ and Track & Trace digital platforms and claims large farmer coverage and certified volumes in 2023–24. Olam reports sustainability support to >830,000 farmers (1.4 million MT procured raw material from supported farmers in 2023) and paid substantial premiums and programme investments. [16], [17], [30]

- Direct‑sourced versus broker‑purchased cocoa (definitions and reported volumes): Olam publicly claims to have achieved 100% traceability of directly sourced cocoa across its global supply chain (September 2020 claim) and to have achieved 100% traceability of its sustainable cocoa supply chain in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana under its 2020 commitment; Olam’s supplementary disclosures state it has farm‑level traceability for 4.8 million metric tonnes of procured volumes. The supplied evidence does not present a single company metric giving the percent split of direct‑sourced versus broker‑purchased cocoa in metric tonnes for each year 2018–2024; the 100% direct‑supply traceability claim pertains to the subset defined as “directly sourced.” [19], [20], [16]

- Origin‑country processing capex (Côte d’Ivoire & Ghana): Olam’s historical and project financing disclosures include a 2010 greenfield announcement for a US$43.5 million processing plant in Abidjan (planned capacity ~60,000 MT) and a later FMO/Proparco/DEG‑backed project with a reported total project size of EUR 50 million for a Côte d’Ivoire processing plant (documented on the FMO project page, with EUR 33.6 million term facility from development financiers). The FMO project documentation specifies planned capacity (69,000 MT annually) and project finance structure; Olam’s corporate disclosures treat the plant as wholly owned by Olam Cocoa. These documented project‑level amounts and capacities are explicit in the supplied evidence. [25], [18]

- Farmer income outcomes and evaluation detail: Olam’s Cocoa Compass reporting provides programme outputs (e.g., Cocoa Compass 2023 reported 44,000 farmers earning a living income — ~13% of the network — and distribution of millions of trees to farmers), and Olam reports USD136 million paid in sustainability premiums and over 64,000 tailored Farm Development Plans. A smaller independent academic impact study from Nigeria (sample 60) reported yield and income gains for pilot farmers associated with Olam programmes, but it is geographically limited and not representative of West Africa as a whole. Olam’s programme outcomes are presented as both monitored internal results (Cocoa Compass) and some independent indicators; methodology details and representative baseline/endline study coverage vary by report and region. [21], [16], [26]

- EUDR / traceability responses (technology, mapping and supply‑map completion): Olam uses Track & Trace, AtSource and GIS/GPS mapping and reports mapping all direct supply chains to the farm plot level for EUDR compliance. Olam’s disclosures claim farm‑level traceability for 4.8 million MT of procured volumes and public statements indicate intensive investment in GIS‑based mapping and GPS‑enabled data collection; independent press reporting highlights upstream supplier data‑collection challenges even where Olam’s internal systems are advanced. The supplied evidence does not include a company statement of a quantified percentage or volume formally excluded as non‑compliant under EUDR screening in 2024. [20], [19], [28]

- Commercial/premium customer positioning: Olam emphasises its integrated global cocoa platform (including the 2015 ADM acquisition) and AtSource traceability/product tagging as commercial differentiators; Olam’s Cocoa Compass and sustainability disclosures position it to meet buyer traceability and sustainability requirements for large manufacturers, but the supplied evidence does not include documented preferred‑supplier contracts with Lindt, Ferrero or Mondelēz in the reviewed materials. [30], [21]

Data‑quality notes (Olam): Olam provides detailed farm‑level traceability claims and project financing documentation (FMO) for specific plants; many sustainability and living‑income aspirational targets are company‑reported via Cocoa Compass and AtSource metrics. Some independent scrutiny (press, limited academic studies) identifies supplier‑level data‑collection challenges that Olam is addressing; representative, independent baseline/endline income evaluation coverage in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana is not fully present in the supplied evidence.

## 4. Cross‑company comparison (synthesis)

- Vertical integration trajectory (2018→2024): All three firms increased upstream integration through (a) investments in local processing capacity, (b) expansion of farmer engagement programmes, and (c) roll‑out of digital first‑mile traceability and mapping to farm level to meet buyer and regulatory demands. Olam’s public claims emphasise 100% direct‑supply traceability for its directly sourced volumes and the largest absolute farm‑level traceability volume (4.8 million MT procured volumes reported in supplementary disclosures), Barry emphasises mapping scale and sustainability premium flows within Forever Chocolate, and Cargill emphasises first‑purchase‑point traceability with explicit investments in local grinding capacity (Yopougon and Tema). [19], [3], [9], [12], [20]

- Direct sourcing / broker reliance (available evidence): The only direct % snapshots in the supplied evidence are: Barry — 40% direct supply (IDH, Dec 2020), Cargill — ~60% direct supply (IDH snapshot), and Olam — claims of full traceability for directly sourced cocoa but no company‑wide published % direct vs broker in the supplied documents. These figures indicate differing public transparency and different historical baselines for direct procurement, but the evidence set lacks a standardised annual metric across 2018–2024 to compute consistent year‑on‑year % direct vs broker for each company. [4], [13], [19]

- Origin‑country processing capex (project‑level comparators): Cargill has the most explicit, recent project‑level capex numbers in the evidence: US$113 million announced in 2019 (US$100M Yopougon + US$13M Tema) and a completed US$100M Yopougon expansion in Nov 2021. Olam documents project‑level financing for an Ivorian processing project (EUR 50M total project size; EUR 33.6M term facility reported) and earlier greenfield capital of US$43.5M (2010 announcement). Barry documents an Abidjan processing unit opened March 2019 that raised processing capacity by >40% by 2022 but the supplied evidence does not present a project‑level capex amount for that facility. [11], [12], [18], [25], [5]

- Farmer income outcomes (comparative evidence and quality): All three report farmer income and yield improvements for programme participants:
  - Barry reports cumulative counts of farmers above a poverty line (e.g., 269,762 farmers no longer in poverty in one report and 557,739 above the poverty line in 2024/25) and premium payments (CHF 43.5M Cocoa Horizons premiums in a reporting year), but independent baseline‑endline methodologies are limited in the supplied evidence (sample‑based Agrilogic survey N=561 is narrow). [1], [3], [23]
  - Cargill reports programme outcomes including yield increases (e.g., 25% increase in some projects) and income increases (e.g., PROCOCO: US$72 → US$239 for participating farmers; another report cites a net income increase of US$194 per farmer), with some project participant counts provided (e.g., 9,625 farmers trained in the Rural Education Project). These are programme monitoring results rather than necessarily independent impact evaluations across all participating regions. [14], [9]
  - Olam/Cocoa Compass reports that 44,000 farmers (13% of its network) achieved a living income in 2023 and that USD136M in sustainability premiums were paid, with other programme outputs (trees distributed, Farm Development Plans). Independent academic evidence is limited and regionally constrained (e.g., a Nigerian pilot study N=60). [21], [16], [26]

  Overall, company monitoring indicates positive income and yield outcomes for program participants, but differences in reporting units (percent above poverty, absolute farmer counts, per‑farmer income deltas), uneven disclosure of sample sizes, and lack of consistent independent baseline/endline studies across the same populations mean cross‑company comparisons should be treated cautiously. [1], [14], [21], [23], [26]

- EUDR readiness and supply‑chain traceability: All three companies invested significantly in digital mapping and first‑mile traceability tools to meet EUDR requirements:
  - Barry reports farm‑level traceability levels of ~83% in 2023/24 for its direct supply chain and mapping of 669,174 farm plots in 2023/24, plus Katchilè for batch traceability. Barry states it reached the traceability level required by EUDR for mapped volumes by 2024/25. [3], [4]
  - Cargill reports 100% traceability to the first point of purchase for direct supply and reported 28,000 farms mapped (active) in the direct supply chain, with 76.6% of farmers delivering via digital first‑mile systems in 2024; Cargill began phased EUDR compliance work in 2023. [9], [10], [15]
  - Olam reports mapping all direct supply chains to farm plot level for EUDR and farm‑level traceability for 4.8 million MT of procured volumes, using Track & Trace/AtSource and GIS/GPS tools. [20], [19], [28]

  None of the three companies published, in the reviewed evidence, a company‑level, audited metric of percentage or volume explicitly excluded as non‑compliant under EUDR screening for 2024 (i.e., public tonnes excluded for deforestation non‑compliance were not found in the supplied documents). Where third‑party reporting exists (e.g., CDP for Barry), it indicates limited shares of volumes reported as verified deforestation‑free and some unknown origin shares, highlighting data‑quality and disclosure differences across reporters. [8]

- Premium‑supply competitive positioning: Barry’s renewed long‑term supply agreements with large buyers (e.g., Mars, Unilever) and its substantial sustainability programme scale and premium payment reporting strengthen its claim to supply sustainably certified/premium volumes to global manufacturers. Cargill and Olam’s investments in grinding capacity, digital traceability and supplier services position them to compete for premium contracts requiring farm‑level traceability and EUDR compliance, but the supplied evidence does not include direct declarations of preferred‑supplier contracts with Lindt, Ferrero or Mondelēz for Cargill or Olam in the reviewed materials. Thus, while all three have technical and commercial levers to secure premium manufacturing contracts, the strongest public evidence of renewed long‑term strategic supply agreements (among the reviewed materials) is for Barry. [6], [7], [12], [18], [20]

## 5. Evidence gaps and limits of the supplied evidence

The supplied evidence set is rich in company self‑reported programme outputs and contains some external case studies and project finance pages, but several requested, decision‑critical metrics are missing or inconsistent across sources:

- Standardised annual direct‑sourced vs broker‑purchased split (metric tonnes and %) by company for 2018–2024 is not consistently published in the supplied evidence for all three firms; only snapshots exist (Barry: 40% direct from IDH 2020; Cargill: ~60% direct from IDH case study; Olam: claims of 100% traceability for directly sourced volumes but not a company‑wide direct/broker % split in tonnes). A consistent methodology definition and annual time series is absent. [4], [13], [19]

- Project‑level capital expenditures are explicit for Cargill and Olam (examples above) but not for Barry’s Abidjan expansion (no capex amount in the supplied Barry documents). A full, year‑by‑year capex time series for all origin‑country processing investments (2018–2024) is therefore not available in the evidence. [11], [12], [18], [25], [5]

- Independent, peer‑reviewed baseline–endline impact evaluations with representative sample sizes and counterfactuals for farmer income changes are limited. Company monitoring reports show positive outcomes, and small independent studies exist (e.g., an Olam Nigeria pilot, N=60), but representative independent evaluations for Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana covering the major programmes and enabling apples‑to‑apples cross‑company comparison are not present in the supplied materials. [23], [26]

- Public disclosures of volumes or percentages formally excluded as non‑compliant under EUDR screening (i.e., tonnage rejected/removed from EU supply) are not available in the supplied evidence for any of the three companies. [3], [9], [20], [8]

- Direct publicly disclosed preferred‑supplier agreements between Cargill/Olam and premium chocolate manufacturers (Lindt, Ferrero, Mondelēz) are not contained in the supplied evidence; Barry has documented long‑term agreements with some large customers but not the full universe of premium consumer chocolate manufacturers requested. [6], [7], [12]

## 6. Methodology and data‑quality assessment (how figures were sourced and confidence levels)

- Source types used: company annual and sustainability reports, company press releases, sector case‑studies (IDH), corporate project finance page (FMO), company programme impact documents, independent academic/NGO pieces where present, and trade press. All factual statements in this report are drawn exclusively from the supplied evidence set and are cited accordingly.

- Data‑quality classification used here:
  - High (company audited/finance project docs or external project finance disclosure; clear project‑level amounts and dates): e.g., Cargill 2019/2021 capex announcements and completion; Olam/FMO EUR 50M project documentation. [11], [12], [18]
  - Medium (company self‑reporting in annual/sustainability reports with program metrics but limited independent verification): e.g., Barry/Forever Chocolate mapping, traceability and farmer counts; Olam Cocoa Compass outcomes and traceability MT claims; Cargill Cocoa Promise mapping and first‑mile percentages. [1], [3], [20], [9], [10], [21]
  - Low/limited (small independent studies or descriptive press reporting with limited representativeness): e.g., small academic pilot studies (Olam Nigeria N=60) and limited press assessments of supplier data‑collection challenges. Such sources can illustrate issues but are not sufficient for population‑level inference. [26], [28]

- Specific methodological notes on reported figures:
  - Where companies report “direct supply chain” percentages or “traceability to farm level,” definitions vary; IDH defines direct supply in its case studies and is the source for comparative snapshots (Barry 40%, Cargill ~60% in the referenced case studies), whereas Olam’s 100% traceability claim applies to the subset it defines as directly sourced and sustainable. Users should treat “direct‑sourced” vs “traceable to farm level” as related but distinct concepts without a unified, comparable definition across companies in the supplied evidence. [4], [13], [19]
  - Farmer income figures are primarily programme monitoring outputs; sample sizes and evaluation methodologies are explicitly stated only in some documents (e.g., Agrilogic N=561 for a Barry survey; PROCOCO counts for Cargill; Nigerian pilot N=60 for Olam). Where the company does not publish detailed methodology in the supplied evidence, attribution confidence is lower. [23], [14], [26]

## 7. Implications for premium chocolate supply competition

- Technical readiness and commercial positioning: All three firms have invested in upstream assets (processing capacity) plus first‑mile traceability and farmer programmes — the fundamental capabilities required by premium chocolate manufacturers when contracting for traceable, deforestation‑free, sustainably supported cocoa. Barry’s documented long‑term supply renewals with large customers and its scale of sustainability premium payments give it visible evidence of converting upstream integration into commercial supply agreements; Cargill’s large capex in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana and its first‑purchase‑point traceability system are competitive enablers; Olam’s AtSource/Track & Trace capabilities and its claims of large farm‑level traceability volumes position it strongly on technical traceability. [6], [11], [12], [18], [19], [20], [3]

- Price/quality/premium supply implications (evidence limits): Direct evidence in the supplied materials of how these upstream investments altered contract pricing, quality specifications, or secured formal preferred‑supplier status with premium chocolate brands (Lindt, Ferrero, Mondelēz) is limited. Barry’s long‑term agreements suggest price/volume/premium arrangements with large industrial buyers, but the details (price differentials, quality clauses, exclusive supplier status) are not disclosed in the evidence. For Cargill and Olam, investments plausibly strengthen bids for premium contracts requiring EUDR‑compliant, traceable supply, but the documents reviewed do not provide explicit contract evidence with the named manufacturers. [6], [11], [12], [18], [20]

## 8. Short conclusion

From 2018–2024 Barry Callebaut, Cargill and Olam all intensified vertical integration upstream in West Africa by expanding farmer programmes, investing in origin‑country processing capacity, and deploying digital first‑mile traceability to satisfy sustainability buyers and upcoming regulatory demands. Cargill and Olam present clear project‑level processing investments (Cargill: US$113M announced in 2019 with US$100M Yopougon expansion completed in 2021; Olam: documented FMO‑backed EUR 50M project and earlier US$43.5M greenfield); Barry documents capacity expansion in Abidjan (March 2019) but does not disclose a project capex figure in the supplied evidence. On tracing direct sourcing, IDH case studies give a snapshot (Barry 40% direct, Cargill ~60% direct) while Olam claims full traceability of its directly sourced volumes but lacks a supply‑wide direct/broker % in the provided documents. All three report farmer income gains for programme participants, but company monitoring dominates the evidence and independent, representative baseline–endline evaluations are limited, constraining cross‑company causal comparisons. Finally, Barry’s documented long‑term supply agreements (e.g., Mars, Unilever) provide the clearest public evidence of converting upstream integration into large customer supply relationships among the reviewed materials; comparable publicly disclosed contract evidence for Cargill and Olam with premium chocolate manufacturers in the supplied set is not available.

# CI/CD approach comparison for a 200+‑service fintech (50–100 prod deployments/day)

Executive summary
- Recommendation: Buildkite with dynamic pipeline generation and hosted agents (or hybrid: self‑hosted agents for sensitive workloads, hosted agents for high-throughput non‑sensitive builds) most directly minimizes developer wait time while reducing platform-engineering maintenance, and offers the clearest ecosystem support for progressive delivery (Argo/ArgoCD/Helm plugins and rollback tooling). Key trade-offs: higher per‑minute hosted-agent cost vs. better out‑of‑the‑box dispatch latency, and Enterprise features (audit/export) are on higher tiers. Evidence and reasoning below support this selection and provide alternatives (GitHub Actions with reusable workflows; GitLab CI with DAGs) when cost, vendor consolidation, or feature parity push the decision elsewhere. Recommendation is conservative about compliance-sensitive data: consider self‑hosted agents or private Buildkite clusters for regulated workloads.

## 1. Scope, approach, and primary assumptions
- Scope: polyglot microservices (Java, Go, Python), ~200+ repositories/services, ~50–100 production deployments/day, pipelines defined per service. “Typical service” definition taken from the brief: 15‑minute build, 8 parallel test jobs, 3 deployment stages (canary, promote, final).
- Explicit modeling assumptions (used below; all numerical assumptions marked as such and not presented as additional factual claims):
  - Two test-duration scenarios modeled because test runtimes were not specified:
    - Short-tests: each parallel test job = 5 minutes → pipeline compute time = build (15) + tests (5) + deploys (assume 3 + 1 + 1 = 5) = 25 minutes.
    - Long-tests: each parallel test job = 15 minutes → pipeline compute time = build (15) + tests (15) + deploys (assume 10 + 3 + 3 = 16) = 46 minutes.
  - SaaS-hosted runner per-minute pricing used from vendor docs (GitHub, GitLab, Buildkite) and representative self‑hosted VM pricing using AWS m5.xlarge and m5.large on‑demand hourly rates as a simple baseline (sources listed in References).
  - Queue/runner startup behavior modeled using public queue/initialization observations (see Performance section). Where platform metrics gave SLOs or sample results those guided median/p95 estimates; where exact percentiles were absent, conservative ranges are shown and explicitly labeled.
- Evidence coverage: all platform feature claims, pricing figures, queue/initialization observations, and case studies are taken from the referenced documentation, blogs and case studies in References.

## 2. Performance (pipeline wall‑clock time)
Model goal: produce median and p95 end‑to‑end times for the “typical service” in SaaS‑hosted and self‑hosted runner scenarios, accounting for queue/startup and cache/IO overheads described in public reports.

Summary of relevant platform behaviors (single citation each):
- GitHub Actions: hosted runner concurrency increased (up to 1,000 for larger runners) and documented runner initialization variability; community reports show runner initialization and pod Pending delays for self‑hosted Kubernetes, and AWS guidance reports EC2 instance readiness up to ~2 minutes for self‑hosted runners [11]. GitHub Actions cache semantics and limits are documented separately [12], and cache-related init latency improvements have been reported after optimization [3]. (Citations: GitHub limits [11]; actions/cache & cache rate-limits [12]; depot runner-init improvements [3]; AWS self-hosted runner guidance [13].)
- GitLab CI: shared SaaS runners create fresh VMs per job and default cache behavior causes download+reupload on many jobs; GitLab.com SLO aims for 90% of CI jobs to start within 120s (i.e., p90 ≤ 120s) [1], [9].
- Buildkite: hosted agents provision on demand, dispatched “within a matter of seconds” per documentation; self‑hosted agents support warm images, pre‑pull, and autoscaling patterns for low queue times; Buildkite also advertises high per‑job performance and provides dynamic pipeline generation APIs [5], [2], [7].

(References quoted in each paragraph above: Buildkite hosted agents [5]; SeatGeek self‑hosted optimizations [2]; depot.dev [3]; GitHub limits & cache [11], [12]; GitLab SLO & cache behavior [1], [9]; Buildkite dynamic pipelines [7].)

Modeling methodology (how numbers were computed)
- End‑to‑end time = queue waiting time + runner startup/init time + pipeline compute time (build + tests + deploy steps) + cache/artifact overheads where applicable.
- Queue/startup medians and p95s were taken or inferred from vendor SLOs and community measurements; cache/artifact overheads used reported examples (e.g., a redundant cache upload ~30s in a GitLab setup) to demonstrate realistic tails rather than optimistic minima [1].
- Two compute scenarios (short/long) described in Assumptions were used to produce example totals. These are illustrative models intended to show relative platform differences given documented startup/queue behaviors.

Performance results — SaaS‑hosted runners (median / p95)
- Buildkite (hosted agents)
  - Rationale: Buildkite documentation: hosted agents are provisioned on demand and jobs are dispatched “within a matter of seconds” → very low queue latency [5].
  - Modeled numbers (examples):
    - Short‑tests (25 min compute): median ≈ 25.1–25.3 minutes (queue/startup seconds), p95 ≈ 25.5 minutes (allowing tens of seconds for cache attach/startup) [5].
    - Long‑tests (46 min compute): median ≈ 46.1–46.3 minutes, p95 ≈ 46.6 minutes.
  - Evidence note: Buildkite hosted agents attach cache volumes at initiation and startup can take “a few seconds, varying with cache size and recency” [5].

- GitHub Actions (hosted)
  - Rationale: GitHub-hosted runners have low median queue times for many orgs (runs‑on benchmarks showed queue p50 in the ~10–29s range for several providers) but initialization p99s have been observed and improved with caching patterns; hosted concurrency can be large (up to 1,000) reducing queueing at scale [4], [3], [11].
  - Modeled numbers:
    - Short‑tests (25 min): median ≈ 25.2–25.6 minutes (add ~10–30s median queue + runner init), p95 ≈ 26–27 minutes (allowing runner init p99/39s and occasional cache pulls) [4], [3].
    - Long‑tests (46 min): median ≈ 46.2–46.6 min, p95 ≈ 47–48 min.
  - Evidence note: self‑hosted/workflow-specific initialization variability can increase p95 substantially; a tuned hosted scenario gives modest overheads [3], [4].

- GitLab CI (GitLab.com shared runners)
  - Rationale: GitLab shared runners use fresh VMs and default cache behavior leads to download & reupload per job unless tuned; GitLab’s SLO states 90% of CI/CD jobs should start within 120s → p90 ≤ 120s, making p95/median wider than Buildkite’s documented “seconds” [1].
  - Modeled numbers:
    - Short‑tests (25 min): median ≈ 25.3–26.5 minutes (median queue/startup varied; conservative median ≈ 30–90s depending on load), p95 ≈ 27–27.5+ minutes or higher (if hitting cache reupload and fresh NVD downloads for heavy scans as observed needs of tens of minutes in worst cases for dependency scans) [1].
    - Long‑tests (46 min): median ≈ 46.3–47.5 min, p95 similarly extended when caches are missed or large downloads occur [1].
  - Evidence note: sample GitLab sagas show cache uploads could add ~30s per job, and certain scans (e.g., OWASP NVD without API key) can cause cold downloads that add 20–30 minutes in extreme cases unless mitigated [1].

Performance results — Self‑hosted runners (median / p95)
- Buildkite (self‑hosted)
  - With warm images, pre‑pulled container images, and autoscaling pods, SeatGeek / Buildkite best practices show very low queue/p95 counts; Buildkite docs describe long‑running agents for warm starts and large disk caches to lower startup time [2], [6].
  - Modeled numbers:
    - Short‑tests: median ≈ 25.0–25.1 min, p95 ≈ 25.3 min (seconds-level startup).
    - Long‑tests: median ≈ 46.0–46.2 min, p95 ≈ 46.5 min.
  - Evidence note: pull times for very large images still matter and self‑hosted runners must manage disk cache limits [2].

- GitHub Actions (self‑hosted)
  - Rationale: documented realities: a job remains queued until the EC2 instance is ready (up to ~2 minutes), and community reports of larger init delays exist; Kubernetes pending pods can create additional uncounted delays [13], [3].
  - Modeled numbers:
    - Short‑tests: median ≈ 25.5–27 min (add ~0.5–2 min median for provisioning), p95 ≈ 27–30+ min (up to ~2 min EC2, and reports of longer Pending/init delays) [13], [3].
    - Long‑tests: median ≈ 46.5–48 min, p95 ≈ 48–50+ min.

- GitLab CI (self‑hosted)
  - Rationale: self‑hosted GitLab runners on Kubernetes can achieve very low queue times if correctly configured; SeatGeek moved p98 queue time from >3 minutes to <4 seconds with an optimized Kubernetes runner setup [2].
  - Modeled numbers:
    - Short‑tests: median ≈ 25.0–25.1 min, p95 ≈ 25.2–25.4 min (with warm pools and pre‑pulls).
    - Long‑tests: median ≈ 46.0–46.2 min, p95 ≈ 46.5 min.

Synthesis and practical implications (performance)
- Best latency (median and tail) out of the box: Buildkite hosted agents; they advertise seconds‑level job dispatch and several case studies describe dramatic build-time reductions when switching to optimized Buildkite hosted/self‑hosted agent strategies [5], [21].
- With platform engineering effort (warm pools, pre‑pull, caching), self‑hosted runners on GitLab or GitHub can reduce tails to single-digit seconds, but that requires active engineering investment and operational capacity. SeatGeek’s example shows dramatic improvements are achievable with Kubernetes runner orchestration and pre‑pulls [2].
- GitLab SaaS shared runners can show longer tails unless caching and cache‑policy are tuned because of cache reupload defaults and the possibility of large external downloads in pipeline jobs [1].

## 3. Cost (estimated per 1,000 pipeline runs)
Method: compute runtime minutes per pipeline (models above: 25 and 46 minutes), multiply by 1,000 runs to get total minutes, then apply vendor per‑minute SaaS pricing (vendor docs) or representative self‑hosted VM cost (AWS on‑demand m5.xlarge or m5.large) as baseline. All per‑minute prices and VM hourly rates are taken from vendor docs and referenced sources.

Key pricing facts used (single citation each):
- GitLab compute minutes: $10 per 1,000 minutes (i.e., $0.01/minute) for GitLab CI/CD compute minutes on GitLab.com [9].
- GitHub hosted runner pricing reported in public materials: Linux runner rates commonly cited at $0.008 per minute in available pricing summaries and guides used here for modeling (private repos paid minutes) [31].
- Buildkite hosted Linux agent pricing: Small (2 vCPU, 4GB) $0.013/minute (per Buildkite pricing page) [6].
- Representative self‑hosted VM cost for modeling: AWS m5.xlarge on‑demand ~$0.192/hr (~$0.0032/min) and m5.large ~$0.096/hr (~$0.0016/min) [27].

(Each of the four items above are taken from vendor docs or representative VM pricing in References [9], [31], [6], [27].)

Cost results per 1,000 pipeline runs (computed examples)
- Scenario A — Short-tests (25 minutes avg):
  - Total minutes per 1,000 runs = 25,000 minutes.
  - GitLab SaaS (compute minutes): 25,000 * $0.01 = $250 [9].
  - GitHub-hosted: 25,000 * $0.008 = $200 [31].
  - Buildkite-hosted (Small): 25,000 * $0.013 = $325 [6].
  - Self‑hosted baseline (m5.xlarge at $0.192/hr ≈ $0.0032/min) fully utilized: 25,000 * $0.0032 ≈ $80 of raw compute; note this omits storage, egress, HA, management time and extra agents to reduce queue — see sensitivity below [27].

- Scenario B — Long-tests (46 minutes avg):
  - Total minutes per 1,000 runs = 46,000 minutes.
  - GitLab SaaS: 46,000 * $0.01 = $460 [9].
  - GitHub-hosted: 46,000 * $0.008 = $368 [31].
  - Buildkite-hosted: 46,000 * $0.013 = $598 [6].
  - Self‑hosted baseline (m5.xlarge): 46,000 * $0.0032 ≈ $147 [27].

Cost sensitivity (key drivers and how they change cost)
- Concurrency and utilization: self‑hosted economics assume high utilization. If the platform-engineering team sizes runner pools for low queue time (many idle instances), self‑hosted cost rises; conversely, aggressive autoscaling + spot instances reduces cost but increases operational complexity (SeatGeek reported cost reductions using optimized Kubernetes runners and capacity reservations) [2].
- Average run time: the per‑minute SaaS pricing makes pipeline shortening the single biggest lever for reducing SaaS cost (cost scales linearly with run minutes). The examples show a 2× increase in average runtime (25→46 min) nearly doubles SaaS cost.
- Runner type: GitHub hosted vs. GitLab compute minutes vs. Buildkite hosted per‑minute pricing differ; Buildkite hosted is more expensive per minute but yields lower queue/tail latency; self‑hosted compute cost (raw VM) is materially lower per minute but requires ops effort.

Evidence gaps (cost)
- Public sources do not publish the complete TCO for sustained self‑hosted Buildkite agent fleets (operational FTEs, storage/egress), nor exact per‑GB artifact storage/egress rates for Buildkite hosted artifacts; those gaps are noted below.

## 4. Operational overhead / maintenance burden
Goal: compare expected maintenance effort to manage pipeline definitions across 200+ services, including drift control, onboarding time, and developer UX for editing pipelines.

Evidence‑based observations (single citation per item):
- GitLab: DAGs (needs) and cache policy tuning can cut pipeline time; however, GitLab’s default cache behavior causes redundant uploads and larger pipelines may have longer MR pipelines unless optimized; public migration/maintenance estimates for GitLab self‑hosted indicate 1–2 FTE for medium orgs to run self‑hosted GitLab (including CI/CD) [1], [31].
- GitHub Actions: reusable workflows are a mechanism to centralize steps; self‑hosted runners require 0.25–0.5 FTE for maintenance for medium orgs in public guidance; GitHub best practices emphasize OIDC, caching, and runner pools [31], [32].
- Buildkite: dynamic pipelines allow programmatic generation and reduce YAML duplication; Buildkite provides migration tooling and case studies show organizations cut build times and setup time with Buildkite [7], [20], [21].

(Mapped citations: GitLab cache/DAG blog [1]; GitLab self-hosted maintenance FTE estimate [31]; GitHub self-hosted maintenance FTE and best practices [31]/[32]; Buildkite dynamic pipelines and migration/case studies [7], [20], [21].)

Quantitative maintenance estimates (evidence + modeling)
- GitLab self‑hosted (200+ services):
  - Evidence: self‑hosted GitLab maintenance typically 1–2 FTE for a medium org [31].
  - Expected weekly maintenance hours: 40–80 hours of one or more SREs for platform upkeep plus platform‑team effort to maintain templates and tune caching (consistent with 1–2 FTE).
  - Pipeline template complexity: GitLab DAGs can centralize but require YAML tuning and cache policy controls across services to avoid pipeline slowdowns [1].
- GitHub Actions (using reusable workflows):
  - Evidence: self‑hosted runner operations ~0.25–0.5 FTE for medium orgs; reusable workflows centralize code reducing duplication [31], [32].
  - Expected weekly maintenance hours: 10–20 hours platform time (0.25–0.5 FTE) for runner fleet and shared workflow maintenance; additional time per repo to onboard templates and permission management.
  - Reuse & drift control: reusable workflows are strong but still require careful versioning and depend on repository admin permissions and OIDC/secret configs for each org [32].
- Buildkite (dynamic pipelines + hosted agents):
  - Evidence: dynamic pipeline generation explicitly reduces repeating YAML because pipelines are created programmatically; Buildkite migration services and case studies show companies reduced setup friction and build/runtime significantly after adopting Buildkite [7], [20], [21].
  - Expected weekly maintenance hours: public sources do not provide a precise FTE estimate for Buildkite platform ops at this scale; case studies show major improvements but do not publish maintenance hours. This is an evidence gap (see Evidence Gaps).
  - Reuse & drift control: dynamic pipelines centralize pipeline generation code (single generator) which can manage templating and enforce standards programmatically; this reduces per‑repo YAML drift and onboarding time compared to individually maintained YAML files [7].

Developer experience and editing workflows
- GitHub Actions: reusable workflows + local tools and OIDC patterns are supported, and PR feedback loops are standard; however, local dry‑run tooling and runner initialization differences (some init latency not counted in queue metrics) can cause developer confusion around perceived pipeline time [3], [11], [12].
- GitLab CI: DAGs with needs give flexible parallelism, but cache behavior and reupload of caches must be managed; authors have achieved significant speedups by changing cache policies and keys [1].
- Buildkite: dynamic pipelines enable repository templates generated by a single script/tooling which reduces repetitive edits and the number/size of YAML files; Buildkite also supports previewing pipelines via pipeline upload APIs and has migration tooling to convert from other CI formats [7], [19].

Operational reliability (pipeline breakages & fix time)
- Evidence provides per‑org variance rather than universal rates. Case studies (PlatOps/Buildkite) show organizations reached high pipeline success rates after standardization (PlatOps fintech reported 99.9% pipeline success) but that required centralized templates and tooling [20], [21]. Quantitative frequency and mean‑time‑to‑fix for 200+ services at the specified deployment rate are not publicly reported — evidence gap (see Evidence Gaps).

## 5. Security, secrets rotation, and compliance
Key, documented platform capabilities:
- GitLab CI supports integration with AWS Secrets Manager via the aws_secrets_manager keyword and supports per‑secret configuration (region, role ARNs) enabling short‑lived credentials and scoped secrets [14].
- GitHub Actions supports OIDC federated identity integration with cloud key vaults (example: Azure Key Vault via federated identity) to avoid storing long‑lived credentials in Actions secrets and to allow short‑lived tokens per workflow run [15].
- Buildkite offers HashiCorp Vault plugins and Azure Key Vault integration (plugins and examples), and Buildkite’s tooling supports redaction of secrets from logs and injecting secrets at job time [13], [16].
- Audit logging: Buildkite provides an organization audit log (Enterprise customers) with event types and event export (and GraphQL access) [16]; GitHub Enterprise supports audit log streaming for enterprise activity [31]; GitLab currently has a noted gap in pipeline execution auditing per an open issue requesting richer immutable pipeline execution audit events [17].

(Citations: GitLab secrets manager [14]; GitHub OIDC/Azure Key Vault blog [15]; Buildkite Vault/KeyVault plugins [13]; Buildkite audit log doc [16]; GitLab issue on pipeline audit [17]; GitHub audit streaming [31].)

Secrets rotation and operational complexity
- Native/first‑class rotation:
  - GitHub OIDC + cloud vaults: OIDC allows issuance of short‑lived cloud credentials without storing secrets in the platform; this pattern reduces operational complexity and supports per‑run ephemeral credentials [15].
  - GitLab’s secrets integration with AWS Secrets Manager can select versions and use roles, enabling rotation without pipeline code changes if the pipeline pulls the latest secret versions [14].
  - Buildkite’s Vault plugin supports AppRole/AWS/JWT auth and can fetch secrets at job runtime; redaction support is provided [13].
- Practical recommendation for fintech compliance: use an external enterprise vault (HashiCorp Vault / AWS Secrets Manager / Azure Key Vault) with ephemeral retrieval via OIDC or agent‑based authentication; configure pipelines to reference vault paths rather than in‑repo secrets and ensure redaction in CI logs [13], [14], [15].

Audit trails, retention, and export for compliance
- Buildkite: Enterprise audit log stores events indefinitely with UI retention up to 12 months and the ability to stream events to e.g., EventBridge for SIEM ingestion [16].
- GitHub: Enterprise audit log streaming exists and can be used for evidence export; streaming buffers and delivery semantics are documented [31].
- GitLab: evidence indicates a gap — pipeline execution auditing is not comprehensive and an issue has been raised to add an immutable pipeline execution audit event [17].
- Regulatory note: PCI‑DSS and financial regulators require long retention and tamper‑resistant audit trails; Buildkite and GitHub Enterprise provide streaming and export mechanisms that can be used to meet these needs; GitLab SaaS users should plan for additional export/archival strategies or evidence of pipeline execution to meet strict audit requirements [16], [31], [17], [29].

## 6. Rollback orchestration and progressive delivery
Platform & ecosystem capabilities
- Argo Rollouts and Flagger: both are production‑grade progressive delivery tools supporting canary and blue/green strategies and automated rollback on health metrics; Argo Rollouts integrates with Istio and supports traffic splitting and analysis templates; Flagger automates rollouts and integrates with different ingress controllers and monitoring solutions [18], [19], [8].
- Buildkite: provides deployment plugins for ArgoCD/ArgoCD rollouts, Helm, and AWS Lambda with rollback capabilities and collects health checks/logs as artifacts — enabling programmatic progressive delivery flows inside pipelines [7], [22].
- GitHub Actions: no built‑in automatic rollback feature but workflows can implement conditional rollback steps using workflow logic and continue‑on‑error as documented in community examples [3].
- GitLab: while GitLab CI/CD supports deployment orchestration pipelines, the public evidence in this dataset emphasizes pipeline speed and cache behavior rather than native Rollout orchestration — therefore for robust progressive delivery it is common to use Argo Rollouts or Flagger integrated with GitLab‑driven pipelines (evidence of Argo Rollouts+Istio examples and Flagger capabilities exist) [19], [18].

Implementing automated rollback on health metrics (how it looks)
- Argo Rollouts (analysis templates + automated rollback):
  - Recommended flow: CI builds and publishes the image → GitOps (ArgoCD) or direct k8s manifest update creates an Argo Rollout resource with canary steps and AnalysisTemplate that queries Prometheus (success‑rate, latency) → Argo automatically advances or aborts/rolls back based on thresholds [19], [18].
  - Evidence shows Argo Rollouts can be configured with setWeight/pause/analysis sequences and auto‑rollback when error_rate exceeds threshold (examples provided) [19].
- Buildkite example integration:
  - Use Buildkite’s ArgoCD plugin to apply rollouts and collect analysis artifacts; Buildkite plugins include rollback features and can annotate builds with logs/health metrics [7].
- GitHub Actions / GitLab CI approach:
  - Use a workflow/job to call Argo Rollouts/Flagger or to run deployment scripts; then use a monitoring step (Prometheus query or external canary analysis) and conditional rollback step in the workflow. Community examples show conditional rollback steps in GitHub Actions by examining monitoring results and invoking a rollback command when thresholds are violated [3], [18].

Developer/operator ergonomics
- Buildkite: dedicated plugins for ArgoCD/Helm and explicit support for collecting logs as artifacts make progressive delivery ergonomics straightforward; dynamic pipelines allow per‑service custom steps while enforcing standard rollout patterns from the pipeline generator [7], [22].
- GitHub Actions: flexible but requires more custom workflow logic; lack of native rollback means platform teams need to provide well‑tested reusable workflows and helper actions to make progressive delivery ergonomic at scale [3], [15].
- GitLab CI: supports driving Argo/Flagger workflows from pipelines; pipeline execution audit gaps should be considered when operators require immutable proof of rollout actions for compliance [17], [18].

- Buildkite adopters and outcomes: Intercom, PagerDuty, REA Group, Shopify, Elastic, Reddit reported large build‑time improvements or increased deployment frequency after adopting Buildkite; Intercom reduced tests from 25→3 minutes enabling 150 daily deployments; Elastic cut pipeline run time from 3 hours to 55 minutes [21].
- Revolut: supports ~1,200 microservices with a 15‑person DevOps automation team enabling self‑service pipelines and templates; this demonstrates that standardization + self‑service templates scale efficiently for very large microservice footprints [22].

Interpretation

Short migration/implementation checklist for recommended approach (Buildkite + dynamic pipelines)

   - Run a pilot with 10 representative services to measure real builds/tests and tune caching/warm images; use Buildkite hosted agents initially to assess dispatch latency and per‑minute cost [5], [6].

   - Use hosted Buildkite agents for majority tests to minimize queue latency; for regulatory workloads, deploy self‑hosted agents inside the VPC with pre‑pulled images and warm pools [5], [2].

   - Ensure pipelines publish artifacts and monitoring queries (Prometheus) and that pipeline steps block or fail to trigger automatic rollback steps when thresholds are exceeded [19].

   - Store pipeline generator code in a single repo with versioned releases; use repository‑level constraints and automated checks to prevent ad hoc pipeline drift [7], [21].

## 9. Assumptions, calculation method, and sensitivity analysis
- Key assumptions called out earlier: two test-duration scenarios (short/long), per‑minute prices from vendor docs, representative VM prices for self‑hosted. Where public evidence indicated variable startup times or SLOs, conservative estimates were used.
- Calculation method: multiply per‑pipeline average minutes by 1,000 and multiply by per‑minute pricing for SaaS; for self‑hosted use VM per‑minute cost as baseline (note: ignores HA, idle capacity, and engineering labor).
- Sensitivity highlights:
  - If average pipeline minutes fall by 20–50% (via caching, split tests, or faster build images), SaaS costs fall proportionally; Buildkite’s higher per‑minute cost can be offset by developer-time savings from lower queue/tail latency.
  - If strict compliance requires private runners for all workloads, hosted agents may be unavailable for sensitive workloads and self‑hosted cost + ops FTE increase — GitHub and GitLab self‑hosted ops estimates suggest additional FTE time is required [31], [2].
  - Queue/tail behavior is sensitive to runner warm pools and pre‑pull strategies; SeatGeek’s optimizations reduced avg queue time from 16s → 2s and p98 from >3 minutes to <4s — showing that platform engineering investment materially reduces p95 [2].

## 10. Evidence gaps (items not available in the sources)
- No published precise FTE estimates for Buildkite platform operations at the 200+ service scale (Buildkite case studies show operational improvements but don’t publish maintenance FTEs). This prevents exact FTE numeric comparison for Buildkite.
- No granular public breakdown of artifact storage/egress pricing for Buildkite hosted artifacts sufficient to include in per‑1,000 pipeline cost models.
- No dataset giving empirical pipeline breakage frequency and mean‑time‑to‑fix at the specific scale (200+ services; 50–100 daily deployments) across the three platform configurations.
- Precise typical test durations per test job were not provided in the brief; two modeling scenarios were used to illustrate cost and performance sensitivity.

## 11. Final recommendation and trade‑offs
- Best fit: Buildkite with dynamic pipelines + hybrid runners (hosted for high throughput, self‑hosted in VPCs for regulated workloads), with Argo Rollouts/Flagger for canary automation and HashiCorp Vault/Azure/AWS Key Vault for secrets.
  - Pros: lowest out‑of‑the‑box dispatch/tail latency, dynamic pipelines reduce YAML drift, out‑of‑the‑box plugins for Argo/Helm + rollback, Enterprise audit/export features, strong case studies for scaling builds and deployments [5], [7], [21], [16].
  - Cons: higher per‑minute hosted agent cost vs. GitHub/GitLab; some Enterprise features (audit log retention, SSO) are on Enterprise plan; hosted agents outside private network may not meet compliance — mitigate with hybrid self‑hosted agents for sensitive workloads [6], [16], [5].
- Reasonable alternatives:
  - GitHub Actions with reusable workflows — attractive for lower per‑minute cost and tight GitHub integration; requires platform engineering investment for warm pools/self‑hosted runners to reach low p95 and additional reusable workflow + action libraries for progressive delivery [31], [3].
  - GitLab CI with DAG pipelines — gives integrated SCM+CI features and can be tuned (cache policy and needs) to reduce pipeline time; GitLab.com shared runner tails and caching defaults require deliberate platform tuning, and GitLab SaaS has a noted pipeline execution audit gap to address for strict compliance [1], [17].

# Impact of Rubber Leaf’s Supply‑Model Shift on Gross Margin — Q1 2023 vs Q1 2024

Executive summary
- Reported gross margin fell from 21.2% in Q1 2023 to approximately −6.66% in Q1 2024, a deterioration of ~27.9 percentage points (a ~131% relative decline versus Q1 2023). The Q1 2024 cost of sales shown in the available filings includes factory‑relocation losses presented within cost of sales, but the findings do not disclose a relocation loss amount for Q1 2024. A relocation loss of $190,703 is reported for the three months ended March 31, 2025 (for reference). Removing a relocation loss equal to $190,703 from Q1 2024 cost of sales (scenario) would reduce the Q1 2024 gross loss to approximately −0.20% (near break‑even), meaning most of the reported margin deterioration would be explained by a one‑time relocation charge of that size; however, even after that adjustment an underlying margin shortfall versus Q1 2023 remains (~21.4 percentage points). Key remaining drivers consistent with an indirect supply model are higher third‑party logistics, vendor margins and inventory adjustments, lower direct‑model volume/mix, and idle‑capacity costs. The analysis below shows all calculations, identifies evidence gaps, and lists follow‑up data requests.

## 1) Reported figures and computed gross margins (method and sources)
- Q1 2023 (reported)
  - Net sales (reported): 3,931.8 (as reported in the company Q1 2023 press release) and gross profit = 835.5, with gross profit = 21.2% of net sales (company disclosure) [1].
  - Use company’s reported gross‑profit percent (21.2%) as the Q1 2023 reported gross margin [1].

- Q1 2024 (reported)
  - Revenue (reported): $2,954,607 for the three months ended March 31, 2024; Cost of sales (reported): $3,151,232 for the three months ended March 31, 2024 (company filing) [2].
  - Computation (gross margin = (Revenue − COGS) / Revenue):
    - Gross profit (Q1 2024) = 2,954,607 − 3,151,232 = −196,625
    - Reported Q1 2024 gross margin = −196,625 / 2,954,607 = −0.066565 ≈ −6.66% (rounded) [2].

- Year‑over‑year change (reported margins)
  - Absolute change (percentage points): −6.66% − 21.20% = −27.86 percentage points.
  - Relative percent change vs Q1 2023: (−27.86 pp) / 21.20% = −1.3137 → −131.4% (the margin has a ~131% relative decline from Q1 2023) [1], [2].

(Sources for Q1 2023 metrics and Q1 2024 revenue/COGS cited together here) [1], [2].

## 2) Factory‑relocation loss: presence, location in statements, and quantification
- Presentation in financials
  - The filing notes that a loss on factory relocation is presented within the Cost of Sales section of the company’s 10‑Q (i.e., relocation costs are included in reported cost of sales rather than booked separately below gross profit) [2].
- Quantification for Q1 2024
  - The research findings do not include a relocation‑loss dollar amount explicitly reported for the three months ended March 31, 2024. Therefore the relocation loss amount for Q1 2024 is Not Disclosed in the available findings.
  - For reference, the findings do report a loss on factory relocation of $190,703 for the three months ended March 31, 2025 (i.e., the 2025 quarter) and also show cost‑of‑sales and cost‑of‑revenues composition language that confirms relocation/idle capacity are reflected within cost of sales; however, that 2025 relocation amount cannot be treated as Q1 2024’s relocation loss without explicit disclosure [2].

(Source: presentation of relocation loss in cost of sales and the 2025 relocation amount are from the same filing) [2].

## 3) Adjusted Q1 2024 gross margin (removing relocation loss) — feasibility and scenarios
- Feasibility note: Because the findings do not disclose the Q1 2024 relocation loss amount, an exact, evidence‑based single adjusted Q1 2024 gross margin cannot be calculated from the available evidence. Two types of adjustments are therefore shown:
  - A) Reference adjustment using the relocation loss reported in a later period (Q1 2025) for comparison: $190,703 (reported for Mar 31, 2025) — shown only as a scenario (the evidence does not state that same amount applied to Q1 2024) [2].
  - B) Sensitivity scenarios using hypothetical but plausible relocation‑loss sizes to show how adjusted Q1 2024 gross margin would vary if relocation costs of different magnitudes had been included in reported Q1 2024 cost of sales.

- Scenario calculations (all use reported Q1 2024 revenue = 2,954,607 and reported total cost of sales = 3,151,232) [2].
  - Baseline (reported): COGS = 3,151,232 → reported gross margin = −6.6565% (as above).
  - Scenario 1 — Remove relocation loss = $0 (i.e., assume no relocation loss included): adjusted COGS = 3,151,232 − 0 = 3,151,232 → adjusted gross margin = −6.66% (no change).
  - Scenario 2 — Remove relocation loss = $100,000: adjusted COGS = 3,051,232 → adjusted gross margin = (2,954,607 − 3,051,232) / 2,954,607 = −96,625 / 2,954,607 = −3.27%.
  - Scenario 3 — Remove relocation loss = $190,703 (Q1 2025 reported relocation loss, shown for reference): adjusted COGS = 3,151,232 − 190,703 = 2,960,529 → adjusted gross margin = (2,954,607 − 2,960,529) / 2,954,607 = −5,922 / 2,954,607 = −0.20%.
  - Scenario 4 — Remove relocation loss = $300,000: adjusted COGS = 2,851,232 → adjusted gross margin = (2,954,607 − 2,851,232) / 2,954,607 = 103,375 / 2,954,607 = +3.50%.

(All scenarios use the reported Q1 2024 revenue and cost of sales figures as the starting point) [2].

## 4) Reconciliation table (reported vs adjusted; relocation amount unknown → scenario column included)
- Table format: Metric | Q1 2023 (reported) | Q1 2024 (reported) | Q1 2024 (adjusted — Remove relocation = $190,703, scenario)
  (Table includes the core requested fields. Note: source rows follow the table below.)

Metric | Q1 2023 (reported) | Q1 2024 (reported) | Q1 2024 (adjusted, L = $190,703 scenario)
--- | ---:| ---:| ---:
Reported revenue | 3,931.8 (as reported in Q1 2023 press release) | $2,954,607 [reported] | $2,954,607 (same)
Reported cost of sales | 3,096.3 | $3,151,232 [reported] | Adjusted COGS = $3,151,232 − $190,703 = $2,960,529
Reported gross margin | 21.2% (company reported) [=835.5/3,931.8] [1] | −6.66% (computed) [2] | −0.20% (computed after removing $190,703; scenario) [2]
Relocation loss amount (disclosed) | Not reported for Q1 2023 | Not disclosed for Q1 2024 in the findings; relocation loss is presented within Cost of Sales in the filings. For reference: $190,703 relocation loss is reported for three months ended Mar 31, 2025 (not Q1 2024) [2]. | $190,703 (scenario amount — Q1 2025 reported figure used for scenario only) [2]
Absolute difference (reported vs adjusted) | n/a | n/a | Reported − adjusted margin = −6.66% − (−0.20%) = −6.46 percentage points (improvement of 6.46 pp when removing $190,703)
Relative difference (reported vs adjusted) | n/a | n/a | Reported margin improves ~97% of the reported deficit when removing $190,703 (6.46 pp improvement relative to 6.66 pp reported shortfall)
YoY margin change before adjustment | − | −27.86 pp (−6.66% − 21.2%) | −27.86 pp (same baseline)
YoY margin change after adjustment (L = $190,703) | − | −21.40 pp (−0.20% − 21.2%) | −21.40 pp

Sources for table entries: Q1 2023 press release figures and reported gross‑profit percent [1]; Q1 2024 revenue and COGS and disclosure that relocation loss is presented in cost of sales, plus Q1 2025 relocation amount for reference [2].

## 5) Sensitivity / scenario analysis (summary and implication)
- Purpose: show how adjusted Q1 2024 gross margin would move if a one‑time relocation charge of varying size were included in reported COGS.
- Key scenarios (using reported Q1 2024 revenue 2,954,607 and reported total COGS 3,151,232) [2]:
  - L = $0 → adjusted margin = −6.66% (no change).
  - L = $100,000 → adjusted margin ≈ −3.27% (partial recovery, still negative).
  - L = $190,703 → adjusted margin ≈ −0.20% (near break‑even).
  - L = $300,000 → adjusted margin ≈ +3.50% (positive margin restored).
- Interpretation:
  - If a relocation loss in Q1 2024 were in the $150k–$200k range (the single explicit relocation figure available from a later quarter is $190,703), then removing that one‑time cost would largely explain the steep reported drop in gross margin and would leave underlying gross margin near zero (i.e., the one‑time relocation cost would account for most of the reported gross‑margin decline).
  - If relocation costs in Q1 2024 were materially larger (e.g., $300k), removing them would more than restore a positive gross margin for the quarter; if materially smaller (e.g., <$100k), a meaningful underlying gross loss would remain even after adjustment.
  - Because the Q1 2024 relocation loss is Not Disclosed in the available findings, conclusions about whether margin pressure is structural versus one‑time are sensitive to the (unknown) relocation amount; however, a relocation charge on the order of ~$190k would explain most of the reported Q1 2024 margin deterioration.

## 6) Qualitative assessment — are remaining margin effects consistent with an indirect supply model?
- Evidence on cost structure and supply‑model mechanics
  - Company disclosure indicates two supply models (direct and indirect/Model B) and that cost of revenues includes raw materials consumed, manufacturing costs, third‑party logistics and distribution costs (packaging, freight, transportation, shipping and handling), and inventory adjustments due to defectives and inventory counts [2], [3].
  - The company’s filings and annual discussion note that the shift away from direct‑model sales and factory relocation/idle capacity contributed to lower gross profit and higher losses in the period (annual commentary cites losses due to factory relocation and idle capacity) [4].
- Which cost items/operational metrics in the evidence would drive remaining margin change after removing relocation loss
  - Third‑party logistics, freight and packaging: Cost‑of‑revenues explicit line items include third‑party logistics and related transportation/shipping/handling costs; moving to an indirect supply model typically increases reliance on third‑party intermediaries and LOGISTICS costs, which are present in the company’s cost composition [2].
  - Vendor margins / purchase prices: In the indirect model the company purchases raw materials and equipment through named third parties; margins or markups by these intermediaries and any increase in input prices could raise COGS (research findings note the company purchases main raw materials from third parties under indirect supply) [2].
  - Inventory adjustments and defectives: Cost of revenues explicitly includes inventory adjustments due to defectives and counts; increases here (including write‑downs during relocation or model transition) would depress gross margin [2].
  - Reduced direct‑model volume / mix: The company reported reduced demand from the direct supply model; lower volume of higher‑margin direct sales or adverse product mix can lower aggregate gross margin (annual commentary) [4].
  - Idle capacity: Management cited idle‑capacity losses related to the factory transition which are reflected in gross results [4].
- Conclusion on structural vs one‑time:
  - Removing a relocation charge of a plausible magnitude (e.g., the $190,703 reference amount from Q1 2025) would materially narrow or nearly eliminate the reported Q1 2024 gross loss, indicating a substantial portion of the reported deterioration may be one‑time relocation‑related costs.
  - However, even after removal of a $190k relocation charge the adjusted Q1 2024 margin remains much lower than Q1 2023 (≈ −0.20% vs 21.2%); that remaining shortfall is consistent with structural effects expected from a move to an indirect supply model (higher third‑party logistics and vendor margins, inventory adjustments, lower direct‑model volumes/mix, and idle capacity). The evidence therefore supports a mixed conclusion: one‑time relocation costs likely account for a large share of the reported drop, but underlying operational changes associated with the indirect model plausibly continue to exert downward pressure on gross margin.

Sources used for qualitative assessment: cost of revenues composition & relocation presentation [2]; description of direct vs indirect models and expectations around Model B rates and operations [3]; annual commentary on relocation/idle capacity and gross loss increase [4].

## 7) Evidence gaps and limits
- Q1 2024 relocation loss amount: The facts do NOT include a specific dollar amount for a factory‑relocation loss in the three months ended March 31, 2024. The only explicit relocation‑loss dollar in the findings is $190,703 for the three months ended March 31, 2025 — not Q1 2024 — so it cannot be assumed equal to the 2024 charge without confirmation [2].
- Unit and presentation consistency: The Q1 2023 press release reports figures as 3,931.8 / 3,096.3 / 835.5 (no explicit unit label in the provided facts); Q1 2024 figures are reported as full‑dollar amounts (e.g., $2,954,607). The findings do not state the units explicitly for the Q1 2023 figures (e.g., thousands vs dollars). This creates ambiguity for direct numeric comparisons of levels; ratio comparisons (gross margin percentages) remain valid because they are unitless, but confirmation of units in the original Q1 2023 release/filing is required for unambiguous dollar‑level reconciliation [1], [2].
- Detailed cost‑of‑sales breakout for Q1 2024: No line‑by‑line COGS breakdown for Q1 2024 (raw materials vs logistics vs relocation vs inventory write‑downs) is provided in the findings. The presence and magnitude of relocation, idle capacity and inventory adjustments within COGS is noted qualitatively but not quantified for Q1 2024 [2], [4].
- Volumes and product mix: No unit volume or mix data for Q1 2023 vs Q1 2024 is in the findings, so the impact of lower direct‑model volume or mix shifts cannot be quantified precisely from the available evidence [3], [4].

## 8) Follow‑up data requests (to close uncertainties and produce a definitive adjusted margin)
Please provide the following items from corporate filings or internal reporting (preferably with exact 10‑Q page/footnote references):
1. The Q1 2024 Form 10‑Q (or quarterly financial statements and accompanying notes) pages/notes that disclose cost of sales line‑items and any component labeled “loss on factory relocation” (exact dollar amount for the three months ended March 31, 2024) and the explicit statement that the relocation loss is included within cost of sales (if already present, give page/footnote number). (Needed: to compute the exact adjusted Q1 2024 gross margin.)
2. A detailed cost‑of‑sales (COGS) schedule for Q1 2024 showing raw materials consumed, manufacturing costs, third‑party logistics & distribution, inventory adjustments (defectives/write‑downs), idle capacity costs and relocation costs as separate line items or sub‑components (with dollar amounts).
3. Confirmation of the units reported in the Q1 2023 press release (i.e., whether 3,931.8 and 3,096.3 represent $3,931,800 or $3,931.8) so that dollar‑level YoY reconciliations are consistent.
4. Volume and ASP / price per unit (or revenue per major product family) for Q1 2023 and Q1 2024 to quantify mix and volume effects on gross margin.
5. Any management commentary, MD&A section or earnings call transcript excerpt that quantifies the expected ongoing (recurring) incremental per‑unit cost impacts of the indirect supply model (e.g., incremental freight per unit, typical vendor markup percentages) and the expected duration of relocation‑related idle costs.
6. If available, a reconciliation schedule prepared by management (or in the 10‑Q footnotes) that reconciles reported COGS to COGS excluding nonrecurring relocation and idle capacity items for Q1 2024 and adjacent quarters.

## 9) Short conclusion
- The reported Q1 2024 gross margin (≈ −6.66%) is a large deterioration from Q1 2023 (21.2%). The filings show relocation losses are included in cost of sales, but the findings do not disclose the Q1 2024 relocation loss amount needed to compute a single definitive adjusted Q1 2024 margin. Scenario analysis using a relocation number available for Q1 2025 ($190,703) shows that removal of a relocation charge of that magnitude would materially reduce the reported Q1 2024 gross loss (to roughly −0.20%), implying the one‑time relocation cost could explain the bulk of the reported deterioration. Even after that adjustment, a significant gap versus Q1 2023 remains, and the remaining shortfall is consistent with expected ongoing effects of moving to an indirect supply model (higher third‑party logistics, vendor margins/markup, inventory adjustments and lower higher‑margin direct sales). Definitive attribution between one‑time relocation charges and structural margin effects requires the detailed Q1 2024 COGS breakout and confirmation of the relocation loss amount requested above.
