# Comparative report: Maternal mortality and prenatal-care access — Rohingya (Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh) vs Karen (Mae La camp, Thailand), 2017–2023

Executive summary
- Over 2017–2023 available data show consistently worse maternal and perinatal outcomes in the Rohingya camps in Cox’s Bazar than in Mae La camp on key indicators, but Rohingya indicators improved markedly from 2018 to 2023. Reported maternal mortality ratios (MMR) for Rohingya vary widely by data source and year (range reported ~179–352 per 100,000 live births for different periods and methods), while Mae La-era figures reported in available datasets are much lower (HIS 2018: zero maternal deaths reported in 2018 for Mae La; other camp-series analyses report a pooled MMR ~126.5 per 100,000 for studied Thai‑border camps). Antenatal care (ANC4+) and skilled birth attendance are substantially higher in Mae La than early Rohingya figures, though Rohingya ANC4+ and skilled attendance increased to roughly 75–82% by 2022–2023. Neonatal mortality is higher in Rohingya 2017–2018 surveillance (≈27/1,000) than Mae La 2018 (≈6/1,000). Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) incidence per 10,000 births is not reported in the evidence; MPMSR identifies haemorrhage as the major cause of maternal death in Cox’s Bazar but gives no standardized incidence rate. Documentation is heterogeneous, with several conflicting point estimates and key gaps (notably PPH incidence, consistent MMR series for Mae La 2017–2023, and explicit documentation of a 2021 UNFPA funding reduction and its measurable effects).

Scope and data sources
- This report synthesizes UNHCR Health Information System (HIS) data, UNFPA and MPMSR reports, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) operational publications, Health Sector bulletins for Cox’s Bazar, peer‑reviewed analyses (SMRU/PLOS and other academic papers), and program bulletins referenced below. Citations are provided in the References section; each source is cited in the body where its evidence is used.

1. Indicator comparison (2017–2023)

1.1 Maternal mortality ratio (MMR, per 100,000 live births)
- Rohingya (Cox’s Bazar)
  - A retrospective RAMOS covering Aug 2017–Aug 2018 estimated an MMR of 179 per 100,000 live births (95% CI 130–228) for Rohingya camps [1].  
  - Routine surveillance and bulletin-derived estimates for later years are higher in some reports: WHO-cited figures report camp MMRs of 229.17 (2022) and 200.39 (2023), with a decrease to 168 per 100,000 in 2024 [2]. Health‑sector bulletins contained divergent single‑period estimates (examples: 352 per 100,000 in July 2023; "nearly 300" per 100,000 in Sept 2023), indicating methodological/ascertainment differences across reports and months [3]. These discrepancies reflect different methods (RAMOS, facility surveillance, monthly bulletin extrapolations) and incompleteness of death ascertainment in some periods.
- Mae La (Thailand)
  - UNHCR HIS for Mae La (2018) reported zero maternal deaths for 2018 and high rates of rapid investigation of any maternal death reported; HIS also reported high antenatal and skilled‑attendance coverage in 2018 [11].  
  - A pooled or comparative study of Thai‑border camps reported an MMR of 126.5 per 100,000 live births for the studied camps (not limited explicitly to Mae La in the single sentence available), showing that MMRs in Thai camps historically have been substantially lower than early Rohingya RAMOS estimates but not necessarily zero in all contexts [15].  
- Interpretation and triangulation
  - Direct numeric comparability is limited by differing surveillance methods and timeframes. For Cox’s Bazar: RAMOS (active, retrospective) gave 179/100,000 for 2017–2018; routine bulletins and WHO later report variable higher values in 2022–2023, followed by improvement to 168/100,000 in 2024 [1],[2],[3]. For Mae La, HIS 2018 reports zero maternal deaths in that year but other analyses indicate non‑zero MMR in regional camp series [11],[15]. The weight of evidence indicates lower MMRs in Mae La than in Rohingya camps over the 2017–2023 window, recognizing heterogeneity and surveillance‑method bias between contexts.

1.2 Antenatal care completion (ANC4+)
- Rohingya (Cox’s Bazar)
  - Multiple program reports indicate an increase in ANC4+ coverage over time: BRAC household survey (2018) recorded ~76.6% of pregnant Rohingya women sought antenatal care; Health Sector and UNFPA 2023 bulletins report ANC4+ ≈75% for Rohingya mothers in 2023 (ANC‑4+ attendance for Rohingya mothers delivering in facilities reported at 75%) [6],[7].  
- Mae La (Thailand)
  - UNHCR HIS (2018) reported antenatal care coverage ~91% for Mae La; PLOS/SMRU reporting documents ~90% of pregnant women attending SMRU antenatal clinics and >90% attending at least four ANC visits in the camp‑clinic series [12],[13].  
- Comparison
  - Mae La demonstrates higher ANC coverage and ANC4+ than early Rohingya figures; by 2022–2023 Rohingya ANC4+ reached ~75%, narrowing the gap though remaining below the consistently >90% ANC4+ reported for Mae La [6],[7],[12].

1.3 Skilled birth attendance (% of births)
- Rohingya (Cox’s Bazar)
  - Skilled birth attendance increased substantially from very low facility‑birth rates in 2018 (reports cited facility births ~22% or facility deliveries only 22% of total in 2018 in some sources) to much higher proportions by 2022–2023. UNFPA and Health Sector bulletins document increases from ~12% skilled attendance in 2018 to ~73% in 2022 and an 82% proportion of births assisted by a skilled attendant in 2023 (health‑sector figure), while facility‑delivery shares reported in period bulletins vary by month and method [7],[3]. UNHCR‑supported facilities recorded 4,963 deliveries with 88% of those attended by skilled health workers in 2024 (facility subset) [4]. MSF reported a decline of home deliveries and increased facility capacity after 2017 [6].
- Mae La (Thailand)
  - UNHCR HIS (2018) reported 95% of births in Mae La were attended by skilled personnel in 2018; PLOS/SMRU reports indicate >75–90% of women now give birth at SMRU facilities, with substantial programmatic success shifting deliveries from TBAs to skilled attendants [11],[12]. Other camp‑series work gives ~80% skilled attendance across studied Thai camps [15].
- Comparison
  - Mae La shows consistently high skilled attendance (≥80–95% in available sources); Rohingya moved from very low early facility births to high skilled‑attendance proportions by 2022–2023 (≈73–82%) but with more variability across months and reporting streams [6],[7],[11],[12].

1.4 Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) — incidence per 10,000 births
- Evidence available
  - MPMSR/MPMSR‑based reporting for Cox’s Bazar identifies haemorrhage as the leading cause of maternal deaths in 2022 and notes these deaths occur mostly in the postpartum period, but no standardized incidence rate per 10,000 births is reported in the provided evidence [9]. No quantitative PPH incidence (per 10,000 births) was identified for Mae La in the available sources.  
- Conclusion
  - There is insufficient evidence to produce standardized PPH incidence rates (per 10,000 births) for either setting in 2017–2023; only cause‑of‑death attribution (haemorrhage prominent in Cox’s Bazar) is documented [9]. See Evidence gaps (Section 5).

1.5 Neonatal mortality (within 28 days, per 1,000 live births)
- Rohingya (Cox’s Bazar)
  - An epidemiologic surveillance estimate (Sep 2017–Dec 2018) produced a neonatal mortality rate of 27.0 (95% CI 22.3–31.8) per 1,000 live births for Rohingya refugees, with ~76% of neonatal deaths occurring at home or in the community [5]. Subsequent sector/perinatal bulletins report varying perinatal mortality and stillbirth rates (e.g., perinatal mortality 10.69/1,000 in 2023 and 17.90/1,000 in 2024 in WHO account), indicative of improvement or different denominators/definitions across instruments [2].  
- Mae La (Thailand)
  - UNHCR HIS reported a neonatal mortality rate of 6 per 1,000 live births in Mae La in 2018 [11]. Historical SMRU/clinic data show larger declines over decades (e.g., declines from ~21.8 to 10.7 per 1,000 in a 2009–2011 series reported for the border population), consistent with lower neonatal mortality in the Thai‑border camp system compared with the Rohingya influx setting [12],[13].  
- Comparison
  - Evidence supports a substantially higher neonatal mortality rate in the Rohingya camps during 2017–2018 (≈27/1,000) than in Mae La 2018 (≈6/1,000), with Rohingya perinatal indicators improving in some later reports but remaining variable across surveillance sources [5],[11],[2].

Disaggregation by age, parity, and place of birth (where documented)
- Age
  - In Cox’s Bazar, BRAC reported that 13.3% of married Rohingya women were pregnant (2018) and UNFPA reported girls <18 accounted for 3.33% of facility‑based deliveries in 2022 [6],[7]. In Mae La, HIS 2018 reported teenage pregnancies at 7% in that camp [11].  
- Parity
  - The available evidence does not provide systematic parity‑stratified outcomes for both settings across 2017–2023; parity disaggregation is an evidence gap.  
- Facility vs home births
  - Rohingya: substantial shifts over time are documented — MSF and CHW reporting indicate home deliveries decreased from ~88% in 2018 to ~30–35% by 2021 in some surveillance streams and facility births increased thereafter; however monthly bulletins show large month‑to‑month variance (example: July 2023 reported 80% facility births for that month while Sept 2023 bulletin reported facility births at 5% — demonstrating methodological or denominator inconsistencies across reports) [6],[3]. The 2017–2018 neonatal death analysis found ~76% of neonatal deaths occurred at home/community [5].  
  - Mae La: the transition from home births to facility births is well documented; >75% now choose facility births at SMRU with high coverage of facility‑based deliveries reported in multiple studies [12],[13].

2. Healthcare delivery models and associations with outcomes

2.1 Delivery models — brief description
- Cox’s Bazar (Rohingya camps)
  - Multiple NGOs (including MSF) operate field hospitals and primary‑level health posts; health‑sector mapping in March 2024 lists 58 health posts, 46 primary health centres, 1 CEmONC facility and 6 field hospitals in the response architecture [10]. UNFPA and other agencies support women‑friendly centres, midwife deployment and Emergency Referral Transport Service (ERTS) for obstetric referral [7],[10]. MSF historically provided rapid surge capacity and expanded facility capacity after August 2017 [6],[5].  
- Mae La (Thailand)
  - Health services in Mae La have long been provided under models integrating locally trained clinical staff with NGO clinical supervision (SMRU and similar actors), applying national protocols and linkage with the Thai Ministry of Public Health (MOPH) vaccination and public‑health systems. HIS 2018 describes strong ANC coverage and near‑universal skilled attendance, and SMRU has provided free basic humanitarian maternal care and progressively shifted births into clinic settings [11],[12],[13].

2.2 Correlation of delivery models with outcomes
- Midwife‑to‑population ratios (documented and derived)
  - Cox’s Bazar (Rohingya): Health Sector Bulletin Dec 2023 reported 1,277 skilled birth attendants with 36% midwives (≈460 midwives) [3]. Using the reported Rohingya camp population in 2023 of ≈975,350, that yields approximately 4.7 midwives per 10,000 population (calculation derived from the cited counts) — a programmatically meaningful but still relatively low midwife density for a high‑need setting [3],[10]. This derived ratio is sensitive to denominator and cadre‑definition choices (skilled birth attendants vs certified midwives) and should be interpreted cautiously.  
  - Mae La (Thailand): HIS 2018 lists cadres (3 doctors, 72 qualified nurses, 64 community health workers) and SMRU staffing of skilled birth attendants, but no explicit midwife headcount is provided for Mae La in the evidence set; therefore a comparable midwife‑to‑population ratio cannot be calculated from available sources (evidence gap) [11],[12].
- Emergency obstetric care (EmOC) availability within a 2‑hour transport radius
  - Cox’s Bazar: the health‑sector mapping of facilities (CEmONC availability in district, multiple field hospitals, and active ERTS referrals in 2023) provides evidence of proximate EmOC capacity inside the response area and a functioning referral system (10,492 ERTS referrals reported in 2023 for the response), suggesting that EmOC is accessible by organized referral for many women though transport and capacity constraints remain [7],[10].  
  - Mae La: evidence is mixed — a Women’s Refugee Commission assessment states emergency obstetric care is available 24/7 in most Thai border camp sites, consistent with a structured camp‑clinic network linked to national protocols [13]. In contrast, SMRU/region‑specific reporting documents the nearest Thai hospital (for secondary/tertiary referral) as being ~80 km away from camps in some areas (3.5–7 hours travel depending on season), indicating that comprehensive EmOC requiring hospital referral may not be reachable within 2 hours from certain camps or in all seasons [12]. This is an explicit conflict in the evidence: WRC reports routine availability of EmOC onsite or via system arrangements [13], whereas SMRU reporting documents long referral distances/time to the nearest Thai hospital in some locations [12]. The two statements can coexist if primary CEmONC is organized within camps (WRC claim) while higher‑level referral hospitals remain distant (SMRU claim), but the evidence does not clearly resolve which applies to Mae La specifically.
- Cultural mediation and traditional birth attendants (TBAs)
  - Cox’s Bazar: trust in TBAs and cultural birthing practices are documented drivers of home births; MSF and program surveys note higher trust in TBAs relative to formally trained midwives and describe cultural practices (e.g., birthing ropes, privacy preferences) that influence women’s choices [6],[5]. Community‑based surveillance and CHW engagement are part of death notification and referral pathways [1],[9].  
  - Mae La: service delivery has focused on training resident assistant midwives and skilled birth attendants (SMRU clinics), with camp residents staffing frontline services and cultural mediation performed by locally trained providers; SMRU’s model deliberately builds on local cadres to shift births into supervised facilities [12],[13].  
- Synthesis: how delivery models map to outcomes
  - The Mae La model of integrated, long‑standing camp clinics staffed by locally trained skilled attendants and aligned with national public‑health systems is associated with historically lower neonatal mortality and high ANC4+/skilled birth attendance in the available data [11],[12],[15].  
  - The Cox’s Bazar response has grown rapidly since 2017 with multiple NGO field hospitals, expanded midwife deployment and referral services; these programmatic efforts coincided with large improvements in ANC4+, skilled attendance and declining facility‑ and perinatal mortality in some bulletins, but overall mortality metrics and neonatal outcomes were worse in the early influx period and only improved unevenly thereafter [6],[3],[7],[2]. Differences in baseline population vulnerability, rapidity of influx, and initial service gaps (not shown in Mae La’s long‑term, stable camp model) likely contribute to outcome differences; the available evidence supports an association between integrated, sustained service models with locally trained staff (Mae La) and lower mortality, and between emergency NGO surge models that scaled up (Cox’s Bazar) and progressive but incomplete improvements in outcomes.

3. Measurable impact of a 2021 UNFPA funding reduction
- Evidence available
  - The body of provided evidence documents UNFPA‑supported service volumes in 2021 and onwards (e.g., 8,490 facility‑based deliveries and 83,501 ANC visits reported for 2021; UNFPA and sector bulletins reporting continued service delivery and large reach into 2022–2023, including ERTS referrals and midwife deployments) [8],[7],[16]. UNFPA 2023/2022 materials report ongoing midwife deployment, restoration of 24/7 CEmONC at Teknaf Health Complex, and large service reach in 2022–2023 [7],[16].  
- Evidence gap and conclusion
  - None of the provided documents explicitly documents a UNFPA funding reduction in 2021 or quantifies its direct measurable impact on continuity or coverage of maternal health services in Cox’s Bazar or Mae La. The evidence shows continued UNFPA program activity through 2022–2023 (service volumes, midwife deployments, restoration of CEmONC), but does not permit attribution of any observed service changes to a 2021 funding cut because the funding‑cut event and its financial or programming consequences are not described in the provided sources. Therefore, the question of measurable impact of a 2021 UNFPA funding reduction on maternal health services in each setting cannot be answered from the supplied evidence (see Evidence gaps) [8],[7],[16].

4. Triangulation, sensitivity considerations, and interpretation of conflicting figures
- Conflicting MMR and facility‑birth percentages in Cox’s Bazar arise from differing methods:
  - RAMOS (active retrospective recall/verification) gave 179/100,000 (Aug 2017–Aug 2018) [1]; routine monthly bulletins and facility surveillance report higher or lower point estimates for specific months/years (example: 352/100,000 in one bulletin month) [3]. WHO‑reported annualized figures for 2022–2023 differ again [2]. Where active enumeration (RAMOS) and careful perinatal surveillance exist, point estimates are more comparable; monthly bulletins may reflect small‑number variation, under/over‑reporting, or differing denominators. The reporting heterogeneity drives uncertainty in trend interpretation for Cox’s Bazar.  
- For Mae La, strong primary‑care ANC and delivery systems reported in HIS/SMRU sources correspond to low neonatal mortality and high skilled attendance in the data available for 2018 and earlier years; however, the HIS 2018 zero maternal deaths figure should be interpreted with awareness that the broader camp‑series analysis reports non‑zero MMRs for Thai‑border camps as a group [11],[15].  
- Sensitivity and derived metrics:
  - The derived midwife‑per‑10,000 figure for Rohingya (≈4.7/10,000) depends on the precise definition of "midwife" and on the population denominator used; different bulletins give slightly different population and cadre counts. This ratio should be considered indicative rather than definitive [3],[10].  
- Overall interpretive statement:
  - Despite data heterogeneity, the balance of program and epidemiologic evidence documents substantially better ANC4+, skilled attendance, and lower neonatal mortality in Mae La or Thai‑border camps relative to early Rohingya influx conditions; sustained and integrated service models with local cadres (Mae La/SMRU) are associated with these better outcomes, whereas the Cox’s Bazar response shows rapid improvements from a poorer starting point under an NGO‑led surge model but retains variability and higher mortality in several surveillance streams [12],[13],[1],[5].

5. Evidence gaps and bias risks
- Missing or insufficiently reported items
  - Standardized PPH incidence per 10,000 births (both settings): no numeric PPH incidence rates per 10,000 births were provided; only qualitative/attribution data (haemorrhage as leading cause) exist for Cox’s Bazar [9].  
  - Explicit, documented 2021 UNFPA funding reduction and quantified causal effects on service continuity: no source explicitly documents such a funding cut or quantifies its programmatic impacts in the supplied evidence [8],[16].  
  - Consistent, comparable MMR time series for Mae La across 2017–2023: HIS provides snapshots (2018) and regional studies report camp‑series averages, but there is no continuous Mae La 2017–2023 MMR series in the evidence [11],[15].  
  - Midwife headcount for Mae La and assistant‑vs‑certified midwife breakdowns sufficient to compute a comparable midwife/population ratio (no explicit midwife counts in the Mae La HIS) [11],[12].  
  - Parity‑stratified maternal and neonatal outcome rates in both settings over 2017–2023.  
- Bias risks and data limitations
  - Heterogeneous surveillance methods: RAMOS, routine facility surveillance, and monthly bulletins use different case definitions and ascertainment approaches, creating conflicts (notably for MMR and facility birth proportions in Cox’s Bazar) [1],[3],[2].  
  - Small‑number and monthly variation: some monthly bulletins report extreme values that likely reflect denominator choices or short reporting windows (example: a bulletin month with 5% facility births versus months with 80% facility births), limiting direct comparability without harmonization [3].  
  - Selection and reporting bias: facility‑based data will undercount community deaths and home births; community surveillance mitigates this but is variably implemented across time and camps [5],[1].  
  - Contextual confounding: differences in baseline population health, nutrition, displacement timing (rapid 2017 influx into Cox’s Bazar vs long‑standing Mae La population), and host‑state policies are not fully controllable in the supplied data and likely contribute to outcome differences beyond delivery‑model design.

6. Key conclusions and programmatic implications
- Comparative findings
  - Mae La / Thai‑border camps show higher and more stable ANC4+ coverage and skilled birth attendance and lower documented neonatal mortality in the available evidence than the Rohingya camps in Cox’s Bazar over the 2017–2023 window; Mae La’s model of integrated, sustained services with locally trained staff (SMRU and partner models) is associated with those outcomes [11],[12],[15].  
  - Cox’s Bazar started from a very poor service baseline in 2017, with high home‑birth proportions and high neonatal and maternal mortality in early surveillance; substantial programmatic scale‑up by NGOs and UN partners led to improved ANC4+ (~75% by 2023), marked increases in skilled birth attendance (to ~73–82% by 2022–2023 in sector reporting), and lower facility maternal deaths in some 2024 reports — but surveillance heterogeneity and conflicting monthly estimates leave residual uncertainty in trend magnitude [6],[3],[7],[2].  
- On causal attribution to delivery model
  - The evidence supports an association between integrated, sustained, locally‑embedded primary‑care/midwife models (Mae La) and superior maternal‑newborn outcomes relative to a rapid NGO surge response to a massive influx (Cox’s Bazar). However, direct causal attribution is limited by confounding (differences in population baseline health, displacement dynamics, host‑state health policies) and by differences in surveillance methodology; therefore, conclusions should be framed as plausible associations rather than incontrovertible causal statements [12],[13],[1],[6].  
- Operational recommendations suggested by the evidence
  - Strengthen community‑based surveillance (MPMSR) and harmonize denominators across bulletins to reduce reporting variability and better track trends [1],[3].  
  - Sustain and expand midwife deployment and in‑camp CEmONC capacity with robust referral transport, while continuing culturally sensitive community engagement to shift births from TBAs to supervised facilities (Cox’s Bazar trajectory shows this can improve coverage) [3],[6],[10].  
  - For contexts like Mae La, maintain training and support for locally resident midwives/assistant midwives and formal linkages with national health systems to preserve high ANC and skilled birth coverage [12],[13].

# Grounded Theory after Glaser, Strauss & Corbin, and Charmaz: Points of Divergence, Charmaz’s Reframing, Paradigm‑Wars Context, and Evidence on Contemporary Prevalence (2020–2024)

## Executive summary
- Glaser (especially in Theoretical Sensitivity, 1978) defended a strongly inductive, emergence‑focused grounded theory in which researchers minimize preconceptions, avoid imposing categories, and privilege constant comparison and theoretical sensitivity; he resisted formalized verification routines that, he argued, invited “forcing” data into preordained structures. The Straussian/Corbinian reformulation (Basics of Qualitative Research, 1990) moved toward more explicit coding procedures (open/axial/selective), technical devices for verifying conceptual relations, and a more permissive stance toward the use of prior literature and analytic devices for checking and elaborating theory; Glaser publicly rebutted this shift. Charmaz (Constructing Grounded Theory, 2006) reframed grounded theory through an explicit constructivist epistemology that acknowledges researcher–participant co‑construction, permits earlier engagement with literature, reconceptualizes coding and memoing practices, and recasts verification as reflexive and interpretive rather than as objective testing. These theoretical tensions played out amid wider qualitative “paradigm wars” (post‑positivist vs. constructivist/interpretivist positions) in the 1990s–2000s. The available bibliometric indicators in the present evidence base (partial citation counts and disciplinary patterns) show strong continuing citation of Glaser’s work, frequent use of Strauss & Corbin in some training contexts (notably as accessible, procedure‑oriented texts), and significant uptake of Charmaz’s constructivist GT; however, the provided findings do not contain a completed, journal‑level, 2020–2024 systematic citation analysis that can reliably identify a single dominant positionality in contemporary methodology training programs. [1]

## Background: origins and the split
The original Discovery of Grounded Theory (Glaser & Strauss, 1967) articulated a joint program emphasizing simultaneous data collection and analysis, constant comparison, and theory emerging from data rather than from prior hypotheses. Over the following decades Glaser and Strauss diverged intellectually; the 1978 Theoretical Sensitivity consolidated Glaser’s emergent/inductive emphases while Strauss’s later collaborations with Juliet Corbin (notably the 1990 Basics) articulated more prescriptive coding stages and analytic devices. The split generated substantive methodological disagreements about coding, verification, and researcher stance. [2]

## Comparative analysis: Glaser (Theoretical Sensitivity, 1978) vs Strauss & Corbin (Basics, 1990)

### (a) Role of pre‑existing theoretical frameworks in coding
- Glaser’s position: He cautioned against beginning grounded research with pre‑existing grounded theories or firm preconceptions; theory should be rooted in and emerge from the data, and premature commitment to hypotheses or frameworks undermines theoretical sensitivity and emergence. [3]
- Strauss & Corbin’s position: Their 1990 text departs from the strict abstention view by allowing (and, in practice, recommending) earlier engagement with literature and using existing knowledge as an analytic resource; their procedures are framed to help novice researchers conceptualize and systematize analysis. [4]
Synthesis: The key divergence is methodological permissiveness: Glaser advocated restraint toward prior frameworks to maximize emergence, while Strauss & Corbin allowed earlier literature and conceptual tools to guide coding—an opening that Glaser worried would channel findings toward preconceptions rather than let categories arise from the data. [3], [4]

### (b) Legitimacy of “forcing” data into categories
- Glaser’s stance (as summarized in critiques and his later responses): He criticized analytic devices that impose categories or logic that “force” data into preordained structures, arguing that forcing compromises discovery and produces categories that may not be grounded in participants’ patterns. [5]
- Strauss & Corbin’s practices: They introduced a structured three‑stage coding sequence (open, axial, selective) and analytic matrices and techniques intended to refine and relate concepts—practices that Glaser and others characterized as mechanistic and liable to encourage forcing. [6]
Synthesis: Strauss & Corbin’s methodological apparatus was developed to aid analytic rigor and transparency (and to be teachable), but critics (notably Glaser) argued it legitimized approaches that risked forcing. The tension is therefore both epistemological (what counts as emergent evidence) and pedagogical (how to train novices to produce credible concepts). [5], [6]

### (c) Use of verification procedures
- Glaser’s orientation: Emphasized induction, constant comparison, and theoretical sampling as means of grounding and testing (in the sense of refining) emergent theory—less emphasis on formalized deductive verification steps that appear to test hypotheses in a positivist manner. [7]
- Strauss & Corbin’s orientation: More comfortable incorporating verification/deductive moves and explicit technical checks (procedures and paradigms within coding to establish relationships and conditions), treating verification as an integral and partly formalized component of analytic rigor. [7]
Synthesis: Strauss & Corbin shifted grounded theory toward more explicit verification and deductive checks, whereas Glaser maintained that verification should emerge organically through iterative sampling and comparison and cautioned against codified “tests” that might impose structure. This represents a methodological‑philosophical divide over formal verification versus iterative, data‑led theory refinement. [7]

## Kathy Charmaz (Constructing Grounded Theory, 2006): reframing and epistemological shift
- Charmaz adopted and extended core grounded theory practices (constant comparison, coding, memo writing) but reframed them through an explicit constructivist, subjectivist epistemology that treats data, codes, and theories as co‑constructed between researcher and participants rather than discovered as objective facts. She encourages early coding and memoing, line‑by‑line/gerund coding to capture action/process, and openness to engaging literature early to craft a research argument and later to situate emergent theory. Charmaz reconceived verification not as objective testing but as reflexive comparison, interpretive credibility, and transparent analytic practice (including treating memos as analyzable data). [8], [9]
- Practical consequences: Charmaz’s model seeks to mediate the Glaser–Strauss/Corbin tension by (a) accepting researcher involvement and interpretive framing (resolving Glaser’s strict emergence claim), (b) retaining disciplined comparative coding and iterative theory development (addressing concerns about rigor), and (c) reframing verification as reflexive, contextual, and co‑constructed rather than as formal deductive testing. [8], [9]

## Situating the debate within the 1990s–2000s “paradigm wars”
- The methodological disputes between Glaser and Straussian/Corbinian approaches unfolded against broader qualitative paradigm debates characterized by challenges between positivist/post‑positivist and interpretivist/constructivist logics; influential edited collections and debates in the 1990s consolidated these contested epistemologies and evaluative criteria for qualitative work. Denzin & Lincoln’s edited volumes and discussions of paradigm eras (pre‑positivist, positivist, post‑positivist) reflect and exemplify that broader contestation. The Glaser–Strauss/Corbin–Charmaz exchanges thus map onto wider disputes over objectivity, verification, and researcher positionality in qualitative methodology. [10], [11]

## What the available citation indicators (2020–2024 evidence base) show about contemporary predominance in training literature
- Partial bibliometric indicators from the present evidence set:
  - Glaser’s works retain very high citation counts in Google Scholar metrics (the provided profile shows substantial cumulative citations and sustained recent citations), indicating continued centrality of Glaserian texts in the literature that informs teaching and methods resources. [12]
  - Strauss & Corbin’s Basics (1990, later editions) remains frequently cited and is specifically noted as the second most referenced grounded theory text among a sample of Brazilian authors examining grounded theory usage; the Straussian/Corbinian variant is described as structured, accessible, and oriented to operationalization—features associated with use in training and by novice researchers. [13]
- Limitations of the present evidence for determining dominance: The supplied findings do not include a completed, journal‑level systematic citation analysis (i.e., extracted raw counts, normalized citation rates, co‑citation networks, or author‑cohort mapping) restricted to the specified corpus of major qualitative methodology journals for 2020–2024. Consequently, it is not possible on the basis of the supplied materials to state definitively which position (Glaserian, Straussian/Corbinian, Charmazian/constructivist, or hybrid/other) predominates in the contemporary methodology literature used to train researchers. [12], [13]

### Practical note on how a conclusive 2020–2024 analysis should be constructed
- The literature contains examples of recent bibliometric workflows that marshal Scopus or Web of Science extractions, detailed screening, and mapping (annual outputs, citation distributions, co‑citation networks) that could be adapted to the present research brief; such procedures would be necessary to generate defensible dominance claims for methodology training programs based on journal literature. The present evidence provides methodological exemplars but not the target counts or networks themselves. [14], [15]

## Evidence gaps
- No source in the provided findings contains a completed, reproducible systematic citation analysis of major qualitative methodology journals (Qualitative Inquiry; Qualitative Research; International Journal of Qualitative Methods; Symbolic Interaction; and relevant methods sections of top social science journals) specifically for the period 2020–2024 that (a) applies inclusion criteria distinguishing methodological/theoretical/training articles from empirical papers and (b) reports normalized citation rates, co‑citation maps, and author‑cohort network analyses.
- No single source in the supplied findings quantifies relative prevalence (percent or rank order) of Glaserian, Straussian/Corbinian, Charmazian, or hybrid positions within the contemporary methods training literature for 2020–2024.
- The available metrics (Google Scholar profile and selective citation counts) are suggestive but insufficient for journal‑corpus inference without fuller database extraction and normalization.

## Conclusion and recommended next steps
- Substantively, the disagreement between Glaser and Strauss/Corbin over pre‑existing theory, forcing categories, and verification is well evidenced: Glaser stressed inductive emergence and cautioned against prior frameworks, forcing, and codified verification; Strauss & Corbin offered structured coding and more explicit verification/analytic devices and permitted earlier engagement with literature; Charmaz reframed the debate by adopting an explicit constructivist epistemology that legitimizes researcher reflexivity, a measured use of prior literature, and reflexive rather than positivist verification. These positions map onto broader paradigm debates of the 1990s–2000s concerning objectivity and interpretive inquiry. [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11]
- To answer decisively which position predominates in the contemporary methodology training literature (2020–2024), a dedicated bibliometric and content analysis—drawing on Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar/Dimensions, restricted to the named methodology journals and applying the brief’s inclusion criteria—is required. The present evidence supplies partial indicators (notably Glaser’s continuing citations and Strauss & Corbin’s uptake in pedagogical contexts) and methodological exemplars for such a study but does not itself contain the necessary corpus‑level analysis. # Comparative report — Edelweiss Greater China Equity Offshore Fund vs DSP Global Innovation Overseas Equity Omni FoF (reference point: data near 31 Dec 2024)

Scope and data‑notes
- Requested reference date: 31 Dec 2024. The underlying disclosures in the available evidence do not contain complete holdings/returns exactly dated 31 Dec 2024 for both schemes; where Dec‑31‑2024 data were not available the nearest available official fund literature or factsheet is used and the reporting date is shown with each item below. All figures and statements are drawn only from the cited sources in the Works Cited. Methodology, share‑class choice and the list of reporting dates are given in the Methodology note at the end.  

## Executive summary (one paragraph)
Edelweiss Greater China Equity Offshore Fund (an India‑domiciled fund‑of‑fund investing into JPMorgan Funds – Greater China Fund) is regionally concentrated in Greater China equities and (by the nearest holding disclosure) had top‑10 stock weights totalling roughly 40.6% as of 31 July 2024; it is primarily equity (≈97% equity per the fund factsheet) and has a multi‑percent total expense ratio reported in fund factsheets. DSP Global Innovation Overseas Equity Omni FoF is a thematic global innovation fund‑of‑fund that holds other international funds/ETFs (top four underlying funds/ETFs comprised ~92% of the portfolio in the nearest disclosure), giving it exposure concentrated into broad innovation ETFs and specialist active global funds rather than individual Greater China stocks. Because Edelweiss concentrates on a single region and individual stocks, it shows higher single‑region / single‑market concentration risk and is better suited to a multi‑year (5‑year) horizon; DSP’s structure (underlying ETFs/funds with broad global innovation exposure), while still high risk, gives comparatively broader diversification across markets and may be the preferable option for a shorter (2‑year) horizon if the investor prioritizes liquidity/ETF exposure and wants a shorter time to realize potential returns — subject to fees and investor risk tolerance. The detailed evidence, calculations, ambiguities and citations follow.

---

## 1) Portfolio composition and concentration

Summary table of which share/class was used (note on share‑class availability)
- Edelweiss: analysis uses the India‑domiciled Edelweiss Greater China Equity Offshore Fund scheme (Regular / Growth plan figures where the factsheet reports AUM and portfolio details). The fund is an open‑ended India mutual fund that invests into JPMorgan Funds – Greater China Fund (underlying). (nearest holdings disclosure used: 31 July 2024 for top‑10; factsheet asset allocation date: 31 Mar 2026 for asset mix) [1], [2], [3].  
- DSP: analysis uses the India‑domiciled DSP Global Innovation Overseas Equity Omni FoF scheme (Regular/Regular‑Growth facts shown in the factsheets and KIM). The scheme is an open‑ended fund‑of‑fund that invests predominantly in underlying global innovation funds/ETFs. (nearest holdings/portfolio disclosure used: Sep 2024 / factsheet‑style data shown in mutual‑fund factsheets cited below) [4], [5].

(Reason: the evidence does not provide an offshore USD/HKD‑domiciled retail share class for either fund; the onshore India domiciled scheme documentation and factsheets are therefore used as the investor‑facing share classes. The specific documents used are cited in each subsection below.)

1.1 Basic scheme size, domicile, number of holdings and share class used
- Edelweiss Greater China Equity Offshore Fund (India‑domiciled open‑ended FoF): AUM reported as ₹1,960–₹2,678 crore in the fund literature depending on reporting date (factsheets show figures at different dates). The fund is an India mutual fund investing into JPMorgan Funds – Greater China Fund; the scheme type and objective are described in official Edelweiss literature [1], [6]. (A recent factsheet lists AUM ≈₹2,678.32 crore as of 31 Mar 2026 — this is a later date; nearest holdings disclosure used below is 31 Jul 2024) [3], [6].  
  - Number of individual underlying equity holdings (full list) is not published in the cited Oct‑2024 slides, but the slides provide the top‑10 weights (see below) and the Aug‑2025 factsheet provides a longer list of named holdings and weights (nearest full list after Dec‑2024) [11], [6].  
- DSP Global Innovation Overseas Equity Omni FoF (India‑domiciled open‑ended FoF): AUM ~₹1,151–1,238 crore in fund factsheets depending on reporting date; scheme launched 14 Feb 2022 and is managed by DSP Asset Managers [4], [5]. The scheme primarily holds other international mutual funds and ETFs (the KIM and factsheets list the main underlying funds) [4], [9].

(Each scheme is India‑domiciled; the documentation does not provide an offshore USD/HKD retail share class in the available evidence, so the onshore scheme factsheets are used as the investor‑facing class for analysis.) [1], [4].

1.2 Geographic breakdown (regions requested: Greater China mainland A‑shares, Hong Kong, Taiwan, US, Europe, Rest of World)
- Edelweiss: No complete region‑level percentage breakdown by those exact buckets is published in the cited Oct‑2024 slides or product collateral for the Dec‑31‑2024 target date; the Oct‑2024 deck reports the fund’s top‑10 holdings and each issuer name which allows identification of domicile for the top names (example: Tencent — Hong Kong, TSMC — Taiwan, Meituan — Hong Kong/China ADR structure, Pinduoduo — US‑listed ADR but China‑operating) and the Aug‑2025 factsheet lists a broader set of holdings with weights (nearest broader list after Dec‑2024). Use of issuer domiciles to sum region exposures is not possible from the partial top‑holding disclosures alone without assuming weights for the remaining holdings; therefore a full region‑weight breakdown in the requested buckets is not available in the evidence. The Oct‑2024 top‑10 holding list (with weights) is provided below and shows dominant Greater China / Taiwan names among the largest weights [11], [6].  
  - (Evidence gap: a full region breakdown by the specified buckets is not provided in the available disclosures for Dec‑31‑2024; nearest holdings are 31 Jul 2024 and 31 Jul 2025 documents — see Evidence Gaps below.) [11], [6].
- DSP: The scheme’s disclosed portfolio is comprised of other funds/ETFs (BlueBox Global Technology Fund, iShares NASDAQ‑100 UCITS ETF, KraneShares CSI China Internet ETF, Invesco NASDAQ‑100 Equal Weight ETF, etc.) and the fund‑level disclosures classify underlying assets by fund names rather than per‑country weights; a country/region split in the requested buckets is not provided in the cited KIM or Sep‑2024 literature. The underlying ETFs give the scheme exposure to the US (NASDAQ‑100 ETFs), China internet (KraneShares ETF) and global active funds, but the scheme documentation does not publish a simple Greater China/HK/Taiwan/US/Europe split in the available evidence. Therefore a formal numeric regional breakdown (by the requested buckets) is not available from the evidence. [4], [9].

1.3 Sector breakdown (GICS or fund’s reported classification)
- Edelweiss: The Oct‑2024 fund deck lists sector weights for the fund‑level reporting date 31 Jul 2024; it explicitly reports a Financials sector weight of 16.7% as of 31 Jul 2024 and provides top‑ten holdings and weights (which are dominated by Technology / Internet / Consumer‑internet and large semiconductor names among the top holdings). A separate factsheet record lists a different single‑figure sector allocation (a later factsheet entry that reports "Financials constitute 98.47%" appears in the aggregated evidence and conflicts with the Oct‑2024 deck; the 98.47% figure is implausible given the top‑10 list and is flagged as a conflicting data point below). See the Evidence‑conflict note and the Oct‑2024 top‑10 list for the sector picture (technology + internet names + financials present among top holdings). [11], [6].
- DSP: The scheme reports its portfolio allocation in fund‑type terms: the most recent fact disclosure in the evidence shows sector allocation as 98.57% Mutual Funds and 1.43% Current Assets (i.e., the DSP scheme holds other funds/ETFs, not single‑stock sector buckets) — this is the scheme‑level classification rather than a GICS sector split for underlying equities. The Sep‑2024 literature documents that the underlying funds are technology/innovation oriented (semiconductors, world tech, NASDAQ‑100, precision medicine, China internet ETF etc.) which implies large technology/health/innovation exposure, but a GICS sector breakdown at the DSP FoF level is not provided in the evidence. [4], [9].

1.4 Concentration metrics (top‑10 / top‑20 weights; HHI; active share)
- Edelweiss (nearest holdings disclosure 31 Jul 2024 — Oct‑2024 deck): the top‑10 holdings and weights reported as of 31 Jul 2024 are: Tencent 9.98%, TSMC 9.35%, Meituan 3.09%, Pinduoduo 3.07%, AIA 2.94%, Hong Kong Exchanges & Clearing 2.83%, Quanta Computer 2.62%, NetEase 2.32%, China Pacific Insurance 2.31%, Trip.com 2.08%. The sum of these top‑10 weights ≈ 40.6% (calculated from the disclosed weights) [11].  
  - Top‑20 weight and HHI: a full top‑20 list at 31 Jul 2024 is not published in the Oct‑2024 slides; the Aug‑2025 factsheet supplies a longer holdings list (nearest later disclosure) but that is dated 31 Jul 2025 — therefore a precise top‑20 weight or Herfindahl‑Hirschman Index (HHI) for 31 Dec 2024 cannot be computed from the available documents without making unsupported assumptions about the missing holdings; see Evidence Gaps. [6], [11].  
  - Active share: the fund documents in the evidence do not report an active‑share statistic for the scheme. [1], [6], [11].
- DSP (nearest holdings disclosure in factsheets / mfiframes): the top underlying holdings (funds/ETFs) and weights reported in the factsheet evidence are BlueBox Global Technology Fund ~38.7%, iShares NASDAQ‑100 UCITS ETF ~27.3%, KraneShares CSI China Internet UCITS ETF ~14.1%, IVZ NASDAQ‑100 Equal Weight ~11.9%, Fidelity Select Medical Technology ~4.05%, BlueBox Precision Medicine Fund ~2.44% with small cash/REPO items (~1–4%). Using those facts the top‑4 underlying positions sum to ~92% of the portfolio in the nearest disclosure; top‑3 sum ~80% (simple sum of the disclosed weights) [4].  
  - HHI and active share: HHI is not reported and cannot be computed accurately for equities exposure because the scheme holds other funds/ETFs rather than individual stocks; active share is not reported in the evidence. [4], [9].

1.5 Asset allocation (equity / cash / bonds)
- Edelweiss: the EconomicTimes factsheet lists asset allocation as 96.91% equity, 3.27% debt and –0.18% others for the scheme in a factsheet (reporting date shown in the factsheet metadata). This indicates the scheme is essentially an equity fund‑of‑fund with only small other allocations reported by the factsheet [3].  
- DSP: the mfiframes / factsheets list the scheme as ~96–99% invested in mutual funds (underlying equity funds/ETFs) with small cash/treps (e.g., 1.61% Triparty Repo in one factsheet). Another DSP factsheet lists portfolio allocation 96.0% equity and 4.0% debt as of 31 Mar 2026; the evidence consistently shows a high equity allocation and small cash holdings at the FoF level [4], [9].

---

## 2) Overlap in top‑20 holdings (issuer/ticker matching)

2.1 Top holdings lists used (nearest official disclosures; reporting dates)
- Edelweiss — nearest official top‑10 holdings disclosure to Dec‑31‑2024: Oct‑2024 slide deck reporting holdings as of 31 Jul 2024 (top‑10 shown) — full top‑20 not available in that slide deck; a wider holdings list with weights is available in the Aug‑2025 factsheet (31 Jul 2025). - DSP — nearest official holdings disclosure that gives weights: the DSP factsheet / mfiframes listing (scheme factsheet) and Sep‑2024 DSP literature identify the underlying funds and give weights for the principal underlying holdings (BlueBox Global Technology Fund, iShares NASDAQ‑100 UCITS ETF, KraneShares CSI China Internet ETF, IVZ NASDAQ‑100 EW ACC, Fidelity Select Medical Technology, BlueBox Precision Medicine Fund, plus small cash/REPO). Those underlying funds are the top positions in the DSP FoF in the nearest disclosures to Dec‑31‑2024 [4], [9].

2.2 Full top‑20 lists (as reported)
- Edelweiss: full top‑20 at exactly 31 Dec 2024 is not available in the evidence. The Oct‑2024 deck provides the 31 Jul 2024 top‑10 (above) [11]. The Aug‑2025 factsheet provides a longer list (named holdings with weights) as of 31 Jul 2025; that later list is the nearest fuller published list available in the evidence and is cited where a broader holdings view is needed [6].
- DSP: the DSP factsheet / mfiframes lists the underlying funds and their weights (the fund holds other mutual funds/ETFs). The top underlying positions and weights are shown in the factsheet evidence (BlueBox ~38.7%, iShares NASDAQ‑100 ~27.3%, KraneShares China Internet ~14.1%, IVZ Nasdaq‑100 EW ~11.9%, Fidelity Medical Tech ~4.05%, etc.) — these items constitute the DSP top holdings in the nearest available disclosure [4].

2.3 Overlap computation (match by issuer name / ticker)

- Structure difference: Edelweiss is a FoF that (at the fund level) holds an active Greater China equity fund (JPMorgan Greater China), hence its top holdings are individual Greater China / Taiwan / Hong Kong equity names via the underlying fund’s portfolio; DSP is a FoF that holds multiple underlying funds/ETFs (including passive UCITS ETFs and active offshore funds) — the DSP FoF’s top holdings are other funds/ETFs rather than direct stock tickers, which reduces direct ticker overlap but can create indirect economic overlap through the ETFs’ holdings (e.g., KraneShares China Internet ETF holding Tencent/Alibaba) [1], [4], [11].

## 5) Interpretation and horizon recommendation (strictly tied to the evidence)

Summary recommendation up front:
- For a 2‑year investment horizon: DSP Global Innovation Overseas Equity Omni FoF is the preferable choice from the evidence for most investors who require a shorter horizon and want broad innovation exposure via underlying ETFs/funds (subject to fee tolerance), because the DSP FoF’s exposure is primarily via large underlying ETFs/funds (offering immediate multi‑fund diversification, daily liquidity at the scheme level, and no exit load in the factsheets) and its top holdings are funds/ETFs rather than concentrated single‑country stock bets (as reported in the scheme factsheet evidence). [4], [9].
- For a 5‑year investment horizon: Edelweiss Greater China Equity Offshore Fund is the more suitable choice from the evidence for investors willing to accept single‑region concentration to seek potential long‑term Greater China recovery / growth, because the fund explicitly targets Greater China equities via the JPMorgan underlying fund and shows concentrated stock exposure (top‑10 ≈40.6% as of 31 Jul 2024) that typically requires a longer horizon to smooth idiosyncratic regional/stock volatility. [11], [4].

Rationale — numbered, evidence‑linked reasons

Recommendation: DSP for 2‑year horizon — reasons
1. Underlying structure and diversification: DSP’s top holdings are other funds/ETFs (BlueBox Global Technology Fund ~38.7%, iShares NASDAQ‑100 ~27.3%, KraneShares China Internet ~14.1%, IVZ Nasdaq‑100 EW ~11.9% in the nearest factsheet), meaning exposure is delivered through multiple diversified funds and broad ETFs rather than concentrated single stocks — this structure reduces single‑stock liquidity/selection risk for a short horizon relative to a single‑region concentrated stock portfolio as presented for Edelweiss (nearest facts) [4].  
2. Liquidity / exit load: DSP factsheets and KIM report no exit load and low minimums (open‑ended daily liquidity at scheme level), which favors investors who may need to exit within ~2 years; Edelweiss has conflicting disclosures about the exit‑load window (1% exit load within either 90 days or within 365 days depending on the document), which introduces ambiguity on short‑term redemption cost [4], [2], [6].  
3. Shorter‑term return evidence: DSP’s documented recent near‑term performance snapshots in the evidence show strong 1‑yr returns in aggregator factsheets (though exact 31 Dec 2024 alignment is not available); combined with diversification via ETFs and no exit load, the scheme is operationally preferable for a 2‑year holding if the investor accepts thematic/innovation risk and the stated TER (~2% for the regular plan) [4], [13].  
4. Fee tradeoff: DSP’s regular TER is around ~2.03–2.05% in the factsheets — higher than some direct plans elsewhere but acceptable for a FoF that places large weight in active underlying funds/ETFs if the investor values the underlying exposures (this is a judgment the client must make; purely on structural grounds DSP’s underlying ETF trọng reduces single‑stock risk for a short horizon) [4], [9].

Recommendation: Edelweiss for 5‑year horizon — reasons
1. Regional concentration and stock selection tilt: the Edelweiss scheme invests into a single underlying Greater China active fund (JPMorgan Greater China) and the nearest top‑10 holding disclosure (31 Jul 2024) shows large individual stock weights (TSMC and Tencent each ~9–10%), with the top‑10 summing to ≈40.6% — such concentration tends to be higher volatility and better suited to an investor able to hold multi‑year to ride through regional cycles [11].  
2. Long‑term objective alignment: the scheme’s stated objective is long‑term capital appreciation via Greater China equities; the product collateral and factsheets list a suggested longer investment horizon (>3 years in some factsheets) and the fund’s concentrated regional strategy implies a 5‑year+ horizon for potential mean reversion or secular recovery plays to play out [1], [3].  
3. Fee context and active management: the Edelweiss scheme’s TER is in the 1.4–2.4% band across reported dates (and includes underlying fund expense of ~0.76% for the JPMorgan fund) — for an investor confident in the active manager and the Greater China thesis, paying the active expense may be justified over a 5‑year time frame where stock selection can compound (documented TERs and underlying expense are cited in the product materials) [4], [6].

Caveats and ambiguous/marginal areas (data limitations)
1. Expense ratio ambiguity: TERs for Edelweiss differ across documents and reporting dates in the evidence (1.43% direct plan in Feb‑2023 product collateral vs ~1.51% direct plan in Aug‑2025 factsheet vs 1.64% and other aggregator snapshots) — the evidence shows TERs changed across time and that different plan types (regular vs direct) have materially different TERs; investors should confirm the exact TER for the chosen plan and date before decision‑making [4], [6], [2].  
2. Exit load conflict for Edelweiss: one document reports a 1% exit load if redeemed within 90 days, another reports 1% if redeemed within 365 days — this contradiction in the evidence materially affects short‑horizon suitability and must be reconciled with current official fund information before acting [2], [4].  
3. DSP shorter history: DSP launched Feb 2022 and therefore lacks a 5‑year track record — this is a limiting factor when evaluating long‑term performance reliability; the AMFI/KIM evidence confirms the scheme’s relatively short tenure [4], [13].  
4. Indirect economic overlap not captured by issuer‑match: strict issuer/ticker overlap in the top‑20 lists is 0% because DSP reports funds/ETFs as holdings while Edelweiss reports stocks; however the DSP KraneShares China Internet ETF and other underlying funds likely hold many of the same companies economically (Tencent, Alibaba, etc.) — the evidence documents the structural overlap possibility but does not provide contemporaneous underlying ETF holdings at the same date to quantify indirect overlap, so indirect overlap is acknowledged but cannot be numerically reported from the evidence [4], [11].

- Requested reference date: 31 Dec 2024. Based strictly on the reported portfolio structures, concentration metrics and the governance/fee disclosures in the available evidence: for a 2‑year horizon the DSP Global Innovation Overseas Equity Omni FoF is generally better aligned with investors who require shorter‑term access and seek diversified exposure to the innovation theme via ETFs and multi‑fund allocation (no exit load reported in DSP factsheets; underlying ETF/fund structure reduces direct single‑stock concentration risk); for a 5‑year horizon the Edelweiss Greater China Equity Offshore Fund is the preferred choice for investors specifically seeking concentrated Greater China equity exposure and willing to accept higher regional/stock concentration (top‑10 ≈40.6% as of 31 Jul 2024) and potentially longer periods of volatility in pursuit of region‑specific upside — subject to resolving the documented exit‑load and expense‑ratio ambiguities in the current official fund disclosures before investing.
